Submittal transmittals, bid form layouts, and narrative field reports are not models industry guidance offers for describing modifications.

questions.question: A specifier is editing Section 01 26 00 for a project whose general conditions are AIA Document A201. Which set lists the recognized ways to modify the contract documents under A201?

options.A: Change order, work change directive, field order, and written interpretation
options.B: Change order, construction change directive, and minor changes in the work
options.C: Change order, construction change directive, and field order
options.D: Change order, addendum, and minor changes in the work

questions.explanation: Industry guidance identifies three recognized ways to modify contract documents under A201: change order, construction change directive, and minor changes in the work. Work change directives, field orders, and written interpretations come from the EJCDC C-700 list, and addenda are issued before the agreement is executed, so they are not an A201 method of modifying the contract.

questions.question: The owner, contractor, and architect have agreed on an added entrance canopy, a $42,000 increase in the contract sum, and a 10-day time extension. Which AIA form does industry guidance identify as the standard form for documenting this?

options.A: AIA Document G710
options.B: AIA Document G714
options.C: AIA Document G702
options.D: AIA Document G701

questions.explanation: Because all parties agree on the change, the cost, and the time, a change order is the instrument, and industry guidance names AIA Document G701 as its standard form. G710, Architect's Supplemental Instructions, is for minor changes with no sum or time adjustment, and G714 is the construction change directive used when sum or time has not been agreed; G702 is not a modification form industry guidance cites here.

questions.question: On an A201 project, the owner and contractor have settled a revision to the work and its cost, but they still disagree about the extension of contract time the contractor requests. The contractor asks the architect to process a change order now and settle the time later. Under A201, which response is correct?

options.A: Process it; a change order requires agreement only on the change in the work
options.B: Process it; the time adjustment can be added later as a minor change in the work
options.C: Hold it; a change order states agreement on the work, the sum, and the time
options.D: Hold it; a change order may adjust the contract sum or the time, but not both

questions.explanation: Industry guidance describes the A201 change order as a written instrument in which the owner, contractor, and architect state their agreement on the change in the work, the amount of any sum adjustment, and the extent of any time adjustment. With time still disputed, that condition is not met. A single change order can adjust both sum and time, minor changes by definition involve no sum or time adjustment, and agreement on the work alone is not enough.

questions.question: On an AIA A201 project, the contractor emails the owner a change order it drafted for added work that has already been priced and agreed. Under A201, which party is responsible for preparing the change order instrument?

options.A: The architect
options.B: The contractor
options.C: The owner
options.D: The owner and contractor jointly

questions.explanation: Industry guidance, summarizing A201, describes a change order as a written instrument prepared by the architect and then signed by the owner, contractor, and architect. A contractor-drafted, owner-drafted, or jointly drafted owner-contractor document does not match that description.

questions.question: An architect's office prefers to issue minor changes in the work on its own field bulletin form instead of AIA Document G710. Where should the use of that alternate form be indicated?

options.A: Section 01 31 00—Project Management and Coordination
options.B: Section 01 26 00—Contract Modification Procedures
options.C: Section 01 33 00—Submittal Procedures
options.D: Section 01 25 00—Substitution Procedures

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that G710, Architect's Supplemental Instructions, is the standard form for minor changes, but if the architect elects another document, it should be identified in Section 01 26 00—Contract Modification Procedures. Sections 01 25 00, 01 31 00, and 01 33 00 address substitutions, coordination, and submittals, not the instruments for modifying the contract.

questions.question: A specifier is converting Section 01 26 00 from an AIA-based project to a project using EJCDC C-700 general conditions. Which list correctly identifies the recognized ways to change the contract documents under C-700?

options.A: Change order, construction change directive, field order, and minor change in the work
options.B: Change order, work change directive, engineer's supplemental instruction, and minor change in the work
options.C: Change order, work change directive, field order, and minor change in the work
options.D: Change order, work change directive, field order, and written interpretation or clarification

questions.explanation: Industry guidance lists four recognized ways to change contract documents under EJCDC C-700: change order, work change directive, field order, and written interpretation or clarification. Construction change directives and minor changes in the work are the AIA A201 methods, and supplemental instructions belong to the AIA G710 form; under C-700 minor changes are ordered by field order, not listed as a separate method.

questions.question: For change orders under EJCDC documents, which statement correctly matches each party to its role?

options.A: Engineer recommends; owner authorizes; contractor accepts
options.B: Engineer authorizes; owner accepts; contractor recommends
options.C: Engineer accepts; owner recommends; contractor authorizes
options.D: Engineer recommends; owner accepts; contractor authorizes

questions.explanation: Industry guidance describes the EJCDC change order as recommended by the engineer, authorized by the owner, and accepted by the contractor. The other options swap these roles; the contractor neither recommends nor authorizes the change, and it is the owner, not the engineer or contractor, who authorizes it.

questions.question: On a project using EJCDC C-700, the engineer is preparing the instrument to add work with an agreed increase in contract price and time. Which EJCDC form does industry guidance identify as the standard form for it?

options.A: EJCDC C-940
options.B: EJCDC C-700
options.C: EJCDC C-941
options.D: EJCDC C-200

questions.explanation: An agreed adjustment in price and time is made by change order, and industry guidance names EJCDC C-941, Change Order, as the standard form. C-940 is the EJCDC work change directive form, used before the value of the change is established; C-700 is the standard general conditions and C-200 the suggested instructions to bidders.

questions.question: Under the EJCDC C-700 definition, from what point in the project may a change order be issued?

options.A: Only after the notice to proceed has been given
options.B: On or after the effective date of the agreement
options.C: At any time after the bids have been opened
options.D: Only after the notice of award has been issued

questions.explanation: Industry guidance quotes the C-700 definition of a change order as one issued on or after the effective date of the agreement. Bid opening and the notice of award both come before the agreement takes effect, and the definition does not require waiting for a notice to proceed.

questions.question: An engineer on a project using EJCDC C-700 suggests issuing a work change directive to revise the scope of a pump station while bids are still being received. Based on how industry guidance summarizes the C-700 definition of a work change directive, why is this inappropriate?

options.A: It is signed by the owner and issued on or after the agreement's effective date
options.B: It is signed by the engineer and may be issued only after substantial completion
options.C: It is signed by the contractor and issued only after the notice to proceed
options.D: It is signed by the owner and contractor and issued only after bid opening

questions.explanation: Industry guidance, summarizing EJCDC C-700, describes the work change directive as a written directive to the contractor, signed by the owner and issued on or after the agreement's effective date. While bids are still being received no agreement is in effect, so a directive cannot be used; revisions during bidding go out by addendum. The other options misstate who signs it, when it may be issued, or both.

questions.question: During excavation on an EJCDC C-700 project, the contractor uncovers buried foundations not shown in the contract documents. The owner wants work to continue now, with cost and time effects to be negotiated later. Which statement correctly describes the appropriate instrument?

options.A: A field order issued by the engineer, because the change involves no price or time effect
options.B: A change order on EJCDC C-941, because the owner must sign before any added work proceeds
options.C: A work change directive on EJCDC C-940, as evidence that a change order will follow
options.D: A written interpretation by the engineer, because the conditions differ from the documents

questions.explanation: Under C-700, a work change directive can order changes or respond to differing or unforeseen subsurface or physical conditions, and its standard form is EJCDC C-940. It signals that the parties expect a later change order once the price and time effects are negotiated. A field order cannot involve price or time changes, a C-941 change order needs agreed terms, and a written interpretation does not order changed work.

questions.question: On an EJCDC C-700 project, the engineer wants to shift a floor drain 300 mm to clear a beam, with no effect on cost or schedule. The owner's representative is unavailable for two weeks. How should this change be handled?

options.A: The engineer prepares a change order for later signature by owner and contractor
options.B: The engineer gives verbal direction and records it in the next meeting minutes
options.C: The owner issues a work change directive upon returning, before the work proceeds
options.D: The engineer issues a written field order; the owner's signature is not required

questions.explanation: An EJCDC field order is a written order from the engineer for minor changes that do not alter contract price or times. It must be in writing, but it needs neither an executed change order nor the owner's signature. Verbal direction fails the writing requirement, and a work change directive or change order is unnecessary for a change with no cost or time effect.

questions.question: A specifier preparing the Division 01 section on contract modification procedures for an EJCDC-based project wants to cite the standard EJCDC form for field orders. What does industry guidance indicate?

options.A: Use EJCDC C-940 with the owner's signature block deleted
options.B: Use EJCDC C-941 with the price and time entries shown as zero
options.C: EJCDC publishes none, so the job needs its own written format
options.D: EJCDC publishes none, since field orders may be given verbally

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that EJCDC does not have a standard form for field orders, so the project must establish its own written format. Field orders must still be in writing, so verbal direction is not acceptable. C-940 is the work change directive form and C-941 the change order form; neither is meant to be adapted for field orders.

questions.question: A specifier is editing a Division 01 section on modification procedures for a project using ConsensusDocs 200 general conditions. Which set of modification methods matches that document?

options.A: Change order, construction change directive, and minor change
options.B: Change order, work change directive, and minor changes
options.C: Change order, work change directive, and field order
options.D: Change order, interim directive, and written amendment

questions.explanation: Industry guidance lists three methods recognized by ConsensusDocs 200: the change order, the interim directive, and the written amendment. Option A reflects AIA terminology, option B matches the DBIA methods, and option C draws on EJCDC methods.

questions.question: On a ConsensusDocs 200 project, the owner wants a firestopping detail redone; the contractor says the work is extra, but the owner believes it is already required. Which instrument lets the owner direct the work to proceed while the disagreement remains?

options.A: A change order recording the disputed work at no change in price
options.B: An interim directive, ordering the work before any adjustment is agreed
options.C: A written amendment issued by the owner under the general conditions' changes article
options.D: A field order, since the owner considers the work already required

questions.explanation: The ConsensusDocs interim directive directs work before the parties agree on price or time, and industry guidance notes the owner also uses it for work the owner believes is not a change; only the owner must sign it. A change order needs the contractor's signature, which a disputing contractor will not give. The written amendment is not a formal change document in ConsensusDocs 200, and the field order is an EJCDC instrument.

questions.question: An owner's project manager on a ConsensusDocs 200 project needs to order work to begin before price and time adjustments are agreed. Which standard form does industry guidance identify for this purpose?

options.A: ConsensusDocs 202
options.B: ConsensusDocs 200
options.C: ConsensusDocs 203
options.D: DBIA Document No. 500D5

questions.explanation: Industry guidance identifies ConsensusDocs 203 as the standard form for the interim directive, which orders work before the time or price adjustment is agreed. ConsensusDocs 202 is the change order form, ConsensusDocs 200 is the general conditions document itself, and DBIA 500D5 is the design-build work change directive form.

questions.question: A contractor on a ConsensusDocs 200 project refuses to proceed with directed work because it has not countersigned the interim directive. Whose signature is required on that directive?

options.A: The owner and the contractor
options.B: The owner, contractor, and A/E
options.C: The owner, then the contractor on acceptance
options.D: The owner only, as the directing party

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that only the owner is required to sign a ConsensusDocs interim directive, so the contractor's missing signature does not invalidate it. The owner-and-contractor pairing describes the ConsensusDocs change order, and a contractor-party signature on acceptance describes the DBIA work change directive.

questions.question: A specifier searches ConsensusDocs 200 for the procedure and form for a written amendment. What will the specifier find?

options.A: A dedicated changes article with its own standard amendment form
options.B: A brief mention in the order-of-precedence provisions, with no standard form
options.C: A required exhibit to the agreement, completed at contract execution
options.D: A provision in the dispute resolution article, used to record mediation results

questions.explanation: Industry guidance explains that ConsensusDocs 200 does not treat the written amendment as a formal change document; it appears only near the end, where the order of precedence is described, listed alongside change orders. ConsensusDocs also provides no standard form for it. The other options invent a dedicated article, an agreement exhibit, or a dispute-resolution role that industry guidance does not describe.

questions.question: A specifier's draft Division 01 section for a design-build project governed by DBIA Document No. 535 lists the modification methods as change order, interim directive, and field order. What correction is needed?

options.A: Replace interim directive with work change directive, and field order with minor changes
options.B: Replace interim directive with construction change directive, and field order with minor changes
options.C: Replace field order with written amendment, and keep interim directive as drafted
options.D: Replace interim directive with work change directive, and keep field order as drafted

questions.explanation: DBIA Document No. 535 recognizes three ways to change the contract documents: change order, work change directive, and minor changes. The interim directive and written amendment are ConsensusDocs terms, the field order is an EJCDC term, and the construction change directive is an AIA term, so each distractor leaves at least one wrong-family term in place.

questions.question: On a design-build project using DBIA documents, the design-builder's architect asks to sign each change order as the recommending party, as on design-bid-build work. Which form and signatories does industry guidance identify for the DBIA change order?

options.A: DBIA 500D5, signed by the owner alone
options.B: DBIA 500D2, signed by the owner, design-builder, and A/E
options.C: DBIA 500D2, signed by the owner and the design-builder
options.D: DBIA 535, signed by the owner and the design-builder

questions.explanation: Industry guidance names DBIA Document No. 500D2, Design-Build Change Order Form, and states that it requires the signatures of the owner and the design-builder only. Unlike AIA and EJCDC change orders, no separate A/E signature is called for. DBIA 500D5 is the work change directive form, and DBIA 535 is the general conditions document.

questions.question: An owner on a DBIA design-build project issues a work change directive for added paving. Which signatures does the DBIA work change directive require?

options.A: The owner only, as for the EJCDC directive
options.B: The owner, and the design-builder upon acceptance
options.C: The owner and the design-builder's A/E
options.D: The design-builder only, with written notice to the owner

questions.explanation: The DBIA work change directive is prepared and signed by the owner and then signed by the design-builder upon acceptance. An owner-only signature describes the EJCDC directive and the ConsensusDocs interim directive, while written notice to the owner by the design-builder describes the DBIA minor change procedure.

questions.question: After a DBIA work change directive is issued for added site lighting, the owner and design-builder disagree on the cost. What do the DBIA general conditions, as summarized, require next?

options.A: The owner sets the final amount by issuing a second work change directive
options.B: The design-builder records the cost as a minor change with written notice
options.C: The parties negotiate in good faith and record the result in a change order
options.D: The parties execute a written amendment listed in the order of precedence

questions.explanation: DBIA general conditions require the owner and design-builder to negotiate in good faith toward agreement after a work change directive, and the final cost and time agreement is documented in a written change order. The owner cannot fix the amount with another directive, a priced scope change is not a minor change, and the written amendment is a ConsensusDocs concept.

questions.question: An owner's project manager pulls DBIA Document No. 500D2 to direct the design-builder to start added work before the price is settled. What does industry guidance indicate about this choice?

options.A: 500D2 is the change order form; the directive belongs on DBIA 500D5
options.B: 500D2 is correct, but the A/E must also sign it as recommending party
options.C: DBIA has no directive form, so a letter from the owner must be used
options.D: The directive belongs on DBIA 535, the general conditions document

questions.explanation: DBIA 500D2 is the Design-Build Change Order Form, which documents agreed changes. For directing a change before price and time are agreed, industry guidance names DBIA 500D5, Design-Build Work Change Directive Form. DBIA does publish a directive form, the DBIA change order needs no A/E signature, and DBIA 535 is the general conditions rather than a directive.

questions.question: A design-builder working under DBIA general conditions wants to adjust a pipe hanger layout. The adjustment is consistent with the documents' intent and will not materially or adversely affect design, quality, performance, or workmanship. What procedure applies?

options.A: The owner and design-builder must execute a change order on DBIA 500D2
options.B: The owner must issue a work change directive before the work proceeds
options.C: The A/E must issue a written order, binding on both owner and design-builder
options.D: The design-builder may proceed but must promptly inform the owner in writing

questions.explanation: DBIA general conditions let the design-builder make minor changes that keep to the documents' intent and do not harm design, quality, performance, or workmanship, provided it promptly notifies the owner in writing. No work change directive or change order is needed, and a written order by the A/E is the AIA approach to minor changes, not the DBIA one.

questions.question: A specifier is engaged on a federal project whose general conditions were written by the owner rather than taken from AIA, EJCDC, ConsensusDocs, or DBIA. What is the best approach to the Division 01 modification procedures?

options.A: Default to AIA modification forms, since they are the most widely recognized
options.B: Confirm the owner's own modification methods, supporting documents, and forms
options.C: Use EJCDC methods, since they were developed for public works projects
options.D: Adapt the ConsensusDocs 200 methods, since they reflect industry consensus

questions.explanation: Industry guidance notes that entities such as GSA, DOD, and state public works agencies produce their own general conditions. When a standard contract document is not used, the specifier must confirm the applicable modification method, procedures, supporting documents, and forms. Defaulting to AIA, EJCDC, or ConsensusDocs procedures ignores what the owner's own documents require.

questions.question: A state public works agency uses its own non-standard general conditions. With the bid date approaching and the documents still being finalized, the A/E needs to issue revisions. What does industry guidance emphasize for this situation?

options.A: Check for special requirements on modifications made before final bidding
options.B: Hold all revisions until after award and process them by change order
options.C: Issue revisions on standard AIA forms, since pre-bid procedures are uniform
options.D: Issue revisions as field orders, since no contract yet exists to modify

questions.explanation: For non-standard contract documents, industry guidance cautions the specifier to watch for any special requirements that apply to modifications made before final bidding or contract negotiation. Holding revisions until after award, assuming AIA pre-bid procedures apply, or using field orders before a contract exists all bypass that check.

questions.question: Which public project most clearly falls within the 'other' category of contract modification methods, where the specifier must confirm the applicable method, procedures, and forms?

options.A: A county courthouse using AIA A201 general conditions
options.B: A municipal water plant using EJCDC C-700 general conditions
options.C: A state university lab using ConsensusDocs 200 general conditions
options.D: A military base using Department of Defense general conditions

questions.explanation: The 'other' category covers general conditions produced by entities such as GSA, DOD, and state or other public works agencies, where a standard contract document is not used. A public owner that adopts AIA A201, EJCDC C-700, or ConsensusDocs 200 is using a standard document, so that family's modification methods apply; the deciding factor is the document, not whether the owner is public.

questions.question: An architect issues AIA G709 to price a revised storefront layout. The contractor immediately stops storefront installation, claiming the request suspends that work. How should the architect respond?

options.A: The request is informational only and neither orders the change nor stops the work
options.B: The request suspends affected work until the change order is signed
options.C: The request acts as a construction change directive once the contractor receives it
options.D: The request obligates the contractor to begin the proposed change without delay

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that a change order proposal request, such as AIA G709, is for information only; it does not instruct the contractor to carry out the proposed changes or to stop work in progress. It merely solicits the contractor's proposed adjustment of contract sum, time, or both. It does not convert into a construction change directive or require the contractor to begin the change.

questions.question: An architect with broad contract-administration duties signs a change order and tells the contractor the change is now authorized, though the owner has not yet signed. Which principle does industry guidance state that applies across AIA, EJCDC, ConsensusDocs, and DBIA?

options.A: The A/E's signature authorizes the change; the owner's confirms funding
options.B: The contractor's signature authorizes it once the A/E has recommended it
options.C: Only the owner has the authority to execute a change order
options.D: Either the owner or the A/E may execute it once both have been notified

questions.explanation: Industry guidance describes it as an axiom of AIA, EJCDC, ConsensusDocs, and DBIA that only the owner has authority to execute, or authorize, a change order. The A/E signs to recommend the change and the contractor signs to accept it; neither signature authorizes it, and the A/E cannot execute in the owner's place.

questions.question: An A/E wants to obtain the contractor's proposed adjustment in contract sum and time for a possible revision, without directing any work. Which AIA document does industry guidance cite for initiating this?

options.A: AIA Document G701, Change Order
options.B: AIA Document G714, Construction Change Directive
options.C: AIA Document G710, Architect's Supplemental Instructions
options.D: AIA Document G709, Work Changes Proposal Request

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states the A/E can start a change order proposal request with AIA Document G709, Work Changes Proposal Request, which describes the proposed change and asks for a proposed adjustment without directing work. G701 records an agreed change, G714 directs work before agreement, and G710 issues supplemental instructions rather than requesting pricing.

questions.question: An owner wants a lab equipment vendor to furnish fume hoods and also build them into the walls and ductwork on site. How should the vendor's work be contracted?

options.A: Under a purchasing contract with the owner, listing installation as a special service
options.B: Under a subcontract agreement between the vendor and the construction contractor
options.C: Under a purchasing contract with the owner, later assigned to the A/E for administration
options.D: Under a purchasing contract, with the construction contractor coordinating the vendor's site work

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that when the goods contractor must take part in actual construction, the goods are furnished and installed under a subcontract between the goods contractor and the construction contractor, not under a purchasing contract. Purchasing contracts involve little or no on-site work, special services such as technical assistance do not extend to building items into the work, and coordination by the construction contractor does not change that.
questions.source: introduction to specifying for the purchase of goods

questions.question: A specifier preparing purchasing documents for an owner's FF&E package is asked why the documents use the term goods. The term keeps the specifications consistent with which source of terminology?

options.A: The Uniform Commercial Code
options.B: The Federal Acquisition Regulation
options.C: The MasterFormat numbering system
options.D: The construction contract's general conditions

questions.explanation: Industry guidance explains that purchasing specifications use the term goods because the Uniform Commercial Code, which governs most purchasing contracts, uses the same term, keeping the specifications consistent with applicable law. The FAR, MasterFormat, and construction general conditions are not the source industry guidance gives for this terminology.
questions.source: introduction to specifying for the purchase of goods

questions.question: A university's facilities department buys the same light fixtures from fourteen vendors to maximize competition, but struggles with inconsistent quality. Under the traditional management theory described, which action is recommended?

options.A: Split orders evenly among the vendors to spread supply risk
options.B: Transfer fixture purchasing to the construction contractor on each job
options.C: Rebid every order among all fourteen vendors on a short-term basis
options.D: Reduce the number of suppliers used for the same or similar products

questions.explanation: Industry guidance notes that maintaining many suppliers for the same or similar products often costs more to manage than the savings competition produces, and it makes quality and consistent performance harder to control. Reducing the supplier count is the recommended action; spreading orders across all vendors, rebidding short-term, or shifting purchasing to contractors does not address that.

questions.question: An owner has negotiated long-term contracts with a few preferred suppliers to gain cost savings. Under the traditional management theory industry guidance describes, what accompanies these large purchase commitments?

options.A: Reduced oversight, since long-term partners are trusted to self-manage
options.B: Periodic rebidding of each order to a broad pool of competing suppliers
options.C: More rigorous tracking of their timelines and quality
options.D: Fewer quality requirements, offset by the lower negotiated prices

questions.explanation: Under the traditional management theory, the large commitments made to a few preferred suppliers come with more rigorous and detailed tracking of their timelines and quality, along with higher quality and performance requirements. Relaxing oversight, returning to broad rebidding, or lowering quality requirements contradicts that approach.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects how supply chain management concepts, as industry guidance describes them, view the acquisition function?

options.A: As a support function that responds to requisitions as they arrive
options.B: As a transactional function judged mainly by the unit prices it manages to obtain
options.C: As one part of a larger system linking customer needs and supplier capabilities
options.D: As an independent unit that operates apart from the organization's other processes

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that supply chain management concepts recognize acquisition does not operate in a reactive vacuum; it is a component of a broader management system that creates value by merging customer needs and supplier capabilities with the organization's value-added processes. Responding to requisitions as they arrive is the reactive view, and treating acquisition as price-driven or separate from other processes contradicts that view.

questions.question: A purchasing agent has formally notified a vendor that it is the successful bidder for an equipment package. The vendor asks whether a legally binding agreement now exists. Under typical procurement steps, what is the correct answer?

options.A: Yes; the agreement becomes legally binding when the award is made
options.B: No; it is formed at contract execution, the step after award
options.C: Yes; the agreement became legally binding when the bids were opened
options.D: No; the agreement becomes binding only when the goods are delivered

questions.explanation: In the typical procurement steps, Award (step 4) is when the buyer formally awards the contract, and Execution of Contract (step 5) is when the buyer enters a legally binding agreement with the goods contractor. Bid opening and delivery are not the points industry guidance identifies for a binding agreement.

questions.question: During the bid/proposal evaluation step of a goods procurement, the buyer tabulates the submissions. What does the buyer review them for?

options.A: Responsiveness and responsibility
options.B: Lowest price and earliest delivery
options.C: Completeness and lowest cost
options.D: Qualifications and references

questions.explanation: During the bid/proposal evaluation step, industry guidance says the buyer tabulates and reviews all bids or proposals for responsiveness and responsibility. Price, delivery, completeness, and references may matter in a given procurement, but they are not the review criteria industry guidance names for this step.

questions.question: In the bidding or accepting-proposals step, bidders receive the complete set of procurement documents. Which item does industry guidance list among the contents of that project manual?

options.A: The bid tabulation from prior procurements
options.B: The notice of award
options.C: The buyer's evaluation scoring sheets
options.D: Certifications and representations

questions.explanation: The list of project manual contents for the bidding step includes certifications and representations, alongside items such as the instructions, bid forms, contract conditions, and specifications. Bid tabulation and evaluation belong to the later evaluation step, and the notice of award follows evaluation.

questions.question: A county's purchasing office publishes a Notice to Bidders for library shelving. In typical procurement steps, which step does this document represent?

options.A: Step 4, Award
options.B: Step 2, Bidding or Accepting Proposals
options.C: Step 1, Solicitation
options.D: Step 3, Bid/Proposal Evaluation

questions.explanation: The first typical procurement step is Solicitation, Request for Bids, or Request for Proposals, which may also be called the Advertisement or Notice to Bidders. Bidding, evaluation, and award follow in steps 2 through 4, so a published notice inviting bids belongs to step 1.

questions.question: An owner pre-purchases lobby light fixtures and wants them to satisfy a cash allowance already carried in the contractor's agreement. Which mechanism does industry guidance identify for this use of purchasing?

options.A: Assigning the purchasing contract to the construction contractor
options.B: Issuing a field order directing the contractor to accept the owner's fixtures
options.C: Converting the allowance to a unit price based on the fixture count
options.D: Assigning the purchasing contract to the A/E for administration

questions.explanation: Among the uses of purchasing, industry guidance lists acquiring goods to fulfill cash allowances in a construction contract by assigning the purchasing contract to the construction contractor. A field order cannot involve price, so it cannot settle an allowance; converting to a unit price does not fulfill the allowance; and assignment to the A/E is not the mechanism described.

questions.question: An owner is buying long-lead switchgear under a purchasing contract for installation by the construction contractor. Late delivery could expose the owner to delay claims from the construction contractor. What does industry guidance suggest considering in the purchasing documents?

options.A: Liquidated damages in the construction contract, payable by the goods contractor
options.B: Liquidated damages in the purchasing contract that reflect that claim exposure
options.C: A waiver of delay claims by the construction contractor in the purchasing contract
options.D: Transfer of delivery responsibility to the A/E under its design contract

questions.explanation: Industry guidance warns that when the owner buys goods for installation by the construction contractor, the owner may become liable to that contractor for late or incomplete delivery, and this possibility should be considered when setting liquidated damages in the purchasing contract. Placing damages in the construction contract, seeking a waiver, or shifting delivery to the A/E does not address the exposure as industry guidance describes.

questions.question: Commercial kitchen equipment will be bought under a purchasing contract and set in place by the construction contractor. Which task can properly be assigned to the goods contractor in the purchasing documents?

options.A: Setting and connecting the equipment as the installer of record
options.B: Building the equipment's concrete pads and wall blocking on site
options.C: Field checking and testing the equipment after others install it
options.D: Erecting the exhaust hood and ductwork during construction

questions.explanation: Purchasing documents may include special services such as field checking or testing goods after installation by others, start-up, and training, but industry guidance notes these activities stop short of on-site construction or installation by the goods contractor. Setting equipment as installer, building pads and blocking, or erecting hoods and ductwork are construction activities.

questions.question: Comparing a purchasing project manual with a construction project manual, a specifier finds most differences are readily apparent. In which documents do the more subtle differences occur?

options.A: The solicitation and procurement instructions
options.B: The conditions of the contract
options.C: The bid or proposal forms
options.D: Division 01—General Requirements

questions.explanation: Industry guidance lists several purchasing documents that differ from their construction counterparts, including the solicitation, bid forms, agreement, contract conditions, and Division 01. Most differences are obvious, but the subtler ones occur in the conditions of the contract.
questions.source: purchasing contract and construction contract differences

questions.question: To save time, a specifier proposes reusing the Division 01 sections from a recent construction project manual, unchanged, in a purchasing project manual for laboratory equipment. What does industry guidance indicate?

options.A: Acceptable, because Division 01 is the same for purchasing and construction
options.B: Unacceptable, because purchasing project manuals do not include Division 01
options.C: Acceptable, because only the conditions of the contract differ between the two
options.D: Unacceptable, because Division 01 for purchasing differs from construction

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that the Division 01 General Requirements used for purchasing contracts differ from those used for construction, along with the solicitation, forms, agreement, and conditions. Reusing construction Division 01 unchanged ignores those differences; Division 01 is still part of a purchasing project manual, and the conditions are not the only documents that differ.
questions.source: purchasing contract and construction contract differences

questions.question: A school district requires its contractor to buy classroom casework through the district's established purchase contract. The casework arrives damaged, and the contractor argues it bears no responsibility because the district chose the source. Is the contractor correct?

options.A: Yes; buying through the owner's contract relieves the contractor of product responsibility
options.B: No; the contractor keeps the same responsibilities as for products from other sources
options.C: Yes; responsibility rests with the supplier alone under the owner's contract
options.D: No; responsibility is split equally, as with owner-furnished products

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that when a contractor buys products through the owner's established purchase contract, the contractor is not relieved of the responsibilities it would have for products bought through other sources. The owner's choice of source does not shift product responsibility to the owner or the supplier, and no equal split is described.

questions.question: A project includes contractor-furnished, owner-installed shelving and owner-furnished, owner-installed kitchen appliances needing utility rough-ins. Which section does industry guidance identify for listing these items and the parties' responsibilities?

options.A: Section 01 10 00
options.B: Section 01 64 00
options.C: Section 01 33 00
options.D: Section 01 60 00

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that Section 01 10 00—Summary can list contractor-furnished, owner-installed and owner-furnished, owner-installed products and state each party's responsibilities for them. Section 01 64 00—Owner-Furnished Products is offered only as an alternative for owner-furnished, contractor-installed products, while 01 33 00 (Submittal Procedures) and 01 60 00 (Product Requirements) do not serve this purpose.

questions.question: A specifier is adapting an owner's standard general-conditions definitions article for a purchasing contract for factory-built switchgear. Which group of definitions is most likely to be inapplicable and should be avoided in the purchasing documents?

options.A: Definitions tied to submittals, shop drawings, and product data
options.B: Definitions tied to on-site construction or installation activities
options.C: Definitions tied to payment, delivery, and final acceptance of goods
options.D: Definitions tied to referenced ASTM, ANSI, ASME, or NEMA standards

questions.explanation: Industry guidance warns that definitions in construction documents, especially those tied to on-site construction or installation activities, are not always applicable to purchasing documents, and inapplicable definitions must be avoided. Submittals, payment and acceptance, and reference standards all remain relevant to a goods purchase; industry guidance addresses each of them for purchasing contracts.

questions.question: An owner has a purchasing contract for air-handling units and a separate construction contract under which another contractor installs them. Both project manuals define the term "Provide." Per industry guidance, how should the two definitions relate?

options.A: They must be identical word for word, so one text is copied into both manuals.
options.B: Only the construction contract may define it; the purchasing manual omits it.
options.C: Each contract stands alone, so the definitions need no coordination at all.
options.D: They may differ slightly between the documents but must not conflict.

questions.explanation: Industry guidance recognizes that the same term may be defined in both contracts' documents with slight differences, and it treats avoiding conflict between those definitions as imperative. Requiring identical text overstates the rule, while dropping the term from one manual or skipping coordination ignores the simultaneous-contract situation industry guidance describes.

questions.question: An owner's attorney believes a purchasing contract for kitchen equipment must be closed out before any contract to install that equipment can take effect. Which response reflects industry guidance?

options.A: Both contracts may be in force at the same time for the same products.
options.B: Installation must instead be folded into the purchasing contract itself.
options.C: Installation may be contracted only after title transfers at the plant.
options.D: Installation may be contracted only after final payment for the goods.

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that a purchasing contract and a construction contract that includes installing the purchased goods can both be in place simultaneously for the same products, which is why it stresses keeping their definitions from conflicting. Nothing in industry guidance requires closeout, title transfer, or final payment under the purchasing contract before the installation contract can exist.

questions.question: An owner is purchasing custom-fabricated sunshade assemblies that will be delivered to the site for installation by others. Which bond should usually be required of the goods contractor, and what does it protect against?

options.A: A payment bond, protecting against unpaid claims of the goods contractor's suppliers
options.B: A bid bond, protecting against refusal to sign the purchasing contract after award
options.C: A performance bond, protecting against failure to manufacture, supply, or deliver
options.D: A maintenance bond, protecting against defects found after the goods are installed

questions.explanation: Industry guidance says a performance bond should usually be required, depending on the kind of goods and their intended disposition, because it gives the owner recourse if the goods contractor fails in manufacturing, supplying, or delivering them. Payment, bid, and maintenance bonds address other risks and are not the bond industry guidance identifies for purchasing contracts.

questions.question: Under a purchasing contract, the owner has paid for the first lot of transformers, which are finished but still stored at the goods contractor's plant awaiting shipment. Which insurance stipulation does industry guidance support?

options.A: Property insurance protecting the owner's interest in the paid, undelivered goods
options.B: General liability limits matching those required of every contractor working on site
options.C: Workers' compensation limits for the plant employees who fabricate the goods
options.D: Builder's risk insurance on the goods carried by the installing contractor

questions.explanation: Industry guidance generally discourages insurance stipulations for work at the goods contractor's plant, but it makes an exception for property insurance, required at the owner's request, to protect the owner's interest in goods paid for but not yet delivered. Liability and workers' compensation for plant operations are treated as part of the goods contractor's normal business, and industry guidance does not assign insurance of goods still at the plant to the installer.

questions.question: A purchasing contract requires the goods contractor to deliver rooftop units to the project site, where the construction contractor receives them. Which allocation of insurance responsibility is typical?

options.A: Goods contractor insures in transit and until installation is complete
options.B: Construction contractor insures in transit; owner insures after receipt
options.C: Goods contractor insures in transit; owner insures after delivery
options.D: Owner insures in transit; goods contractor insures until placed in service

questions.explanation: When the goods contractor delivers to a designated location, industry guidance calls for the goods contractor to carry transit insurance during shipment, particularly if payment has already been made. Receipt at the delivery point generally shifts responsibility, and insurance after delivery usually falls to the owner, so extending the goods contractor's coverage to installation or service, or assigning transit coverage to someone else, is inconsistent with recommended practice.

questions.question: A purchasing contract for a packaged chiller plant requires the manufacturer's field technicians to supervise start-up and train the owner's operators on site. Which coverages should the documents require of the goods contractor during these activities?

options.A: Property, transit, and general liability insurance
options.B: Workers' compensation, general liability, and automobile liability
options.C: Builder's risk, workers' compensation, and professional liability
options.D: Transit, automobile liability, and product warranty coverage

questions.explanation: For on-site work such as start-up assistance and owner training, industry guidance notes that the goods contractor's insurable exposure, though smaller than under a construction contract, still exists, so liability coverage similar to a construction contract should be required. Industry guidance names workers' compensation, general liability, and automobile liability; property and transit insurance protect the goods rather than on-site exposure, and builder's risk and professional liability are not in its list.

questions.question: A specifier is drafting purchasing documents for custom millwork panels. Which condition would justify requiring the goods contractor to visit the site?

options.A: The need to obtain a construction permit for installing the panels
options.B: The need to set up temporary storage facilities at the site
options.C: The need to coordinate with the jobsite safety program
options.D: The chance that existing field conditions affect panel production

questions.explanation: Industry guidance limits site visits by the goods contractor to cases where field measurements are needed, technical assistance is specified, or existing field conditions may affect production of the goods. Permits, temporary facilities, and safety are matters industry guidance assigns to the construction contractor, so none of them justifies a site-visit requirement for the goods contractor.

questions.question: When does industry guidance suggest a purchasing contract might need stipulations governing subcontractor relationships?

options.A: When the goods are exceptionally expensive or complicated
options.B: When the goods are delivered to a designated location
options.C: When the owner makes progress payments during fabrication
options.D: When the goods contractor provides on-site start-up services

questions.explanation: Industry guidance notes that subcontractors usually are not involved in a purchasing contract unless the goods are exceptionally expensive or complicated, which is why most purchasing documents omit subcontractor provisions. Delivery location, progress payments, and on-site start-up shape insurance, payment, and acceptance provisions instead of creating a need for subcontractor stipulations.

questions.question: Purchasing documents are being prepared for standard low-voltage switchboards. Which requirement does industry guidance consider appropriate to stipulate for the goods contractor?

options.A: Compliance with all laws regulating the plant's manufacturing processes
options.B: Safety and protection provisions governing fabrication at the plant
options.C: Compliance with applicable industry standards, such as those of NEMA
options.D: Owner supervision of fabrication to verify workmanship at the plant

questions.explanation: Unless unique codes or laws govern, as with nuclear components, pressure vessels, or fire protection systems, industry guidance says it should not be necessary to stipulate compliance with manufacturing-process laws or safety and protection provisions, because fabrication is the goods contractor's own business responsibility. Requiring compliance with applicable standards such as ASTM, ANSI, ASME, or NEMA is what industry guidance calls appropriate, and owner supervision at the plant is not part of its approach.

questions.question: An A/E is preparing the construction documents under which owner-purchased emergency generators will be installed by the electrical contractor. What must the A/E do regarding the purchasing provisions?

options.A: Leave receipt and start-up issues for the two parties to resolve in the field
options.B: Coordinate both contracts so no item is omitted or duplicated between them
options.C: Assign receipt, start-up, and training to the goods contractor by default
options.D: Repeat every purchasing provision in the construction contract so nothing is missed

questions.explanation: Industry guidance requires an A/E who prepares the installation contract documents to coordinate the construction contract's purchasing provisions so the two contracts relate properly and pertinent items are neither omitted nor duplicated. Receipt and handling, utility connections, start-up, and owner training must be clearly stipulated, so leaving them to the field or assigning them to one party by default contradicts recommended practice, and repeating every purchasing provision in the construction contract creates the duplication it warns against.

questions.question: The A/E's responsibilities for a purchasing contract are determined by which factors, and who must thoroughly understand them?

options.A: UCC Article 2 and state law; the goods contractor and the A/E
options.B: The A/E's standard of care; the owner and the construction contractor
options.C: The goods contractor's scope; the owner and the goods contractor
options.D: Project requirements and the owner's desires; the owner and the A/E

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that the A/E's purchasing-contract responsibilities vary with the project requirements and what the owner wants, and that both the owner and the A/E must carefully establish and fully understand them. The other options substitute the UCC, a general standard of care, or the goods contractor's scope, and they name the wrong parties as needing that understanding.

questions.question: Midway through fabrication under a purchasing contract, the owner asks the A/E to travel to the goods contractor's plant to witness shop tests. Neither the A/E agreement nor the purchasing contract addresses this. Which course of action does industry guidance indicate should have been followed?

options.A: Settle with the owner beforehand whether the A/E will attend shop tests
options.B: Treat shop-test witnessing as part of basic contract administration
options.C: Assume the duty applies, since the A/E approved the shop drawings
options.D: Decide on witnessing once fabrication starts and test dates are known

questions.explanation: Industry guidance says the A/E may or may not be obligated to visit the plant, witness shop tests, or verify goods at delivery. Because these items materially affect both the purchasing contract and the A/E's professional services agreement, they must be clarified with the owner in advance. Treating witnessing as a basic service, inferring the duty from shop drawing approval, or deciding it once fabrication is under way all skip that up-front clarification.

questions.question: A specifier is editing the submittal procedures for a purchasing contract for owner-furnished laboratory casework that a separate contractor will install. How should the quantity of approved submittals compare with a typical construction contract?

options.A: Fewer copies, since the goods contractor performs no installation
options.B: The same number, with the goods contractor retaining the records
options.C: More copies than usual, for records and for transmittal to end users
options.D: Electronic copies only, distributed later by the construction contractor

questions.explanation: Industry guidance notes that a greater-than-usual number of approved submittals may be obtained under a purchasing contract, both for records and for passing along to the construction contractor or other end users of the goods. Reducing or merely matching the usual quantity ignores the installer's need for the information, and industry guidance does not shift distribution to the construction contractor.
questions.source: shop drawings, product data, and samples

questions.question: An owner purchased elevator machinery early, and the A/E has already approved the goods contractor's shop drawings. The construction contract for installing the machinery has not yet been bid. What may be advantageous?

options.A: Withholding the approved drawings until the installer is under contract
options.B: Making the approved drawings available to bidders on the installation work
options.C: Returning the approved drawings to the goods contractor until delivery
options.D: Reissuing the drawings for re-approval once the installer is selected

questions.explanation: Industry guidance observes that it may be advantageous to make approved purchasing-contract submittals available during solicitation for the construction contract. Withholding the drawings until the installer is under contract, returning them to the goods contractor, or putting them through re-approval would keep that information from installation bidders and has no basis in recommended practice.
questions.source: shop drawings, product data, and samples

questions.question: How does industry guidance characterize submittal requirements for shop drawings and product data in a purchasing contract?

options.A: Generally omitted, since the goods are fabricated away from the site
options.B: Reviewed and approved by the installing construction contractor
options.C: Replaced by the implied warranties that the UCC attaches to sales
options.D: Similar to construction contracts, with review managed by the A/E

questions.explanation: Shop drawing and product data stipulations in purchasing contracts resemble those in construction contracts, and the A/E typically manages submittal review and approval. Off-site fabrication does not eliminate submittals, the installer is not the reviewing party, and UCC warranties do not substitute for submittal requirements.
questions.source: shop drawings, product data, and samples

questions.question: Why might operation and maintenance manuals be of critical importance under a purchasing contract?

options.A: The goods contractor may have little direct contact with the eventual installer
options.B: The UCC makes delivery of manuals a condition of transferring clear title
options.C: Purchasing contracts generally exclude the A/E from reviewing submittals
options.D: The goods contractor usually performs installation and start-up on site

questions.explanation: Industry guidance explains that because the goods contractor and the eventual installer or erector may have little direct contact, the information delivered through O&M manuals can be critical. The UCC title warranty has nothing to do with manuals, the A/E typically does manage purchasing submittals, and on-site installation by the goods contractor is the exception rather than the rule.

questions.question: During a project manual review, a team member proposes deleting the O&M manual requirement from a purchasing contract for a packaged boiler, arguing that manuals matter mainly in traditional construction contracts. Which response is consistent with industry guidance?

options.A: Agree; manuals belong only in the contract of whoever installs the boiler
options.B: Agree; manuals are needed under purchasing only for owner-installed goods
options.C: Disagree; manuals may be even more critical under a purchasing contract
options.D: Disagree; the UCC requires manuals for every sale of complex equipment

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that O&M manuals, frequently required in traditional construction contracts, might be even more critical under a purchasing contract. Moving the requirement to the installer's contract or limiting it to certain goods ignores that the goods contractor is the source of the information, and industry guidance ties the requirement to the contract documents rather than to the UCC.

questions.question: In traditional construction contracts, industry guidance notes that operation and maintenance manual requirements are particularly common for which type of work?

options.A: Finishes requiring periodic cleaning or care
options.B: Complex equipment or systems
options.C: Products covered by extended warranties
options.D: Products furnished with extra stock materials

questions.explanation: Industry guidance says construction contract documents frequently require O&M manuals, particularly for complex equipment or systems, and then argues the manuals may matter even more for purchased goods. Finishes, warranted products, and items with extra stock may carry maintenance or warranty information, but they are not what industry guidance singles out for the O&M manual requirement.

questions.question: For most purchasing contracts, industry guidance says payment procedures are based on payments at three stages. Which set lists those stages?

options.A: Contract award, delivery to the site, and installation
options.B: Completion of fabrication, shipment, and start-up
options.C: Approval of submittals, shipment, and installation
options.D: Approval of submittals, delivery, and final acceptance

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that, aside from cases needing partial deliveries or progress payments during fabrication, payment is usually made at three points: submittal approval, delivery to the designated location, and final acceptance. The other sets substitute contract award, shipment, installation, or start-up, none of which lists among the three standard payment stages.

questions.question: Owner-purchased chillers were delivered on schedule, but the separate installation contract has slipped by eight months, and the goods contractor is still awaiting final payment because acceptance depends on testing after installation. What provision should the purchasing documents have included?

options.A: Final payment withheld until installation and testing, however long it takes
options.B: Final payment at delivery for all equipment, with no later acceptance test
options.C: A reasonable time limit after delivery, then final payment regardless
options.D: Final payment released only at substantial completion of the installation

questions.explanation: Industry guidance allows final acceptance of equipment to wait until it is installed or placed in service and proven acceptable, but in fairness to the goods contractor it calls for a reasonable time limit between delivery and installation, after which final payment is made even if the item has not been installed and tested. Open-ended withholding or tying payment to the installation contract contradicts that fairness provision, and paying in full at delivery ignores the equipment case.

questions.question: An owner agrees to make progress payments on a large custom switchgear lineup while it is being manufactured and remains under the goods contractor's control. What should the purchasing documents include, and who should furnish the language?

options.A: Protection of the owner's stake in unfinished goods; owner's legal counsel
options.B: Transfer of title to the goods at each payment; the A/E's master specification
options.C: A payment bond securing each progress payment; the goods contractor's surety
options.D: Transit insurance on goods still in fabrication; the owner's insurance adviser

questions.explanation: When progress payments are made while goods are still being manufactured under the goods contractor's control, industry guidance calls for provisions that protect the owner's interest in the partially completed goods and says the contract language should come from the owner's legal counsel. Title transfer, payment bonds, and transit insurance are not the mechanism industry guidance describes, and the A/E, a surety, or an insurance adviser is not the source it names.

questions.question: Which UCC article governs contracts for the sale of goods between buyers and sellers, and which state has not adopted it?

options.A: Article 9; Louisiana
options.B: Article 2; Louisiana
options.C: Article 2; Delaware
options.D: Article 9; Delaware

questions.explanation: Industry guidance identifies Article 2 of the UCC as the law governing contracts for transactions in goods and notes that it has been adopted in 49 states, with Louisiana the exception. Article 9 is not the sales article industry guidance names, and Delaware is not the non-adopting state.

questions.question: Separately from an earlier equipment purchase, an owner contracts with the manufacturer solely for on-site technical assistance and an installation check. Does UCC Article 2 govern this contract?

options.A: Yes, because the services relate to goods sold under a prior contract
options.B: Yes, because Article 2 covers any agreement with a goods contractor
options.C: Only if the contract states a quantity and is signed by the manufacturer
options.D: No, because Article 2 is limited to sales of movable goods, not services

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that Article 2's coverage is limited to sales of movable goods, excluding contracts primarily for services, and it expressly counts technical assistance and installation checks as services. A link to an earlier sale, the identity of the provider, or satisfying the written-contract requirements does not bring a services-only contract under Article 2.

questions.question: A purchasing contract drafted by the A/E is silent on several commercial terms, and the owner assumes the UCC applies only if the contract incorporates it by reference. Which statement is accurate?

options.A: The UCC applies only to public owners that advertise their purchases
options.B: The written contract always prevails over any conflicting UCC provision
options.C: UCC provisions fill gaps and may sometimes override written terms
options.D: The UCC applies only where the parties adopt it by express reference

questions.explanation: Industry guidance cautions that the A/E should know the UCC's basic provisions because they take effect when the written contract does not address a matter and may sometimes override written provisions. Each state adopts the UCC and publishes it with its statutes, so it does not depend on incorporation by reference, is not limited to public owners, and does not always yield to contract language.

questions.question: After delivery, an owner learns that the goods contractor's lender holds a security interest in the delivered goods that was never disclosed to the owner. The purchase order contains no warranty language. Under the UCC, which statement applies?

options.A: The seller generally warrants clear title, free of security interests unknown to the buyer
options.B: No title warranty exists, because the purchase order is silent on warranties
options.C: Title warranties arise only after the goods are installed, tested, and accepted
options.D: The seller warrants title only against those security interests recorded after the delivery

questions.explanation: Industry guidance notes that the UCC attaches express and implied warranties to sales and that a seller generally warrants transfer of clear title, free of any security interest the buyer did not know about. Because this warranty comes from the UCC, it does not depend on warranty language in the purchase order, on installation and acceptance, or on when the interest was recorded.

questions.question: A signed purchase agreement for lighting fixtures leaves several commercial terms open for later agreement or for reasonable commercial practice. Which term must the parties generally settle themselves, rather than rely on the UCC to supply it?

options.A: Price of the fixtures
options.B: Delivery arrangements
options.C: Payment details
options.D: Quantity of fixtures

questions.explanation: Industry guidance explains that the UCC recognizes the practice of leaving terms for later agreement and may supply payment, delivery, and even price when the written contract is silent. Quantity, however, generally must be agreed upon by the parties, so it is the term the UCC will not fill in.

questions.question: A purchase order specifies delivery "FOB destination." According to industry guidance, where are FOB, CIF, and similar shorthand mercantile terms defined, and what do they allocate?

options.A: In the UCC; title, warranty obligations, and final acceptance
options.B: In the UCC; transportation costs, insurance, and risk of loss
options.C: In Division 01; transportation costs, insurance, and risk of loss
options.D: In the general conditions; payment terms, delivery dates, and price

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that FOB, CIF, and comparable mercantile shorthand terms are defined in the UCC and assign responsibility for transportation costs, insurance, and risk of loss. Division 01 and the general conditions are not where industry guidance says these terms are defined, and title, warranty, or price are not what the terms allocate.

questions.question: A purchase contract for goods is signed by both parties, but its terms are grossly unfair to the goods contractor. How should the A/E view the contract's enforceability under the UCC?

options.A: Enforceable, since the UCC defers to whatever terms the parties sign
options.B: Enforceable, as long as the A/E reviewed and approved the terms before signing
options.C: Unenforceable, because the UCC requires the parties to act in good faith
options.D: Unenforceable, because the UCC requires every contract to state a price

questions.explanation: Industry guidance notes that agreements governed by the UCC carry a requirement that the parties act in good faith, so unfair or unconscionable contracts are not enforceable. Signatures or A/E approval do not cure grossly unfair terms, and the UCC does not require a stated price, since it can supply price when the written contract is silent.

questions.question: The goods contractor fails to deliver custom air-handling units as specified. Under the UCC, which remedies are available to the owner as buyer?

options.A: Cancel the contract, purchase substitute goods, and recover damages
options.B: Stop delivery, reclaim the goods, and recover the contract price
options.C: Terminate for convenience and pay only for goods already delivered
options.D: Cancel the contract, stop delivery, and recover liquidated damages only

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that when the seller fails to deliver goods as specified, the buyer may cancel the contract, buy substitute goods, and recover damages. Stopping delivery, reclaiming the goods, and recovering the price are the seller's remedies in the summary, termination for convenience is a construction-contract provision rather than a UCC remedy for breach, and nothing in industry guidance limits the buyer to liquidated damages.

questions.question: Midway through a purchasing contract, the owner becomes insolvent while a shipment of goods is in transit. Which set of options does the UCC give the goods contractor as seller?

options.A: Cancel the contract, purchase substitute goods, or recover damages
options.B: Revoke acceptance, cancel the contract, or recover incidental damages
options.C: Stop delivery, purchase substitute goods, or recover damages
options.D: Stop delivery, reclaim the goods, recover the price, or recover damages

questions.explanation: Industry guidance lists the seller's UCC remedies, when the buyer becomes insolvent or breaches, as stopping delivery, reclaiming the goods, recovering the price, or recovering damages. Cancelling and buying substitute goods are the buyer's remedies, and revoking acceptance is something a buyer does, which lists among buyer breaches rather than seller remedies.

questions.question: An owner wants the purchasing contract for custom fabricated stair assemblies to include a liquidated damages amount far exceeding any delay cost the owner can document. What is the most likely result under the UCC?

options.A: The clause is enforceable because the UCC allows consequential damages
options.B: The clause is unenforceable because the amount is excessive and unsupported
options.C: The clause is enforceable because both parties agreed to the stated amount
options.D: The clause is unenforceable because the UCC bars liquidated damages in sales

questions.explanation: Industry guidance explains that the UCC enforces a liquidated damages clause when the amount is reasonable and verifiable but not when it is excessive and unsubstantiated, as here. The UCC does permit liquidated damages in sales, so a flat prohibition is wrong, and neither mutual agreement nor the availability of consequential damages rescues an unsupported amount.

questions.question: Industry guidance says MasterFormat, SectionFormat, PageFormat, and other CSI organizational tools may be greatly beneficial for purchasing documents under what assumption?

options.A: The goods contractor will also install the goods
options.B: The goods will be bought from a single negotiated source
options.C: The goods are to be procured by competitive bidding
options.D: The owner is a public agency purchasing under the UCC

questions.explanation: Industry guidance frames the value of CSI's organizational tools for purchasing documents on the assumption that the goods will be competitively bid. Installation by the goods contractor, negotiation with a single source, and public ownership are not the condition industry guidance states.

questions.question: An owner will award a purchasing contract for laboratory fume hoods and, at the same time, a construction contract that includes installing them. How should the two project manuals relate?

options.A: They should be similar to each other and carefully coordinated
options.B: They should be merged into one manual under a single contract
options.C: They should use different formats to keep the contracts distinct
options.D: They should be kept independent to avoid conflicting obligations

questions.explanation: When a purchasing contract and an installing construction contract are in force simultaneously, industry guidance says the two project manuals should be similar and must be carefully coordinated. Merging them into one contract, using deliberately different formats, or keeping them independent defeats the coordination industry guidance requires.

questions.question: A specifier proposes organizing an owner's purchasing documents according to CSI conventions. Which rationale does industry guidance give for this approach?

options.A: Construction-contract definitions can then be reused without change
options.B: Formats familiar to goods contractors and suppliers help avoid confusion
options.C: MasterFormat titles were written specifically for purchasing contracts
options.D: CSI formats eliminate the need to coordinate with a construction contract

questions.explanation: Industry guidance reasons that using documents resembling those construction-industry goods contractors and suppliers already know helps avoid confusion, and that CSI's organization, concepts, subject-matter locations, and language can be adapted to purchasing. Construction definitions cannot simply be carried over, since industry guidance says inapplicable ones must be avoided; MasterFormat was not written for purchasing; and industry guidance still requires coordination with any simultaneous construction contract.

questions.question: A specifier is assembling a purchasing project manual for owner-procured laboratory casework and is sorting documents into their groups. Which document does industry guidance list among the procurement requirements rather than with the agreement and conditions?

options.A: Performance bond
options.B: Supplementary conditions
options.C: Bid security form
options.D: Agreement form

questions.explanation: Industry guidance places instructions to bidders, bid forms, bid security forms, pre-bid information, and information available to bidders under the procurement requirements of a purchasing project manual. The performance bond, agreement form, and general and supplementary conditions are named separately as further elements of the manual, not as procurement requirements.

questions.question: An owner's purchasing manager drafts a purchasing project manual for owner-furnished switchgear containing instructions to bidders, a bid form, a bid security form, and technical specifications. Which additional elements should the manual include?

options.A: An agreement form, a performance bond, and general and supplementary conditions
options.B: A payment bond, a maintenance bond, and the seller's standard terms of sale
options.C: A schedule of values, a notice to proceed form, and a closeout certificate
options.D: A labor and material bond, an insurance certificate, and a lien waiver form

questions.explanation: Beyond the procurement requirements, industry guidance says a purchasing project manual should also carry an agreement form, a performance bond, and both general and supplementary conditions. Payment, maintenance, and labor and material bonds, lien waivers, insurance certificates, and schedules of values are not among the elements industry guidance names for the purchasing manual.

questions.question: A specifier is outlining the contents of a purchasing project manual for owner-bought FF&E. Which four categories of documents does a purchasing project manual customarily contain?

options.A: Bidding requirements, contract forms, general requirements, and contract drawings
options.B: Procurement requirements, agreement forms, Division 01 sections, and record documents
options.C: Solicitation documents, purchase order forms, UCC provisions, and product data
options.D: Procurement requirements, contracting forms, conditions of the contract, and specifications

questions.explanation: Industry guidance says a purchasing project manual customarily holds procurement requirements, contracting forms, conditions of the contract, and specifications, paralleling the construction project manual while reflecting purchasing differences. Drawings, product data, UCC provisions, and record documents are not among the categories industry guidance names.

questions.question: A specifier is editing Division 01 for a purchasing contract for factory-finished casework delivered to the owner's warehouse. Which Level 2 section does industry guidance place in the category generally applicable to all purchasing contracts?

options.A: Section 01 20 00—Price and Payment Procedures
options.B: Section 01 40 00—Quality Requirements
options.C: Section 01 70 00—Execution and Closeout Requirements
options.D: Section 01 80 00—Performance Requirements

questions.explanation: The first category, sections that apply to essentially every purchasing contract, consists of 01 10 00 Summary, 01 30 00 Administrative Requirements, 01 40 00 Quality Requirements, and 01 60 00 Product Requirements. Price and payment, execution and closeout, and performance requirements sections form the second category, included only sometimes depending on the goods contractor's activity and the project.

questions.question: A reviewer notices that the Division 01 for a purchasing contract for emergency generators includes Section 01 92 00—Facility Operation. How is that section classified for purchasing contracts?

options.A: Generally applicable to all purchasing contracts, like product requirements
options.B: Sometimes applicable, depending on the goods contractor's level of activity
options.C: Required whenever the goods are furnished by the owner for installation by others
options.D: Generally not applicable, because it relates to on-site activities

questions.explanation: Industry guidance groups 01 50 00 Temporary Facilities and Controls, 01 92 00 Facility Operation, and 01 94 00 Facility Decommissioning as sections that usually do not apply to purchasing contracts, since they concern on-site activities.
