Facility Operation is therefore not in the always-applicable group with product requirements, not in the sometimes-applicable group tied to the goods contractor's activity, and not tied by industry guidance to any disposition method.

questions.question: For a purchasing contract under which the seller will deliver, start up, and demonstrate packaged boilers, a specifier is deciding whether to include Section 01 70 00—Execution and Closeout Requirements. What governs that decision?

options.A: The goods contractor's required level of activity and the project's particular aspects
options.B: Its classification as generally applicable, so it is included in every purchasing contract
options.C: Its classification as generally inapplicable, so it is omitted because it covers site work
options.D: Whether the section is written as a proprietary, descriptive, or performance specification

questions.explanation: Industry guidance lists 01 70 00 Execution and Closeout Requirements in its second category, sections only sometimes applicable to purchasing contracts. Inclusion turns on how much activity the goods contractor must perform and on the particular aspects of the project, so the section is neither automatically included nor automatically excluded. The choice of proprietary, descriptive, or performance specifying is not the factor industry guidance names for this Division 01 decision.

questions.question: A specifier is writing a section for owner-purchased commercial kitchen equipment. The goods contractor must give technical assistance while another contractor installs the equipment, then field-test it after installation. In SectionFormat, where does industry guidance say such special services would typically be stated?

options.A: PART 1—GENERAL, because the services are administrative in nature
options.B: PART 2—PRODUCTS, because the services accompany the goods supplied
options.C: PART 3—EXECUTION, because that part deals with on-site activities
options.D: Division 01 only, because SectionFormat parts address the goods alone

questions.explanation: Industry guidance says PART 3—EXECUTION covers on-site activities and is the part used least in purchasing, yet items about disposing of the goods and any special services the goods contractor must provide would typically be stated there. Neither PART 1 nor PART 2 is identified for those items, and industry guidance does not move them out of the section into Division 01.

questions.question: A purchasing section for loose furniture has no on-site requirements at all. How should the specifier handle PART 3—EXECUTION?

options.A: Delete PART 3 entirely so the section ends after PART 2—PRODUCTS
options.B: Retain the part and simply note “Not Used” under its heading
options.C: Move the delivery and storage articles from PART 1 into PART 3
options.D: Replace PART 3 with a reference to the Division 01 closeout section

questions.explanation: Industry guidance says that when a purchasing section has nothing to state in PART 3, the specifier can simply note Not Used there, so the part stays in place with that notation. Deleting the part, shifting PART 1 articles into it, or substituting a Division 01 reference are not what industry guidance recommends.

questions.question: A specifier prepares two purchasing sections for identical rooftop units. One owner will stockpile the units for its own later use; the other owner will furnish them to a construction contractor for installation. Why might the articles developed in the two sections differ?

options.A: The eventual disposition of the goods is one factor that shapes article development
options.B: MasterFormat assigns a different section number whenever goods go to an installer
options.C: SectionFormat requires a PART 3 only when the owner retains goods for its own use
options.D: Reference standard specifying is not permitted when goods are furnished to an installer

questions.explanation: Industry guidance names five factors that shape the articles under each part of a purchasing section: the basic purchasing procedures, the nature of the goods, the specifying method, the required level of contractor activity, and the eventual disposition of the goods. Stockpiling versus furnishing to an installer is a difference in disposition, so the articles may differ. Industry guidance ties neither section numbering nor the use of PART 3 to owner retention, and it bars no specifying method.

questions.question: An owner purchased lockers and kept them in its own warehouse before handing them to the general contractor for installation. At transfer, several units are missing hardware kits. Who is responsible to the construction contractor for the completeness and condition of the goods at transfer?

options.A: The goods contractor, as the original seller of the lockers
options.B: The A/E, as coordinator of the purchasing and construction contracts
options.C: The construction contractor, once it signs for delivery of the units
options.D: The owner, as the party furnishing the goods to the installer

questions.explanation: When goods are furnished by the owner for installation by others, industry guidance makes the owner answerable to the construction contractor for their suitability, completeness, and condition at the moment of transfer. Only after transfer does the construction contractor take over storage, handling, and installation. Industry guidance does not place this duty on the goods contractor or on the A/E.

questions.question: Owner-purchased rooftop units were furnished to the mechanical contractor, who installed them. A compressor fails during the manufacturer's warranty period, and the owner expects the mechanical contractor to pursue the manufacturer. What does industry guidance suggest about warranties under this method of disposition?

options.A: They transfer automatically to the installer when it accepts the goods at transfer
options.B: They may not transfer to the installer, so the owner may need to retain and enforce them
options.C: They lapse unless the goods contractor itself installs the goods at the project site
options.D: They are best held by the A/E, who may enforce them for the owner until final payment

questions.explanation: Under the furnished-by-owner method, industry guidance cautions that passing the goods' warranties to the construction contractor might be doubtful, so the owner, as original purchaser, may have to keep and enforce them. Industry guidance does not say warranties transfer automatically, lapse because someone else installed the goods, or are held and enforced by the A/E.

questions.question: An owner plans to assign its purchasing contract for long-lead switchgear to the electrical contractor. Which statement describes this method of disposition?

options.A: The owner still pays the goods contractor while the electrical contractor handles installation
options.B: The owner stays responsible to the installer for the goods' suitability and condition at transfer
options.C: The owner may lose part of the cost benefit of buying direct but keeps other inherent advantages
options.D: The A/E and goods contractor drop out after final payment except for warranty obligations

questions.explanation: With assignment, the construction contractor accepts the purchasing contract, much like a purchase order, and takes on receipt, payment, administration, and installation; industry guidance notes the owner may forfeit some of the cost advantage of purchasing but keeps its other inherent advantages. The owner therefore no longer pays the goods contractor. Owner responsibility at transfer describes the furnished-by-owner method, and the A/E dropping out after final payment describes owner retention.

questions.question: An A/E's purchasing documents for laboratory fume hoods state that the hoods will be furnished by the owner for installation by others. The separate construction contract, issued at the same time, is silent on the arrangement. What is the best action?

options.A: Also state the method in the construction contract and define what each contract furnishes
options.B: Rely on the purchasing documents alone, since stating the method once is sufficient
options.C: Leave the goods contractor and construction contractor to work out the interface after award
options.D: Address the disposition method by field order once the construction contract is awarded

questions.explanation: Industry guidance requires the disposition method to be clearly stipulated in the purchasing documents and, when a construction contract is involved, in that contract as well, with procedures firmly established with both contractors. The documents must identify which items, appurtenances, and accessories each contract furnishes and assign responsibility for the rest, which demands close A/E coordination. Relying on one set of documents, leaving the contractors to sort it out, or deferring it to a field order leaves the interface undefined.

questions.question: An owner is buying boxed task chairs to be delivered to its facility, with no assembly or installation by the vendor. Which AIA document is appropriate?

options.A: A151, Standard Form of Agreement Between Owner and Vendor for FF&E
options.B: A751, Invitation and Instructions to Vendors for Quotations for FF&E
options.C: A151 used with A751, since the vendor must inspect the premises
options.D: A152, Purchase Order, with A152 Exhibit A, Terms and Conditions

questions.explanation: Industry guidance directs that when FF&E is only purchased, with no assembly or installation, AIA A152, Purchase Order, should be used with its companion A152 Exhibit A, Terms and Conditions. A151 and A751 each require the vendor to inspect the premises and to assemble or install the FF&E, so they suit purchases that include that work.

questions.question: Owner's counsel asks how two AIA FF&E documents handle a conflict between the document's terms and the UCC. Which statement is accurate?

options.A: A152 says its terms and conditions prevail; A151 does not state which prevails
options.B: A151 says the agreement prevails over the UCC; A152 does not state which prevails
options.C: Both documents state that the UCC prevails over any conflicting contract terms
options.D: Neither document cites the UCC; the law of the project's location governs both

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that A151 refers to the UCC and provides that the agreement takes precedence if the two conflict. A152 also refers to the UCC but is silent on whether its terms and conditions prevail, which rules out the reversed and UCC-prevails statements. Governing by the law of the project's location without citing the UCC is how industry guidance describes ConsensusDocs, not AIA.

questions.question: A specifier converting a CSI-style purchasing project manual to the EJCDC document family notices a terminology difference. Which term does EJCDC use where CSI and AIA use purchasing or sale of goods?

options.A: Acquisition
options.B: Supply
options.C: Procurement
options.D: Furnishing

questions.explanation: Industry guidance notes that EJCDC uses procurement where CSI and AIA speak of purchasing or the sale of goods, which is why EJCDC titles read, for example, Agreement Between Buyer and Seller for Procurement. Acquisition is the federal FAR term, and supply and furnishing are not the label EJCDC adopts.

questions.question: An engineer is assembling the four primary EJCDC purchasing documents for an owner buying pumps for an engineer-designed treatment plant. Which set does industry guidance list?
questions.explanation: Industry guidance identifies the four primary EJCDC purchasing documents as P-200 (Instructions to Bidders), P-520 (Agreement), P-700 (Standard General Conditions), and P-800 (Guide to the Preparation of Procurement Supplementary Conditions). P-400, the bid form, is used alongside them but is not one of the four; P-001 is the commentary; and C-prefixed numbers belong to EJCDC's construction series.

questions.question: A water utility is buying large vertical turbine pumps directly from a manufacturer for an engineer-designed pump station. The manufacturer insists on using its own standard sales order form. What is the best approach for the owner?

options.A: Accept the supplier form and attach the engineer's specifications as an exhibit
options.B: Use the EJCDC construction series, since the goods are engineered equipment
options.C: Accept the supplier form, relying on the UCC to fill any gaps in its commercial terms
options.D: Use the EJCDC procurement documents, which avoid the shortcomings of supplier forms

questions.explanation: Industry guidance presents the EJCDC procurement documents, used when an owner buys goods directly for an engineer-designed project, as an alternative to accepting manufacturers' and suppliers' standard purchase order forms; they avoid the inadequacies of those forms and the trouble of adapting them to the owner's and project's needs. Accepting the supplier's form, even with attachments or UCC gap-filling, is what the EJCDC documents are meant to replace, and the construction series is not the purchasing set.

questions.question: An engineer editing EJCDC P-200 for a procurement wants to confirm the meaning of a capitalized term used throughout the bid package. Where are the terms used in all four primary EJCDC purchasing documents defined?

options.A: In the agreement, EJCDC P-520
options.B: In the general conditions, EJCDC P-700
options.C: In the instructions to bidders, EJCDC P-200
options.D: In the supplementary conditions guide, EJCDC P-800

questions.explanation: Industry guidance explains that the terms used across all four primary EJCDC purchasing documents are defined in the general conditions, which for the procurement set is P-700, Standard General Conditions for Procurement Contracts. The agreement, the instructions to bidders, and the supplementary conditions guide are not where industry guidance locates those definitions.

questions.question: Late in document preparation, an engineer revises the EJCDC P-520 agreement to change the payment terms. What else should the engineer consider?

options.A: Whether P-001, the procurement commentary, must be revised and issued with the bid documents
options.B: Whether bidders must countersign the revised agreement form before bids are opened
options.C: Whether the other primary documents need matching changes, since they are closely integrated
options.D: Whether EJCDC must approve the edit, since P-520 is a copyrighted standard form

questions.explanation: Industry guidance stresses that the EJCDC purchasing documents are closely integrated, with shared terms defined in the general conditions, so changing any one of them may require changes in the others. Industry guidance says nothing about reissuing the P-001 commentary to bidders, having bidders countersign the agreement, or obtaining EJCDC approval of edits.

questions.question: Which document should users of the EJCDC purchasing documents consult for its discussion of the comparable construction contract forms?

options.A: EJCDC C-001, Commentary on the 2018 Construction Series Documents
options.B: EJCDC P-001, Commentary on the 2019 EJCDC Procurement Documents
options.C: EJCDC C-700, Standard General Conditions of the Construction Contract
options.D: EJCDC P-800, Guide to the Preparation of Procurement Supplementary Conditions

questions.explanation: Industry guidance recommends that users of the EJCDC purchasing documents read the relevant parts of EJCDC C-001, the commentary on the 2018 construction series, covering the comparable construction forms. P-001 is the procurement commentary from which paraphrases, C-700 is a construction general conditions form rather than a commentary, and P-800 is the procurement supplementary conditions guide.

questions.question: How does EJCDC P-400, Bid Form for Procurement, relate to the four primary EJCDC purchasing documents?

options.A: It is one of the four, taking the place of the instructions to bidders
options.B: It is a commentary explaining how the four documents should be used
options.C: It is the guide used to draft the procurement supplementary conditions
options.D: It is used in conjunction with them but is not one of the four

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that EJCDC P-400, Bid Form for Procurement, is used together with EJCDC's other procurement documents, while the four primary documents are P-200, P-520, P-700, and P-800. P-400 does not replace the instructions to bidders (P-200), is not a commentary, and is not the supplementary conditions guide (P-800).

questions.question: An owner wants a manufacturer to furnish and also install a specialized conveyor system, and its attorney proposes using the EJCDC purchasing documents unchanged. What is the better course?

options.A: Use the purchasing documents unchanged, treating installation as one of the seller's special services
options.B: Use standard construction contract forms, or modify the purchasing documents to add installation
options.C: Accept the manufacturer's standard sales order, since EJCDC forms cannot address installation
options.D: Use the purchasing documents and have the engineer define installation later by field order

questions.explanation: Industry guidance says the EJCDC purchasing documents are not meant for cases where the manufacturer or supplier must take part in installation; when installation is included, the arrangement resembles a traditional construction contract, so standard construction forms should be used or the primary purchasing documents modified to add installation. Seller special services are limited to assisting the installing entity, industry guidance presents the EJCDC documents as an alternative to suppliers' standard forms, and a field order is not the vehicle industry guidance names.

questions.question: An owner will use the EJCDC purchasing documents to buy identical valve actuators to be shipped in several separate deliveries over two years. How should the needed changes to the primary procurement documents be made?

options.A: Through direct edits to the general conditions text
options.B: Through revisions to the bid form for procurement
options.C: Through the supplementary conditions
options.D: Through a change order issued after the first delivery

questions.explanation: For purchases with multiple deliveries of the same item, industry guidance directs that changes to the primary EJCDC procurement documents be made by supplementary conditions. Editing the standard general conditions text directly, revising the bid form, or issuing a change order after the first delivery are not the methods industry guidance specifies.

questions.question: An engineer is adapting a technical specification section for use with the EJCDC purchasing documents and finds a paragraph reading 'Seller shall perform the Work in accordance with the drawings.' Per industry guidance, what terminology problem does this create?

options.A: Work is a construction-contract term that the EJCDC procurement set does not use
options.B: Seller should read Contractor, the term EJCDC uses for the party furnishing Goods
options.C: Seller should read Vendor, the term EJCDC uses for the furnishing party
options.D: Work should read Special Services, the term EJCDC uses for all seller duties

questions.explanation: Industry guidance notes that Work, a term defined in construction contract documents, is not used in the EJCDC purchasing documents, so a section written for use with them should avoid it. Seller is the correct EJCDC term for the furnishing party, not Contractor or Vendor, and special services cover only site assistance such as instruction or start-up help, not every seller obligation.

questions.question: In the EJCDC purchasing documents, how should a reader interpret a reference to a fabricator or a distributor?

options.A: As another name for the Seller, which has entered into the agreement directly with the Buyer
options.B: As a party under subcontract to a prime construction contractor or to a site subcontractor
options.C: As the Buyer's agent that receives, stores, and later transfers the Goods to the installer
options.D: As a lower-tier supplier to the Seller whose obligations also run directly to the Buyer

questions.explanation: Industry guidance explains that in the EJCDC purchasing documents, anyone called a manufacturer, supplier, fabricator, distributor, or vendor is a party subcontracted to one of the prime construction contractors, or sub-subcontracted to a subcontractor working at the site. The party contracting with the Buyer to furnish the Goods is the Seller, so these labels do not mean the Seller, a Buyer's agent, or a supplier owing duties directly to the Buyer.

questions.question: A construction firm needs to purchase a complex automated storage system, including its installation, for a building project. Which ConsensusDocs purchasing document is intended for this purchase?

options.A: ConsensusDocs 702 alone
options.B: ConsensusDocs 702.1 alone
options.C: ConsensusDocs 702 used with 702.1
options.D: ConsensusDocs 703

questions.explanation: Industry guidance describes ConsensusDocs 703, Standard Purchase Agreement for Non-commodity Goods by a Contractor, as intended for complex goods and, like AIA A151, covering installation. ConsensusDocs 702 and its companion 702.1 are for goods that need no installation, so neither alone nor together do they fit this purchase.

questions.question: An owner's counsel reviewing a ConsensusDocs 702.1 purchase order asks which law governs it. What do the ConsensusDocs purchasing documents provide?

options.A: The UCC governs, because the documents expressly incorporate it throughout by reference
options.B: The agreement governs and takes precedence over any conflicting provision of the UCC
options.C: Laws at the project's location govern, so an adopting state's UCC applies by default
options.D: The law of the seller's home state governs, regardless of where the project is located

questions.explanation: Industry guidance notes that, unlike the EJCDC and AIA documents, the ConsensusDocs purchasing documents do not reference the UCC directly; 702.1 and 703 instead provide that the law where the project is located governs, so the UCC controls by default in a state that has adopted it. Express UCC incorporation, an agreement-over-UCC precedence clause, and a seller's-home-state rule are not what industry guidance describes.

questions.question: ConsensusDocs 702 and 703 are organized very similarly. Why does 703 contain additional insurance, safety, and indemnity provisions?

options.A: It is used only for public-sector buyers
options.B: It also covers installation of the goods
options.C: It directly references the UCC throughout
options.D: It is always paired with the 702.1 terms

questions.explanation: Industry guidance says 702 (used with 702.1) and 703 are organized much alike, but because 703 also includes installation of the goods, it carries extra insurance, safety, and indemnity provisions. Industry guidance does not limit 703 to public buyers, says the ConsensusDocs purchasing documents do not directly reference the UCC, and pairs 702.1 with 702 rather than 703.

questions.question: A specifier on a federal agency project finds that the agency has issued its own acquisition regulation. How does that regulation relate to the FAR?

options.A: It implements or supplements the FAR, which remains the primary document
options.B: It supersedes the FAR for that agency's acquisitions once it is published
options.C: It stands outside the FAR system and governs only internal agency staff
options.D: It replaces the FAR's uniform policies for all other executive agencies

questions.explanation: Industry guidance describes the Federal Acquisition Regulations System as the FAR, the primary document, together with regulations that individual agencies develop to implement or supplement it. An agency regulation therefore operates within the FAR system rather than superseding it, standing outside it, or replacing the uniform policies the FAR provides for all executive agencies.

questions.question: The vision of the Federal Acquisition Regulations System is to deliver which of the following to the customer?

options.A: The lowest-priced product or service obtained through full and open competition
options.B: The highest-quality product or service at the minimum administrative operating cost
options.C: The lowest-priced product or service at the minimum administrative operating cost
options.D: The best value product or service on a timely basis while maintaining the public's trust

questions.explanation: Industry guidance frames the FAR System's vision as providing the customer with the best value product or service, delivered in a timely way, while keeping the public's trust and meeting public policy objectives. Lowest price, highest quality, and minimum administrative cost are not the vision's terms; minimizing administrative operating costs and promoting competition appear among the guiding principles instead.

questions.question: Under the FAR guiding principles cited, customer satisfaction is measured in terms of which three attributes of the delivered product or service?

options.A: Cost, scope, and risk
options.B: Quality, safety, and durability
options.C: Cost, quality, and timeliness
options.D: Scope, safety, and availability

questions.explanation: The first FAR guiding principle in industry guidance is customer satisfaction measured by the cost, quality, and timeliness of what is delivered. The other sets substitute scope, risk, safety, durability, or availability, which does not name for this principle.

questions.question: A federal acquisition team is weighing options for furnishing a new office building. Which practice does industry guidance cite as an example of how the FAR System satisfies the customer?

options.A: Requiring custom-designed products tailored to each agency's needs
options.B: Maximizing the use of commercial products and services
options.C: Awarding contracts primarily on the basis of lowest offered price
options.D: Favoring design-build delivery for facility acquisitions

questions.explanation: The examples of satisfying the customer include maximizing the use of commercial products and services, using contractors with successful past performance or a current superior ability to perform, and promoting competition. Custom-designed products, award chiefly on lowest price, and a preference for design-build are not among those examples.

questions.question: One guiding principle of the Federal Acquisition Regulations System is to conduct business with which three qualities?

options.A: Integrity, fairness, and openness
options.B: Integrity, efficiency, and economy
options.C: Fairness, accountability, and economy
options.D: Efficiency, accountability, and openness

questions.explanation: Industry guidance lists conducting business with integrity, fairness, and openness as one of the FAR System's guiding principles. The other combinations swap in efficiency, accountability, or economy, which does not use in that principle.

questions.question: The FAR is prepared, issued, and maintained jointly by which parties?

options.A: The Secretary of Defense, the Office of Management and Budget, and the Department of Energy
options.B: NASA, the Department of Energy, and the Army Corps of Engineers
options.C: The GSA administrators, the Office of Management and Budget, and the Army Corps of Engineers
options.D: The Secretary of Defense, the GSA administrators, and NASA

questions.explanation: Three parties jointly prepare, issue, and maintain the FAR: the Secretary of Defense, the GSA administrators, and NASA. The Office of Management and Budget, the Department of Energy, and the Army Corps of Engineers are not named as parties to that joint responsibility.

questions.question: A new agency project manager assumes that the roles of government contracting personnel are fixed separately in each contract. Where is the responsibility of each such position described?

options.A: In each contract's general conditions and special clauses
options.B: In the solicitation issued for each individual federal acquisition
options.C: In the FAR, which defines what each of these positions must do
options.D: In the agency's annual procurement plan for each program

questions.explanation: Industry guidance explains that the FAR System includes government personnel assigned to manage and administer federal contracting, and that every one of those positions has a defined responsibility set out in the FAR. Those responsibilities do not come from individual contract clauses, solicitations, or an agency's program plans.

questions.question: At a kickoff meeting, a federal program manager describes the acquisition team as only the government's technical, supply, and procurement representatives. Which participants does this description leave out?

options.A: State and local building officials with jurisdiction over the site
options.B: The customers they serve and the contractors providing products and services
options.C: The private sureties and lenders that finance the contractors' operations
options.D: Congressional oversight staff and the agency's office of inspector general

questions.explanation: Industry guidance defines the acquisition team as all government acquisition participants, including technical, supply, and procurement representatives, plus the customers served and the contractors that furnish the products and services. Limiting the team to government representatives therefore omits customers and contractors; building officials, sureties and lenders, and oversight staff are not named as team members.

questions.question: A head of the contracting activity (HCA) needs to sign a contract personally. What is the HCA's standing with respect to contracting officer authority?

options.A: The HCA must first obtain a separate contracting officer warrant
options.B: The HCA manages the activity but may not sign any contracts
options.C: The HCA is a contracting officer by virtue of the position
options.D: The HCA may sign only after a contracting officer concurs

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that the head of the contracting activity is the official responsible for managing the contracting activity and is a contracting officer by virtue of holding that position. Because the status comes with the position, no separate warrant or concurrence is needed for it, and the HCA is not barred from signing contracts.

questions.question: On a federal courthouse project, the contracting officer is on leave when bids are opened. The agency's facilities director, a senior executive who manages the building program but is not a contracting officer, offers to sign the construction contract so award is not delayed. What is the correct position?

options.A: The director may sign if the contract is below the simplified acquisition threshold.
options.B: The director may not sign; only a contracting officer can sign for the government.
options.C: The director may sign because the director manages the agency's building program.
options.D: The director may not sign, but a contracting specialist on the officer's staff may.

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that only contracting officers may enter into and sign contracts on behalf of the United States, and then only within their delegated authority. A facilities director who is not a contracting officer cannot bind the government, and neither a dollar threshold, a management role, nor substituting a staff contracting specialist who is not a contracting officer changes who may sign.

questions.question: A contractor on a federal project wants to confirm that the contracting officer who will sign a large modification can bind the government for that amount. Which statement about a contracting officer's authority is consistent with industry guidance?

options.A: It is unlimited once the officer is appointed, and the appointment is public.
options.B: It is set case by case in each contract and stated only in that contract's terms.
options.C: It extends only as far as delegated, and the limits are kept confidential in the agency.
options.D: It extends only as far as delegated, and the written limits are available to the public.

questions.explanation: Contracting officers can bind the government only to the extent of their delegated authority; the appointing authority gives them clear written instructions on those limits, and that information is readily available to the public as well as to agency personnel. The authority is therefore neither unlimited nor set contract by contract, and its limits are not kept internal to the agency.

questions.question: A federal contracting officer has a responsive low bid within the government estimate, but a clearance required by agency procedures has not yet been issued, and the construction season is short. What should the officer do?

options.A: Withhold execution until the clearance and all other approvals are in place.
options.B: Execute now, since latitude for business judgment lets the officer waive the clearance.
options.C: Execute now and incorporate the clearance later through a bilateral modification.
options.D: Withhold execution only until the head of the contracting activity concurs verbally.

questions.explanation: Industry guidance bars execution of any contract until the contracting officer ensures that all legal, regulatory, and procedural requirements, including clearances and approvals, have been met. The wide latitude for business judgment exists to carry out the officer's responsibilities, not to skip that precondition, and neither a later modification nor verbal concurrence from the head of the contracting activity substitutes for the missing clearance.

questions.question: On a federal acquisition for construction, a requirement in the FAR part devoted to construction conflicts with a requirement in another FAR part. Which part takes precedence?

options.A: FAR Part 36
options.B: FAR Part 43
options.C: FAR Part 46
options.D: FAR Part 49

questions.explanation: Industry guidance identifies FAR Part 36 as the part containing construction contract requirements and says it prevails over an inconsistent requirement in another part when construction acquisition is involved. Parts 43, 46, and 49 cover modifications, quality assurance, and termination, and none carries that precedence.

questions.question: A single, undivided federal contract covers building a vehicle maintenance facility and supplying some shop equipment; the building work is by far the largest portion. How are the contract clauses selected?

options.A: Use the supply clauses, since equipment is a distinct deliverable.
options.B: Use construction clauses for the building and supply clauses for the equipment.
options.C: Use the clauses applicable to the predominant part of the work.
options.D: Use the clauses for the part with the earliest delivery date.

questions.explanation: Industry guidance directs that a contract combining construction with supplies or services include the clauses applicable to the predominant part of the work. Applying clauses to each portion is the rule only when a contract is divided into parts; because this contract is undivided and building work dominates, construction clauses govern, and supply-based or schedule-based selection has no basis in recommended practice.

questions.question: A federal contract for construction and related services is structured in several separately identified parts, one for building construction and one for post-occupancy services. How do the contract clauses apply?

options.A: Only the predominant part's clauses apply throughout the contract.
options.B: Each part carries the clauses applicable to that part's own work.
options.C: The construction clauses apply to all parts because Part 36 governs.
options.D: The services clauses apply to all parts because services occur last.

questions.explanation: When a contract is divided into several parts, industry guidance says the clauses apply to each portion rather than to the whole. The predominant-part rule addresses contracts that are not divided, and Part 36 precedence resolves conflicting FAR requirements rather than selecting clauses across portions.

questions.question: On a federal building contract, a proposed modification is expected to exceed the simplified acquisition threshold. What must be prepared and furnished to the contracting officer for this modification?

options.A: A contractor-certified schedule of values for the change
options.B: A determination signed by the head of the contracting activity
options.C: A value analysis report prepared by the design A/E of record
options.D: An independent government estimate of construction cost

questions.explanation: Industry guidance requires an independent government estimate of construction cost for each proposed contract and for each modification anticipated to exceed the simplified acquisition threshold. Contractor pricing is not independent, and neither an HCA determination nor an A/E value analysis is the document industry guidance names.
questions.source: special aspects of contracting for construction

questions.question: The A/E firm that designed a new federal laboratory has a construction affiliate that wants to submit a sealed bid for the construction contract. Under the general rule stated, the affiliate:

options.A: should generally not be awarded the contract, given its tie to the designer
options.B: may be awarded the contract if it submits the lowest responsive bid
options.C: may be awarded the contract once the design contract is closed out
options.D: is barred only if the A/E will also provide construction-phase services

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that, in general, no construction contract should be awarded to the firm that designed the project or to its subsidiaries or affiliates. Being low bidder or closing out the design contract does not remove the affiliation, and the prohibition is not limited to designers who stay on for construction-phase services.
questions.source: special aspects of contracting for construction

questions.question: A federal installation has a fixed-price contract underway for a new barracks. The agency proposes a cost-reimbursement contract for utility work on the same site during the same period. This arrangement is:

options.A: generally acceptable, provided both contracts were procured using sealed bids
options.B: generally acceptable, provided the independent estimate shows a cost savings
options.C: generally prohibited, because the two contracts would run concurrently on one site
options.D: generally prohibited, because federal utility work must always be awarded fixed-price

questions.explanation: Industry guidance notes that operating cost-reimbursement contracts concurrently with fixed-price contracts on the same site is generally prohibited; the concern is concurrency on one site, not the kind of work. Sealed bidding and the independent government estimate are separate requirements that do not authorize the combination, and industry guidance sets no rule that utility work must be fixed-price.
questions.source: special aspects of contracting for construction

questions.question: Under FAR Part 43, which of the following actions is accomplished by a bilateral contract modification?

options.A: Issuing a change order under the Changes clause of the contract
options.B: Making a negotiated equitable adjustment resulting from a change order
options.C: Issuing a notice of termination to the contractor for default
options.D: Making an administrative change to the contract's provisions

questions.explanation: Industry guidance lists negotiated equitable adjustments arising from a change order, definitizing letter contracts, and recording other agreements that modify terms as bilateral modifications. Issuing change orders, issuing termination notices, and making administrative changes are all unilateral actions.

questions.question: During construction of a federal facility, the agency's field inspector tells the contractor to add drainage work not shown in the contract documents and says the paperwork will follow. How should this direction be viewed?

options.A: It is binding; the contractor has an obligation to proceed with directed changes.
options.B: It is binding; once the inspector's daily report records the direction, it stands.
options.C: It is improper; only the A/E of record can direct the contractor to add work.
options.D: It is improper; only a contracting officer can execute a modification for it.

questions.explanation: Industry guidance reserves contract modifications to contracting officers acting within their authority, and other government personnel must not direct or encourage work that should be the subject of a modification. The obligation to proceed attaches to change orders from the contracting officer, and neither field reports nor the A/E substitute for that authority.

questions.question: A contractor on a fixed-price federal construction contract receives a change order from the contracting officer but believes the government's proposed price for it is far too low. What course of action does industry guidance support?

options.A: Proceed with the changed work and, if no price is agreed, consider a claim.
options.B: Stop the affected work until a bilateral equitable adjustment has been agreed.
options.C: Proceed only up to the amount allowed by the Limitation of Funds clause.
options.D: Decline the change, since unilateral changes require the contractor's consent.

questions.explanation: On receipt of a change order the contractor may not stop work and must comply; if the parties cannot agree on an equitable adjustment, the contractor may consider initiating a claim. The Limitation of Cost and Limitation of Funds exceptions apply to cost-reimbursement or incrementally funded contracts, not a fixed-price one, and the Changes clause lets the contracting officer make unilateral changes within scope.

questions.question: For a federal project's quality requirements, the contractor proposes language making its accredited third-party testing agency the sole inspecting party and stating that the government will not perform inspections of its own. This language is:

options.A: acceptable, provided the testing agency is independent and nationally accredited
options.B: acceptable, provided another federal agency approves the selected testing agency
options.C: unacceptable, because no contract may bar the government's own inspections
options.D: unacceptable, because only the A/E may perform inspections for the government

questions.explanation: Among the FAR Part 46 obligations industry guidance lists is that no contract precludes the government from performing inspections. The testing agency's independence or another agency's approval cannot remove that right, and industry guidance does not confine government inspection to the A/E.

questions.question: Under FAR Part 46, when and under whose direction must contract quality assurance for a federal agency be conducted?

options.A: Before acceptance, by or under the direction of the A/E of record
options.B: Before acceptance, by or under the direction of government personnel
options.C: After acceptance, by or under the direction of the contractor's QC staff
options.D: After acceptance, during the warranty period, by the contracting officer

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that government contract quality assurance takes place before acceptance and is performed by or under the direction of government personnel. Handing it to the A/E or the contractor's quality control staff, or deferring it until after acceptance, conflicts with that requirement.

questions.question: A federal agency has no quality assurance staff near a remote project site, but another federal agency keeps qualified inspectors nearby. Under FAR Part 46, the owner agency may:

options.A: delegate acceptance to the contractor's quality control manager if the agency certifies that manager
options.B: waive quality assurance if warranty clauses will cover the work after acceptance
options.C: defer quality assurance until after acceptance if its own staff cannot travel sooner
options.D: use the other agency's quality assurance and acceptance services if that is economical

questions.explanation: Industry guidance directs agencies to use other agencies' quality assurance and acceptance services when that is effective, economical, or otherwise in the government's interest. Quality assurance must still occur before acceptance by or under the direction of government personnel, so shifting acceptance to the contractor, substituting warranties, or deferring it are not supported.

questions.question: A specifier drafting a federal guide specification asks whether every federal contract must include a warranty. Under FAR 46.7, which statement is correct?

options.A: Warranty use is not mandatory; benefits must be commensurate with its cost.
options.B: Warranty use is mandatory for all construction contracts under FAR Part 36.
options.C: Warranty use is mandatory above the simplified acquisition threshold amount.
options.D: Warranty use is not mandatory; the contractor elects whether to provide one.

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that a warranty is not mandatory and that the benefits derived from it must be commensurate with its cost to the government. Industry guidance sets no Part 36 or dollar-threshold mandate, and the decision turns on the government's cost-benefit judgment rather than the contractor's election.

questions.question: A federal warranty clause cannot limit the government's rights under an inspection clause with respect to which of the following?

options.A: Patent defects, fraud, or negligent workmanship at acceptance
options.B: Latent defects, abuse, or damage from improper maintenance
options.C: Latent defects, fraud, or gross mistakes amounting to fraud
options.D: Patent defects, gross negligence, or mistakes found at acceptance

questions.explanation: Industry guidance specifies that warranty clauses cannot limit the government's inspection-clause rights concerning latent defects, fraud, or gross mistakes that amount to fraud. Patent defects, negligent workmanship, and gross negligence are not on that list, and abuse or improper maintenance are conditions warranties commonly exclude rather than rights industry guidance preserves.

questions.question: A federal agency's specifier is editing warranty clauses for a construction contract and for a separate supply contract. Regarding the requirement that a warranty apply notwithstanding inspection and acceptance, industry guidance states that:

options.A: only the warranty clauses found in construction contracts must include it
options.B: warranty clauses must include it, except those in construction contracts
options.C: warranty clauses in every type of contract, without exception, must include it
options.D: no warranty clause may extend beyond acceptance by the agency

questions.explanation: Industry guidance says warranty clauses must state that the warranty applies notwithstanding inspection, acceptance, or other contract terms, but it excepts warranty clauses in construction contracts. The rule is therefore neither limited to construction nor universal, and warranties do run past acceptance for a stated period of time or use or until a specified event.

questions.question: A federal construction contractor has fallen so far behind that the contracting officer anticipates it will fail to perform, and partially terminates the contract for default. With respect to the undelivered work, the government:

options.A: owes the contractor's costs for services rendered up to the termination date
options.B: owes the contractor's costs once the TCO determines the amount that is due
options.C: may not terminate yet, since default requires actual rather than anticipated failure
options.D: owes none of the contractor's costs and may recover advance and progress payments

questions.explanation: In a default termination, industry guidance says the government bears no liability for what the contractor spent on work not yet delivered and can recoup the advance and progress payments tied to that work. Payment through the effective date describes termination for convenience, and default may rest on anticipated as well as actual failure to perform.

questions.question: A contracting officer determines that ending part of a federal construction contract is in the government's best interest, with no fault by the contractor. How is the termination effected and what does the government owe?

options.A: Notice of Termination with extent and effective date; services rendered until then
options.B: Notice of Termination stating extent and effective date; all work through completion
options.C: Bilateral modification signed by both parties; costs plus profit on terminated work
options.D: Unilateral change order deleting the work; full contract value of the deleted portion

questions.explanation: For termination for convenience, industry guidance says the contracting officer delivers a Notice of Termination describing the extent of the termination and its effective date, and the government is liable only for services rendered up to that date. It does not owe payment for work through completion, profit on terminated work, or the value of deleted work.

questions.question: After a termination for convenience on a federal construction contract, the termination contracting officer (TCO) must reach a settlement. Which approach does industry guidance say the TCO should take whenever possible?

options.A: Issue a unilateral determination of the amount owed the contractor
options.B: Negotiate a fair and prompt settlement with the contractor
options.C: Cost out the settlement on the prescribed standard form alone
options.D: Refer the settlement to the agency's board of contract appeals

questions.explanation: Industry guidance lists negotiated agreement, TCO determination, costing out under SF 1034, or a combination as settlement methods, but says the TCO should negotiate a fair and prompt settlement when possible. A unilateral determination and SF 1034 costing out are available methods but not the stated preference, and an appeals board is not among the listed methods.

questions.question: Industry guidance lists costing out as one of the methods generally used to settle a federal contract termination. Under which standard form is this costing out performed?

options.A: Standard Form 25
options.B: Standard Form 30
options.C: Standard Form 1034
options.D: Standard Form 1442

questions.explanation: Industry guidance identifies costing out under Standard Form (SF) 1034 as a termination settlement method, alongside negotiated agreement and TCO determination, or a combination of these. SF 1034 is the only form industry guidance names for termination settlement; the other numbers are federal forms used for other purposes.

questions.question: Final payment on a federal construction contract was made in March 2023, but a related claim stayed open until June 2025. Under the federal access-to-records clause, what is the earliest date the contractor may dispose of the records required under the contract?

options.A: March 2026
options.B: June 2026
options.C: June 2028
options.D: March 2030

questions.explanation: The contractor must keep the required books, records, and reports for at least three years after final payment and the closing of all pending matters. Because the claim closed in June 2025, the period runs to June 2028; counting from final payment alone gives March 2026, and the other dates use the wrong period.

questions.question: Under the access-to-records provision summarized, the contractor agrees to give access to its pertinent books and records to which group?

options.A: The owner, the A/E, the surety, or any of their duly authorized representatives
options.B: The contracting officer, the A/E, and the local building official only
options.C: The Comptroller General only, and only after a formal audit is opened
options.D: The owner, federal agencies, Comptroller General, or their authorized agents

questions.explanation: Industry guidance names the owner, the federal agencies, the Comptroller General of the United States, and their duly authorized representatives as the parties entitled to access. The A/E, surety, and local building officials are not named, and access is not restricted to the Comptroller General.

questions.question: A federal auditor reviewing a contractor's records on a federal project asks to excerpt cost records and also requests records of the contractor's unrelated private-sector projects. The access clause:

options.A: covers only records directly pertinent to this contract, which may be excerpted
options.B: covers all of the contractor's business records, which may be excerpted
options.C: covers only records directly pertinent to this contract, examined but not copied
options.D: covers only the cost accounting system itself, examined but not transcribed

questions.explanation: The contractor must provide access to books, documents, papers, and records directly pertinent to the specific contract so the government can audit, examine, excerpt, and transcribe them. Unrelated private work falls outside that scope, and the clause expressly allows excerpting and transcribing, not just examination.

questions.question: A U.S.-manufactured steel stair assembly is predominantly steel. Imported steel accounts for 7 percent of the assembly's cost, and domestic components make up 80 percent of total component cost. Under the Buy American test, the assembly:

options.A: passes, because domestic components exceed 55 percent of component cost
options.B: fails, because foreign iron and steel must be under 5 percent of its cost
options.C: passes, because U.S. manufacture is the only test for steel materials
options.D: fails, because iron and steel materials must be 100 percent domestic

questions.explanation: For materials wholly or predominantly of iron or steel, industry guidance requires foreign iron and steel to be less than 5 percent of the material's cost, in addition to U.S. manufacture. The 55 percent domestic-component test applies only to materials that are not predominantly iron or steel, and industry guidance does not demand 100 percent domestic content.

questions.question: A contractor on a federal project proposes a U.S.-manufactured light fixture that fails the domestic-component cost test. The fixture sells in large volumes commercially, but it would have to be altered to meet the project's requirements. Regarding the commercially available off-the-shelf (COTS) exception, industry guidance indicates that the fixture:

options.A: qualifies, because substantial commercial sales alone establish COTS status
options.B: qualifies, provided alteration costs stay below 55 percent of the item's cost
options.C: does not qualify, because COTS status is granted only on a contractor request
options.D: does not qualify, because the government must be able to buy it unmodified

questions.explanation: Industry guidance requires a COTS item both to sell in substantial quantities commercially and to be available to the government without modification in its commercial form, so a fixture that must be altered fails. Sales volume alone is not enough, the 55 percent figure belongs to the domestic-component test, and the request-and-review process industry guidance mentions covers use of foreign material, not COTS status.

questions.question: An A/E editing a federal agency guide specification finds paragraphs numbered 1.1, 1.1.1, 1.1.2, and 1.1.2.1. This legal-style numbering departs from which CSI convention?

options.A: The PageFormat preferred alphanumeric paragraph arrangement
options.B: The SectionFormat three-part arrangement of section content
options.C: The MasterFormat numbers and titles of the current edition
options.D: The UniFormat elemental arrangement of project descriptions

questions.explanation: Industry guidance notes that although most government guide specifications follow SectionFormat, some agencies number paragraphs in a legal Arabic-numeral style instead of PageFormat's preferred alphanumeric arrangement. Paragraph numbering is a PageFormat matter; SectionFormat governs the parts of a section, and MasterFormat governs section numbers and titles.

questions.question: A specifier moving from private-sector work to a federal agency project plans to state all shop drawing and maintenance information procedures only in Division 01. What agency requirement may conflict with that plan?

options.A: Placing those procedural requirements in agency contract clauses only
options.B: Placing those procedural requirements in drawing general notes sheets
options.C: Placing those procedural requirements in each technical section
options.D: Placing those procedural requirements in a separate Division 00 form

questions.explanation: Industry guidance observes that some agencies require procedural matters for maintenance information and shop drawings to be specified in each technical specification section rather than only in the general requirements. Industry guidance does not describe relocating these procedures to contract clauses, drawing notes, or Division 00 documents.

questions.question: While editing a federal agency's guide specifications, a specifier notices that several section numbers and titles do not match the current MasterFormat edition. Which explanation is consistent with industry guidance?

options.A: The agency's guide specifications are organized by UniFormat, not MasterFormat.
options.B: The agency's numbers can differ from the current edition, at times deliberately.
options.C: The agency's guide specifications must be renumbered to match the current edition.
options.D: The agency's numbers follow SectionFormat, which assigns its own section numbers.

questions.explanation: Industry guidance says most government agencies organize guide specifications by MasterFormat, but their numbers and titles may differ from the current edition, and agencies sometimes deviate intentionally to accommodate unique requirements. Industry guidance does not require renumbering, it names MasterFormat rather than UniFormat as the common link, and SectionFormat governs the arrangement within a section, not section numbers.

questions.question: A federal agency retains an A/E for a new clinic but does not have the A/E prepare the entire solicitation package. Which split of preparation work does industry guidance describe for such cases?

options.A: A/E: procurement requirements and technical sections; agency: general requirements
options.B: A/E: contracting requirements and general requirements; agency: technical sections
options.C: A/E: procurement and contracting requirements; agency: Division 01 and technical
options.D: A/E: general requirements and technical sections; agency: procurement and contracting

questions.explanation: Industry guidance explains that federal agencies usually do not require the A/E to prepare every component of the bid package; in some cases the A/E prepares the general requirements and technical specifications while the agency prepares the procurement and contracting requirements. That is why the A/E must learn agency procedures and expect Division 01 to differ from private-sector practice.

questions.question: A specifier on a federal project looks for the document that serves the role AIA A201 serves on private-sector work. Under which title might that federal document appear?

options.A: Supplementary Conditions
options.B: Instructions to Bidders
options.C: Contract Clauses
options.D: Agreement Form

questions.explanation: Industry guidance notes that federal contract conditions may be titled General Provisions, General Standards, Special Provisions, or Contract Clauses, and all are based on the FAR. Supplementary Conditions, Instructions to Bidders, and an agreement form are different document types, not titles industry guidance gives for federal general conditions.

questions.question: An A/E experienced with AIA-based private work assumes it will administer the construction phase of a federal project, including decisions on change orders. What does industry guidance indicate instead?

options.A: A contracting officer administers the procurement and construction phases.
options.B: The A/E administers construction, while the agency administers procurement.
options.C: The local authority having jurisdiction administers the construction phase.
options.D: The A/E administers both phases, subject to concurrence by the agency.

questions.explanation: On federal projects industry guidance says a contracting officer, either a military officer or a civilian government employee, administers both the procurement and construction phases, so the A/E lacks its usual private-sector authority. Splitting the phases with the A/E, assigning the role to a local AHJ, or keeping the A/E in charge with concurrence all misstate that difference.

questions.question: A federal agency leases floor space in a privately owned office building, and an A/E is designing the tenant improvements. Which statement about building code jurisdiction is correct?

options.A: Only the federal agency has jurisdiction, as both owner and primary regulator.
options.B: Local authorities having jurisdiction have authority over the leased space.
options.C: Local authorities have authority only if the lease expressly names them.
options.D: Only other federal agencies have authority, since local codes never reach federal work.

questions.explanation: Industry guidance explains that local building code authorities lack jurisdiction on federal property, where other federal agencies may have authority instead. On private property leased by a federal agency, however, local AHJs do have jurisdiction, without any condition tied to the lease terms, so the owner-regulator, lease-clause, and federal-only answers misapply the federal-property rule.

questions.question: Federal guide specifications may impose stricter fire protection, security, and durability requirements than typical private-sector specifications. What condition helps explain this?

options.A: Federal agencies adopt local building codes as their maximum requirements.
options.B: Contractors' commercial insurers demand stricter criteria on federal work.
options.C: The FAR requires every federal building to exceed the local building code.
options.D: The federal government self-insures and buys no commercial property insurance.

questions.explanation: Industry guidance ties the more stringent fire protection, safety, security, and durability provisions to the government being self-insuring and not buying commercial insurance for its buildings or contents. Local codes are not a federal ceiling, contractor insurers are not the driver, and industry guidance says only that federal specifications may exceed local codes, not that the FAR always requires it.

questions.question: Federal construction contracts may include provisions such as wage rates, affirmative action, and accessibility standards. What collective term does industry guidance use for this category of provisions?

options.A: Social value regulations
options.B: Special provisions
options.C: Public interest clauses
options.D: Equal opportunity clauses

questions.explanation: Industry guidance groups requirements such as wage rates, affirmative action, small and minority- or women-owned business utilization, and accessibility standards under the term social value regulations. Special Provisions is one possible title for federal contract conditions, and the other two labels are not the term for this group.

questions.question: Which of the following does industry guidance cite as an example of a social value regulation in federal contracts?

options.A: Termination for convenience
options.B: Independent government estimates
options.C: Preference for American shipping
options.D: Access to records and reports

questions.explanation: Industry guidance lists preference for American shipping among its social value examples, together with wage rates, environmental regulations, affirmative action, small and minority- or women-owned business utilization, labor standards, and accessibility standards. Termination for convenience, independent government estimates, and records access are FAR contracting mechanisms, not social value provisions.

questions.question: A specifier reviewing a federal project manual finds requirements for labor standards, use of small businesses, and domestically produced construction materials. What common purpose links these requirements?

options.A: Protecting the government's rights regarding defective work
options.B: Assisting particular industries and other special interest groups
options.C: Ensuring the government can audit the contractor's own costs
options.D: Preventing conflicts among the separate parts of the FAR

questions.explanation: Industry guidance describes social value regulations, which include labor standards, small business utilization, and the Buy American provision, as aimed at assisting particular industries and other special interest groups. Protecting against defective work, auditing costs, and resolving FAR conflicts are the purposes of warranty, records-access, and Part 36 precedence provisions instead.

questions.question: A federal agency is adding a wing to a facility, and the new building automation components must match the existing system's manufacturer. How is the single brand procured?

options.A: The agency prepares a justification and approval document, with technical input from the A/E as needed.
options.B: The A/E names at least three acceptable products and adds a statement that other products are permitted.
options.C: The contractor proposes the matching brand later through the agency's substitution request procedures.
options.D: The A/E specifies performance only, and the contracting officer selects the brand after the contract award.

questions.explanation: Extending or connecting to an existing system is one of the stated exceptions to the federal prohibition on brand names; the agency documents the one-brand purchase with a justification and approval, and the A/E may have to furnish technical input for it. Listing three products describes a different exception that would not guarantee a match, and deferring the brand to substitutions or post-award selection is not the stated procedure.

questions.question: A specifier writing a federal resilient flooring section names two manufacturers' products and adds a statement that products of other manufacturers may also be used. Which change would bring this listing within one of the federal exceptions that permit brand names?

options.A: Delete the statement allowing other manufacturers, since two named products are sufficient.
options.B: Keep both names and attach a justification and approval document supporting the two choices.
options.C: Name a third acceptable product and keep the statement permitting other products.
options.D: Reduce the listing to one brand and identify it by model number as a proprietary requirement.

questions.explanation: Industry guidance permits named products in federal specifications when at least three acceptable products are listed and the text states that other manufacturers' products are allowed, so adding a third name while keeping the open statement satisfies that exception. Deleting the open statement makes the listing more restrictive, a justification and approval document belongs to the one-brand case of matching an existing system, and a single-product proprietary requirement is reserved for cases where no other product can do the job.

questions.question: A federal agency buys a particular manufacturer's brand-name lighting fixture from a multiple-award contract that offers products from many sources. When is the justification for the brand-name item required?

options.A: Before the multiple-award contract is awarded
options.B: When the order for the item is placed
options.C: When the item is first listed on the contract
options.D: When the contract's next option period begins

questions.explanation: On a multiple-award contract, the need for one manufacturer's item is decided at the time of the order, so industry guidance places the justification at order placement. Completing it before award is the rule for a single-source requirements contract, whose brand need is known before that contract is let. Industry guidance also notes that a brand-name item's presence on a multiple-award contract does not make it the only such item available, so its listing is not the trigger, and option periods are not mentioned.

questions.question: An A/E concludes that only one manufacturer's fire alarm control unit, identified by brand name and model number, can perform a required function on a federal project. How is this proprietary requirement handled?

options.A: The agency's contracting authority writes the justification, and the A/E approves its inclusion.
options.B: The A/E includes the unit without any justification as long as the phrase "or equal" is added.
options.C: The contractor justifies the unit in a submittal, and the A/E accepts or rejects the request.
options.D: The A/E provides a technical justification, and the agency approves or disapproves its inclusion.

questions.explanation: Industry guidance treats single-product proprietary specifications as exceptions for federal work, to be used only when no other product can do the task; the A/E must furnish a technical justification, and the agency decides whether the requirement goes into the specifications. The A/E does not approve its own proprietary requirement, an "or equal" phrase contradicts a single-product limit, and the decision is not deferred to contractor submittals.

questions.question: Which list puts the four classifications of reference standards for government construction in their order of preferred usage, most preferred first?

options.A: Private-sector standards, CIDs, federal specifications, military specifications
options.B: Federal specifications, CIDs, private-sector standards, military specifications
options.C: Private-sector standards, federal specifications, CIDs, military specifications
options.D: CIDs, private-sector standards, military specifications, federal specifications

questions.explanation: Industry guidance lists the four classifications in order of preferred usage: private-sector standards, commercial item descriptions (CIDs), federal specifications, and military specifications last. Swapping CIDs and federal specifications is the most tempting slip; the note that federal specifications are being replaced by private-sector standards or by CIDs is consistent with that ranking.

questions.question: A specifier cites a federal specification in PART 2 of a section by its document designation only. What additional information is usually necessary in that citation?

options.A: The issue date of the GSA Federal Supply Service index that lists it
options.B: The particular class or grade of the product within that specification
options.C: The equivalent military specification type and quality designation
options.D: The commercial item description that the specification will replace

questions.explanation: Most federal specifications are classification documents that grade products by physical and functional characteristics, so industry guidance says a reference usually must state the class or grade wanted. Naming an equivalent MIL-SPEC, a replacement CID, or an index date does not tell the contractor which level of the referenced product is required.

questions.question: Which pairing of a government reference document with the body that issues it is correct?

options.A: Military specifications, issued by the GSA Federal Supply Service
options.B: Federal specifications, issued by the US Department of Defense
options.C: Federal standards (FED-STD), issued by ANSI for federal agencies
options.D: Commercial item descriptions, issued and controlled by the GSA

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that the GSA issues and controls CIDs, that the GSA Federal Supply Service issues federal specifications and standards, and that the Department of Defense issues military specifications. The distractors swap those issuers, and ANSI is a private-sector standards developer rather than the source of FED-STD documents.

questions.question: While editing an agency guide section, an A/E finds a referenced federal specification that has not been updated in years; a current ASTM standard covers the same product and meets the agency's needs. What is the best course?

options.A: Keep the federal specification, because agency guide text always takes precedence.
options.B: Cite both documents and let the contractor choose which one will govern the work.
options.C: Use the ASTM reference instead, provided the owner has no objection.
options.D: Replace it with a military specification that covers the same type of product.

questions.explanation: Industry guidance describes government policy as favoring private-sector standards when they exist and satisfy the agency, and it says outdated federal specifications should not be used when a more current standard is available, assuming the owner does not object. Retaining the stale document ignores that policy, letting the contractor pick creates ambiguity, and military specifications rank last in preference.

questions.question: On a federal project, the A/E's mechanical and electrical consultants will produce their sections from separate software with different fonts. Why should the A/E raise this when negotiating its fee?

options.A: The agency may require one typeface for all sections and reject a mixed set.
options.B: The agency may require each consultant to submit its sections under a separate contract.
options.C: The agency may require SpecsIntact, which will not accept sections from other software.
options.D: The agency may limit each discipline to a fixed number of copies for each review.

questions.explanation: One of the fee-negotiation items is whether the agency will insist on a single typeface for every section, because printing produced by different disciplines may be refused as a mixture. Industry guidance does not say the agency splits consultants into separate contracts or that SpecsIntact rejects outside sources, and the number of review copies is a separate negotiation item unrelated to fonts.
questions.source: specification items for consideration during A/E contract fee negotiation

questions.question: A federal project's guide sections cite dozens of criteria manuals and industry standards that the A/E's library lacks. Which fee-negotiation question addresses this?

options.A: Whether the contractor must furnish copies of the standards at the preconstruction meeting
options.B: Whether the references can be deleted from each section to avoid any acquisition cost
options.C: Whether the agency will furnish copies or reimburse the cost of acquiring them
options.D: Whether the A/E may cite older editions already on hand to avoid purchasing new ones

questions.explanation: The list asks whether reference documents will have to be obtained and, if so, whether the agency will provide them or pay back their cost. Shifting the burden to the contractor, deleting references to save money, or relying on outdated editions are not items industry guidance lists, and the last two would also compromise the specifications.
questions.source: specification items for consideration during A/E contract fee negotiation

questions.question: During fee negotiation, an A/E asks a federal agency whether the agency will furnish the front-end documents or the A/E must write them. What related question should the A/E also consider?

options.A: Whether the agency's legal counsel will sign the front-end documents before bidding
options.B: What effect the answer will have on preparing the rest of the contract documents
options.C: How many bidders the agency expects will obtain the front-end documents
options.D: Whether the front-end documents will follow the AIA or the EJCDC document family

questions.explanation: Industry guidance pairs the question of who writes the front-end documents with a follow-up on how that decision will affect producing the remainder of the contract documents, since the split of that work changes the A/E's effort. Legal sign-off, bidder counts, and choice of document family are not items on the fee-negotiation list.
questions.source: specification items for consideration during A/E contract fee negotiation

questions.question: Under typical federal agency policies, how is work on the construction documents divided between the A/E and the agency?

options.A: The agency tailors the guide specifications for Divisions 01-49; the A/E adds procurement and contracting requirements.
options.B: The A/E tailors only Division 01; the agency tailors Divisions 02-49 and adds procurement and contracting requirements.
options.C: The agency's contracting officer tailors Division 01; the A/E tailors Divisions 02-49 and prepares the procurement forms.
options.D: The A/E tailors the guide specifications for Divisions 01-49; the agency adds procurement and contracting requirements.

questions.explanation: Industry guidance describes the A/E tailoring the federal guide specifications for Divisions 01 through 49 to the project, after which the agency incorporates the procurement and contracting requirements before issuing the project for procurement. Reversing those roles contradicts that description, and industry guidance does not split Division 01 from Divisions 02-49 or assign it to the contracting officer. Individual agencies vary, but this is the general pattern.
questions.source: federal government agencies’ construction documents policies

questions.question: An A/E new to federal work asks where the procurement and contracting documents and forms for an agency project originate. Which answer is accurate?

options.A: Each agency publishes its own, or joins other agencies to publish common ones.
options.B: The FAR prescribes one set of forms that every agency must use without change.
options.C: The A/E adapts its standard AIA or EJCDC forms to suit each agency's policies.
options.D: The GSA publishes a single standard set that all construction agencies must use.

questions.explanation: Industry guidance notes that every agency involved in construction has its own policies and procedures, and that each publishes its own procurement and contracting documents and forms or combines with other federal agencies to issue common ones. A single mandatory FAR or GSA form set and the A/E's own commercial forms do not match that description.
questions.source: federal government agencies’ construction documents policies

questions.question: The A/E has finished tailoring the federal guide specifications for Divisions 01-49. When are the procurement and contracting requirements incorporated into the construction documents?

options.A: After bids are opened and before the contract is awarded
options.B: At the 30 percent review, before the A/E edits Division 01
options.C: Before the agency issues the project for procurement
options.D: After procurement closes, when the conformed set is assembled
