questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that the agency incorporates the procurement and contracting requirements into the construction documents after the A/E's tailoring but before issuing the project for procurement. Waiting until bids are opened or until award would leave bidders without those requirements, and nothing in industry guidance ties this step to an early design review.
questions.source: federal government agencies’ construction documents policies

questions.question: What reason have various groups given for recommending uniform development of federal master guide specifications?

options.A: To eliminate the need for A/Es to edit guide specifications for each project
options.B: To cut duplicated effort and costs for contractors, A/Es, and manufacturers
options.C: To replace private-sector reference standards with uniform federal standards
options.D: To require every agency to adopt a single commercial master guide system

questions.explanation: Industry guidance explains that agencies originally built master guide specifications independently and that uniform development was urged to minimize duplication and make doing business with the government easier and cheaper for contractors, A/Es, manufacturers, and others. Guide specifications still must be edited for each project, government policy favors private-sector standards rather than replacing them, and no single commercial system is mandated.

questions.question: A specifier asks why most federal agency specifications can now be obtained online. What development made this possible?

options.A: The GSA Federal Supply Service's online specifications catalog
options.B: NASA's free SpecsIntact download from the Kennedy Space Center
options.C: A FAR requirement that agencies post all their guide specifications
options.D: The advent of NIBS and the WBDG Federal Facility Criteria

questions.explanation: Industry guidance credits the arrival of the National Institute of Building Sciences and the WBDG Federal Facility Criteria with putting most agency specifications online. SpecsIntact is editing software rather than the clearinghouse, the GSA Federal Supply Service is not described as hosting agency guide specifications, and industry guidance cites no FAR posting rule.

questions.question: Among federal agency document policies, which agency uses a commercially available master guide specification system?

options.A: General Services Administration (GSA)
options.B: Naval Facilities Engineering Command (NAVFAC)
options.C: National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)
options.D: Department of the Army, Corps of Engineers (COE)

questions.explanation: GSA is the agency relying on a commercially available master guide specification system. The Corps of Engineers and NAVFAC jointly publish the Unified Facilities Guide Specifications with other agencies, and NASA created SpecsIntact, so none of them is the agency flagged as using a commercial product.

questions.question: What was the origin of the WBDG Federal Facility Criteria?

options.A: It began as the Unified Facilities Criteria, prompted by conflicts among Defense Department design manuals.
options.B: It began as the SpecsIntact system, prompted by a NASA study of errors in editing project specifications.
options.C: It began as the Construction Criteria Base, prompted by problems publishing federal guide specifications.
options.D: It began as a GSA Federal Supply Service catalog, prompted by a study of outdated federal standards.

questions.explanation: Industry guidance traces the WBDG Federal Facility Criteria to the Construction Criteria Base, which grew out of a study of difficulties in publishing federal master guide specifications for construction. The Unified Facilities Criteria are DOD documents reached through the WBDG, SpecsIntact is NASA's editing software, and the GSA Federal Supply Service issues federal specifications, so none of these is its origin.

questions.question: Which organization joins USACE, NAVFAC, and NASA in jointly publishing the Unified Facilities Guide Specifications (UFGS)?

options.A: General Services Administration (GSA)
options.B: Air Force Civil Engineer Center (AFCEC)
options.C: National Institute of Building Sciences (NIBS)
options.D: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)

questions.explanation: Industry guidance names the US Army Corps of Engineers, NAVFAC, the Air Force Civil Engineer Center, and NASA as the joint publishers of the UFGS included in the WBDG Federal Facility Criteria. GSA, NIBS, and NIST appear elsewhere in the federal chapter with other roles (NIST, for example, supplies voluntary product standards through the WBDG), but none is named as a UFGS publisher.

questions.question: Which pairing of an agency with a document reachable through the WBDG system matches the list?

options.A: NIST: Standards for the Treatment of Historic Properties
options.B: NPS: Energy Star manuals for federal buildings
options.C: US Access Board: Unified Facilities Criteria and handbooks
options.D: EPA: Federal Green Construction Guide for Specifiers

questions.explanation: Industry guidance lists the EPA's Federal Green Construction Guide for Specifiers among the documents available through the WBDG Federal Facility Criteria. The other pairings are scrambled: the historic-treatment standards come from the National Park Service, the Energy Star manuals from the EPA, and the Unified Facilities Criteria from DOD, while the US Access Board supplies guidelines and standards.

questions.question: A small A/E firm with its first UFGS-based project asks how to obtain SpecsIntact. Which statement is accurate?

options.A: It is licensed by USACE to firms holding a federal design contract.
options.B: It is sold through the GSA Federal Supply Service with UFGS updates.
options.C: It is a free download from NASA's Kennedy Space Center website.
options.D: It is issued by NIBS only to registered WBDG Federal Facility users.

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that NASA created SpecsIntact and that it can be downloaded free from the NASA Kennedy Space Center website. It is not a USACE license, a GSA product, or a NIBS registration benefit, even though UFGS sections are formatted for editing within it.

questions.question: How does SpecsIntact handle the editor's notes in a UFGS section?

options.A: It embeds the notes in the section body and can delete them during printing.
options.B: It keeps the notes in a separate companion file linked to each paragraph number.
options.C: It shows the notes only in its online help, never in the section text.
options.D: It requires the user to delete the notes manually before final processing.

questions.explanation: Industry guidance explains that SpecsIntact places notes within the body of the specification section and includes a feature that removes them when the section is printed. Notes are therefore not stored in a separate file or confined to help screens, and manual deletion is unnecessary because note deletion is one of the program's listed features.

questions.question: An A/E evaluating SpecsIntact for a UFGS project wants to know what the software does. Which pair of capabilities is among SpecsIntact's features?

options.A: Automatic MasterFormat section renumbering and cost reports
options.B: Reference verification and testing requirement reports
options.C: Spell checking and product substitution request tracking
options.D: Drawing cross-referencing and keynote list generation

questions.explanation: Industry guidance lists verification that the references at the front of each section are cited, and generation of testing requirement reports, among SpecsIntact's features, along with submittal lists, paragraph renumbering, and note deletion. Cost reports, MasterFormat renumbering, substitution tracking, and drawing keynote lists are not on that list.

questions.question: An A/E is about to sign its first design contract with a federal agency. Which three determinations about the agency's master guide specifications should the A/E make before entering into the contract?

options.A: Whether they follow MasterFormat, whether they cite current standards, and who maintains them
options.B: Whether they are proprietary, whether reviewers accept edits, and when they were last revised
options.C: Whether they cover renovation work, how long they run, and whether the A/E may reformat them
options.D: Whether they exist, whether their use is required, and whether editable copies are free

questions.explanation: Industry guidance advises the A/E, before contracting, to find out whether the agency has master guide specifications, whether using them is mandatory, and whether editable copies come at no charge. The other combinations raise concerns that industry guidance either addresses elsewhere or not at all, and none matches those three threshold determinations.
questions.source: using federal government master guide specifications

questions.question: Which variable is chief among those affecting how long it takes an A/E to produce project specifications from a federal agency's guide specifications?

options.A: The number of review submittals the agency requires during design
options.B: The number of drawing sheets in the agency's construction documents
options.C: The A/E's familiarity with the agency's required methods of specifying
options.D: Whether the agency distributes its guide specifications electronically

questions.explanation: Industry guidance names the A/E's degree of familiarity with the agency's prescribed specifying methods, such as heavy reliance on reference standards and generic descriptions instead of brand names, as the chief variable. The number of reviews and the form of the guide specifications are fee-negotiation considerations, and drawing count is not mentioned, so none of these is the chief factor.
questions.source: using federal government master guide specifications

questions.question: An agency's guide specifications use section numbers and titles that differ considerably from the current edition of MasterFormat. What is the A/E usually expected to do?

options.A: Renumber every section to the current MasterFormat edition
options.B: Follow the numbering and titling the agency defines
options.C: Use the numbering from the A/E's own office master guide
options.D: Use MasterFormat for new sections and agency numbers for others

questions.explanation: Industry guidance acknowledges that agency guide specifications may depart from CSI practice and MasterFormat, and it says that when they do, the A/E is usually expected to use the agency's numbers and titles. Converting to MasterFormat, substituting the office master's scheme, or mixing systems would depart from what the agency requires.
questions.source: using federal government master guide specifications

questions.question: After finishing edits to an agency guide section, the A/E notices the index at the front of the section. Unless the agency requires otherwise, what does industry guidance say to do with it?

options.A: Keep it and update its page references
options.B: Move it into the project manual's table of contents
options.C: Convert it into a list of the section's editing notes
options.D: Delete it from the section

questions.explanation: Industry guidance directs that the index at the front of each section be removed once editing is finished, unless the agency instructs otherwise, and notes that SpecsIntact can generate an index electronically. Retaining and updating it, relocating it to the table of contents, or converting it to notes are not the guidance.

questions.question: An agency requires paper submittal of marked-up guide sections, and a junior specifier plans to mark retained text with a highlighter. Why should this be avoided?

options.A: Some highlighting reproduces as solid black on photocopies.
options.B: Agency reviewers reserve highlighting for their own comments.
options.C: Highlighted text is read as deleted text by most agency reviewers.
options.D: Highlighting is reserved for bracketed choices the A/E must make.

questions.explanation: Industry guidance warns against using a highlighter on review copies because some highlighting copies as solid black and obscures the text. The other reasons are invented; the related guidance is that handwritten changes be dark enough to scan clearly and that agency electronic-markup rules be followed.

questions.question: When editing the list of references at the beginning of an agency guide section, which approach follows industry guidance?

options.A: Keep every standard on the master list so that the agency's reference record stays complete
options.B: Keep all listed standards but label the ones no longer cited as for information only
options.C: List only standards still cited, each with its current issue date unless told otherwise
options.D: List only standards still cited, omitting dates so that the latest edition always governs

questions.explanation: Industry guidance says the references list should be trimmed to the standards that remain in the edited text, and each should carry its current issue or revision date unless there is a specific reason for an older one or the agency directs otherwise. Retaining uncited standards, with or without labels, contradicts that instruction, and dropping dates removes the edition control industry guidance calls for.

questions.question: A federal project needs a section for which the agency has no guide specification, and the A/E's office master version names a single manufacturer. What is the best course?

options.A: Insert the office master section unchanged, keeping the A/E's own format, numbering, and named product
options.B: Prepare a new section in agency format and numbering, open to competition among current standard products
options.C: Ask the agency to write the section, because agencies are obligated to furnish all of the technical sections
options.D: Omit the section and describe the work in general notes on the drawings to avoid naming any product

questions.explanation: When no agency guide specification exists, industry guidance makes the A/E responsible for preparing the section from other resources, conforming to the agency's format and numbering, avoiding proprietary or restrictive requirements, and basing it on standard products and current models. Reusing the single-manufacturer office section violates those requirements, shifting the work to the agency contradicts the A/E's stated responsibility, and dropping the section leaves required work unspecified.

questions.question: At which design-phase milestones does a federal agency often want reviews of the A/E's documents?

options.A: 30, 60, and 90 percent, plus final completion
options.B: 35, 65, and 95 percent, plus final completion
options.C: 25, 50, and 75 percent, plus final completion
options.D: 30, 50, and 90 percent, plus final completion

questions.explanation: Industry guidance lists 30, 50, and 90 percent reviews followed by a final completion review as the milestones agencies commonly want during design. The other sequences are plausible-sounding intervals that do not match recommended practice, which ties specific submittal content to each of its four stages.

questions.question: For the 30 percent design review on a federal project, which submittal matches one of the options industry guidance describes for that stage?

options.A: A marked-up copy of the agency guide specifications with unneeded pages deleted
options.B: A single section in final form as a sample of the completed specifications
options.C: A list of sections generated from the agency's master list of section titles
options.D: A typed rough draft of every specification section needed for the project

questions.explanation: At 30 percent, industry guidance calls for either a section list drawn from the agency-furnished master list of titles or outline specifications identifying products. A marked-up guide specification and a typed rough draft are 50 percent options, and a single final-form sample section is a 90 percent option.

questions.question: At the 90 percent review, an A/E will resubmit its marked-up copy of the agency guide specification. What should this resubmittal contain?

options.A: Every page of the guide, even pages that may be deleted later
options.B: The pages being kept, with any deleted pages removed from the set
options.C: The paragraphs revised in response to 50 percent comments
options.D: The sections reviewers flagged, with the written responses

questions.explanation: Industry guidance specifies that a 90 percent resubmittal of the marked-up guide specification cover the complete document with all of its pages, even those that may eventually be dropped. Removing deleted pages, sending only revised paragraphs, or limiting the set to flagged sections would not give reviewers the complete document industry guidance describes for that milestone.

questions.question: Reviewers return no comments on the final typed electronic copy of a federal project's specifications. What happens next?

options.A: The A/E advertises the project for bids.
options.B: The agency advertises the project for bids.
options.C: The A/E makes a compliance-check submittal.
options.D: The agency schedules another 90 percent review.

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that if reviewers have no comments on the final electronic copy, the agency then advertises the project for bids. Advertising is the agency's act rather than the A/E's, a compliance check is associated with significant changes rather than a clean final review, and there is no reason to repeat an earlier milestone.

questions.question: On a federal project, the fire protection reviewer and the HVAC reviewer issue comments that conflict with each other. Who should resolve the conflict?

options.A: The A/E's project specifier
options.B: The agency's contracting officer
options.C: The agency's project manager
options.D: The lead architectural reviewer

questions.explanation: Industry guidance recognizes that separate discipline reviewers can produce conflicting requirements and assigns their resolution to the agency's project manager. The A/E must respond to comments but does not arbitrate between agency reviewers, and industry guidance does not give that role to the contracting officer or to any one discipline's reviewer.

questions.question: A plumbing reviewer's comment on a federal project is minor, and the A/E has already made the requested change. How should the A/E respond to the comment?

options.A: Not at all, since the revised documents show the change
options.B: Orally, at the next scheduled review meeting
options.C: In writing, but only if the A/E disagrees with it
options.D: In writing, usually on a form the agency provides

questions.explanation: Industry guidance requires a written response to every reviewer comment, typically on an agency-furnished form, regardless of how minor the comment is or whether the A/E agrees. Relying on the revised documents alone, answering orally, or responding only to disputed comments falls short of that requirement.

questions.question: After incorporating review comments, the A/E has made significant changes to a federal project's drawings and specifications. What is usually required?

options.A: A compliance-check submittal
options.B: A repeat of the 30 percent review
options.C: A new A/E fee negotiation
options.D: A justification and approval document

questions.explanation: Industry guidance notes that a compliance-check submittal is usually required after significant changes. Restarting the review cycle at 30 percent is not called for, fee renegotiation is not described as automatic, and a justification and approval document relates to brand-name procurement rather than design review.

questions.question: A federal agency requires printed review copies of the contract documents to go to several reviewing offices. How is responsibility for distributing them determined?

options.A: By the agency alone, because review copies become government records
options.B: By the terms of the agreement, so it should be addressed in negotiation
options.C: By the A/E alone, because it produces and prints the review documents
options.D: By the FAR, which assigns review distribution to the contracting officer

questions.explanation: Industry guidance says either the A/E or the agency may handle distribution of review copies, depending on their agreement, and because the task affects time and expense it should be considered during negotiation. Assigning it automatically to one party, or to the contracting officer under the FAR, is not supported by industry guidance.
questions.source: distribution of documents for the review process

questions.question: A local military facility contracts directly with a local A/E for a building project that is not subject to USACE district jurisdiction. Which specifications might the A/E use?

options.A: The installation's own guide specification version, or the A/E's office master
options.B: The USACE Washington, DC, guide specifications, used without any local modification
options.C: The USACE district office's supplemented and modified guide specifications
options.D: The WBDG Federal Facility Criteria masters, used in place of agency guides

questions.explanation: Industry guidance explains that when a local military facility contracts directly with a local A/E for work outside USACE district control, the facility may have its own version of the guide specifications or may let the A/E use its office masters. The DC-published guides and the district-supplemented versions describe the normal USACE route, not this direct-contract case. WBDG is a distribution channel for jointly published guides, not a mandated replacement.

questions.question: An A/E accustomed to private-sector work plans to adapt its office masters, which list three named manufacturers per product, for its first federal agency project. Given the policies most federal agencies share, what should the A/E expect?

options.A: Three named manufacturers plus an "or equal" clause are the norm
options.B: Named manufacturers are acceptable in Part 2 if they are listed alphabetically
options.C: Naming manufacturers or brands is barred except in special circumstances
options.D: Named manufacturers are required wherever the agency guide is silent

questions.explanation: One of the common traits industry guidance lists for federal agencies is that the A/E may not name manufacturers or brand names for products except in special circumstances. The private-sector habit of listing three manufacturers with an or-equal clause, or listing them alphabetically in Part 2, does not carry over. Nothing in industry guidance makes naming mandatory where a guide is silent.

questions.question: An A/E is preparing the project manual for a federal agency. Given the policies most federal agencies share, how are procurement and contracting requirements most often handled?

options.A: The A/E drafts them from its office masters for agency review
options.B: The agency issues them separately and keeps them out of the manual
options.C: The A/E adapts AIA or EJCDC forms to meet federal requirements
options.D: The agency issues its own and requires them in the manual

questions.explanation: Industry guidance notes that most federal agencies publish their own procurement and contracting requirements and require that they be bound into the project manual. The A/E therefore does not draft them from office masters or adapt private-sector AIA or EJCDC forms. They are also not kept outside the manual; inclusion is required.

questions.question: At a kickoff meeting, an owner suggests that a performance bond and the contractor's insurance are interchangeable, since each shields the owner from occurrences beyond its control. How should the A/E characterize the two?

options.A: Seemingly similar purposes, and essentially the same protection method
options.B: Seemingly similar purposes, but very different protection methods
options.C: Clearly different purposes, but essentially the same protection method
options.D: Clearly different purposes, and very different protection methods

questions.explanation: Industry guidance acknowledges that bonds and insurance may look as if they serve similar purposes, since both protect a party against acts and events largely outside its control, but stresses that their methods of protection are very different. They are therefore not interchangeable. Calling the methods the same, or calling the purposes clearly different, contradicts that overview.

questions.question: A specifier is sorting bond requirements within a project manual. How are the three basic construction bond types classified?

options.A: Bid bond as a procurement requirement; performance and payment bonds as contract documents
options.B: Bid and performance bonds as procurement requirements; payment bond as a contract document
options.C: Bid bond as a contract document; performance and payment bonds as procurement requirements
options.D: All three as procurement requirements until the owner-contractor agreement is executed

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that the bid bond, when used, is a procurement requirement, while performance and payment bonds are classified as contract documents. The bid bond secures the bid itself, whereas performance and payment bonds back the contractor's obligations under the contract. The other options shift one or more bonds into the wrong category.

questions.question: An owner wants a two-year maintenance bond on a new roofing system, in addition to the standard bonds for the project. Where are bonds of this kind generally called for?

options.A: In the instructions for procurement, alongside the bid bond
options.B: In the supplementary conditions, with the performance bond
options.C: In the individual specification section covering that work
options.D: In the owner-contractor agreement, with the payment bond

questions.explanation: Industry guidance distinguishes the three basic bonds from other bonds, such as warranty or maintenance bonds, which are generally required by individual specification sections. The instructions for procurement address bid bonds, and the supplementary conditions address performance and payment bonds, so neither is the usual home for a work-specific maintenance bond.

questions.question: A surety's premium for performance and payment bonds is based on the bonded contract amount and generally falls within what range?

options.A: Between 1 and 5 percent
options.B: Between 2 and 10 percent
options.C: Between 0.1 and 0.5 percent
options.D: Between 0.3 and 2 percent

questions.explanation: Industry guidance gives the typical premium as roughly 0.3 to 2 percent of the bonded contract amount, varying with the type of risk, the financial strength of the principal and any indemnitors, past claims history, and the extent of the project. The higher ranges overstate typical bond cost, and 0.1 to 0.5 percent understates the upper end.

questions.question: A contractor seeking performance and payment bonds is a closely held corporation. With whom does the surety typically have a separate indemnity agreement?

options.A: The obligee, which agrees to share any losses with the surety
options.B: The principal and its individual owners, officers, or operators
options.C: The principal only, since its owners are shielded from liability
options.D: The first-tier subcontractors that the principal intends to use

questions.explanation: Industry guidance explains that the surety usually holds a separate indemnity agreement with the principal and, when the principal is closely held, with its individual owners, officers, or operators as well. The corporate form does not shield those individuals under that arrangement. The obligee is the owner being protected, not an indemnitor, and subcontractors are not parties to it.

questions.question: Comparing a surety bond with an insurance policy, which statement correctly describes the surety's position?

options.A: The surety accepts primary responsibility to pay valid claims, as insurers do
options.B: The surety absorbs losses as a priced risk, recovering them through premiums
options.C: The surety is liable only secondarily and expects reimbursement from indemnitors
options.D: The surety shares liability equally with the principal from the very outset of work

questions.explanation: Industry guidance compares the surety to a cosigner: the principal stays primarily liable, and the surety is only secondarily liable after the principal defaults. In theory the surety should not pay out of its own pocket because the principal and individual indemnitors must reimburse it. Primary responsibility for claims is the insurer's model, which contrasts with suretyship.

questions.question: With its bid, a contractor proposes to furnish performance and payment bonds through a wealthy private individual instead of a bonding company. How is such an offer generally handled?

options.A: Reject it; the surety should hold a license in the project's state
options.B: Accept it if the individual's net worth exceeds the penal amount
options.C: Accept it if the individual is licensed in the contractor's home state
options.D: Reject it unless the A/E verifies the individual's AM Best rating

questions.explanation: Industry guidance says the surety should be licensed by the insurance department of the state where the project is located, and offers to bond through an individual or an unlicensed company should generally be rejected. Personal net worth does not substitute for that licensing, and licensing in the contractor's home state is not the stated test. AM Best rates insurance companies, so it is not a remedy for an individual surety.

questions.question: An owner's insurance advisor wants sureties whose Best's Key Rating Guide classification, suggests that the carrier is financially excellent. Which minimum rating fits that description?

options.A: B+ or better
options.B: B or better
options.C: C- or better
options.D: A- or better

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that an A- or better rating in Best's Key Rating Guide suggests a financially excellent carrier. The guide's classes run from A for superior down to C- for fair, so B-level and C- ratings fall below the threshold industry guidance associates with excellent financial strength.

questions.question: An A/E is preparing bidding documents for a federal agency project and must identify which sureties are acceptable to the government. Which source applies?

options.A: Best's Key Rating Guide, limited to sureties holding A- or better ratings
options.B: The Treasury's Bureau of the Fiscal Service annual certified listing
options.C: The Standard & Poor's and Fitch annual ratings of surety companies
options.D: The approved surety roster kept by each USACE district office

questions.explanation: Industry guidance notes that the federal government applies its own surety criteria, with the Treasury Department's Bureau of the Fiscal Service publishing an annual list of certified sureties acceptable for federal work. Best's, Standard & Poor's, and Fitch ratings are private rating services useful on other projects but are not the federal acceptance list. Industry guidance does not describe any USACE district surety roster.

questions.question: The federal government's annual list of sureties acceptable for federal projects is published in which document?

options.A: The January 1 Federal Register
options.B: The July 1 Federal Register
options.C: Best's Key Rating Guide
options.D: The WBDG Federal Facility Criteria

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that the US Treasury Department's Bureau of the Fiscal Service publishes its listing of certified sureties for federal projects each year in the July 1 Federal Register, and also posts it on the Treasury website. January 1 is a near-miss date. Best's Key Rating Guide is AM Best's private rating publication, and WBDG distributes federal guide specifications, not surety listings.

questions.question: A specifier is placing bond requirements in the project manual. Where do bid bond information and performance and payment bond requirements belong, respectively?

options.A: Supplementary conditions; procurement requirements
options.B: Procurement requirements; Division 01 general requirements
options.C: General conditions; supplementary conditions
options.D: Procurement requirements; supplementary conditions

questions.explanation: Industry guidance places bid bond information in the procurement requirements because it governs the bidding process, and it puts performance and payment bond requirements in the supplementary conditions. Division 01 and the general conditions are not the locations industry guidance gives for either item, and the first option reverses the correct pairing.
questions.source: obtaining bond information from the owner

questions.question: An A/E is designing its fourth branch library for the same municipal owner and plans to copy the bond requirements from the previous library's documents into the new manual. What is the best course of action?

options.A: Request this project's bond information early enough to include it
options.B: Reuse the prior requirements unless the owner objects in writing
options.C: Ask the low bidder's surety to set the requirements after bid opening
options.D: Issue the prior requirements now and correct them later by addendum

questions.explanation: Industry guidance directs the A/E to request bond information for each project, even for a repeat client or an owner building multiple projects, and to do so early enough for the owner to respond before the project manual is completed. Reusing old requirements by default, deferring to a bidder's surety, or planning to fix them by addendum all skip that owner request.
questions.source: obtaining bond information from the owner

questions.question: An architect uses AIA Document G612, Owner's Instructions to the Architect, to collect the owner's bonding requirements. Which description of the form is accurate?

options.A: Part A: bidding procedures, including bid bond information
options.B: Part B: construction contract, including insurance requirements
options.C: Part B: bidding procedures, including bid bond information
options.D: Part A: construction contract, including bid bond information

questions.explanation: Industry guidance describes G612 as a two-part form: Part A relates to the construction contract and requests the project's insurance and bond requirements, while Part B relates to bidding procedures and includes bid bond information. Options that put bidding procedures in Part A, the construction contract in Part B, or bid bond information in Part A reverse that structure.
questions.source: obtaining bond information from the owner

questions.question: A bond requirement on a small commercial project drew only two bids, and several capable local contractors chose not to bid at all. What is the most likely explanation?

options.A: Bid bonds were billed separately, making bidding too costly for them
options.B: Bond premiums had to be paid by the bidders before bids were opened
options.C: Bidders lacking established surety relationships were discouraged
options.D: Bonds exposed bidders personally to mechanic's liens on the project

questions.explanation: Industry guidance notes that on residential and small commercial contracts, some contractors have no established relationship with a surety and may be discouraged from bidding by a bond requirement; screening out contractors who cannot qualify is one function of the requirement. The premium is carried in the bid price rather than paid before opening, and bonds protect against liens rather than create lien exposure.

questions.question: Among the advantages of a fully bonded project listed, which one is attributed to the indemnity agreement?

options.A: Added incentive for the contractor's principals to perform properly
options.B: Protection of the owner against mechanic's liens on the project
options.C: Protection of the owner against withdrawal of a favorable bid
options.D: Satisfaction of statutory requirements for publicly funded work

questions.explanation: Industry guidance credits the indemnity agreement with motivating the contractor's principals to perform, because they may be personally liable to the surety for amounts it pays. Lien protection flows from payment of subcontractors and suppliers, protection against bid withdrawal comes from the bid bond, and meeting statutory requirements is an advantage of bonding generally.

questions.question: An owner with no separate legal counsel or insurance adviser follows the A/E's informal comment that bonds are unnecessary, and the contractor later defaults. What exposure does this create for the A/E?

options.A: The A/E becomes the obligee under any replacement performance bond
options.B: The A/E takes on the surety's duty to complete the defaulted work
options.C: The A/E must refund the fees it earned for bidding-phase services
options.D: The owner may claim the A/E's advice on bonding was insufficient

questions.explanation: Industry guidance warns that unless the owner is expressly cautioned, it may rely on the A/E's statements without further investigation, especially without its own counsel, and may later argue the A/E's bonding advice was inadequate if an unbonded contractor defaults. That is why the owner should always be told to get an attorney's or surety adviser's counsel. The A/E does not become an obligee or a surety.

questions.question: Under a traditional bid bond with a penal amount of 5 percent of the bid, the selected bidder at $2,000,000 refuses without justification to sign the contract. The next-lowest bid is $2,150,000. The most the owner can recover from the surety is:
questions.explanation: Industry guidance lets the owner seek the difference between the principal's bid and the next-lowest bid, but only up to the bid bond's penal amount. The difference here is $150,000, while the penal amount is 5 percent of $2,000,000, or $100,000, so recovery is capped at $100,000. The other figures either ignore the cap or combine the numbers incorrectly.

questions.question: The selected bidder declines to sign the contract. In which situation would the bid bond most likely be discharged, leaving the surety with no liability?

options.A: The bidder finds its price far below the others but proves no mistake
options.B: The owner accepted the bid after the stated acceptance period expired
options.C: The other bidders have withdrawn, so the owner must rebid the work
options.D: The owner tenders an agreement at the exact price and terms bid

questions.explanation: Industry guidance lists late acceptance beyond the time set in the procurement documents as a condition that can discharge the bid bond, along with a proven mistake or a unilateral change in terms by the owner. A low price without a provable mistake is exactly the reluctance the bond guards against. Withdrawal of other bidders increases the surety's exposure, and a tender on the bid terms does not justify refusal.

questions.question: Under a traditional bid bond, the selected bidder refuses without justification to sign, and every other bidder has already withdrawn, so the owner must rebid the work. For what may the surety be responsible?

options.A: The cost of rebidding only, with no liability for any price difference
options.B: Nothing, because no next-lowest bid remains to set the owner's damages
options.C: The full penal amount, regardless of the outcome of the reprocurement
options.D: The difference to the low rebid price, and possibly the rebid's cost

questions.explanation: Industry guidance addresses this case directly: when the owner must rebid, the surety answers for the difference between the principal's bid and the low bid on the reprocurement and may also owe the cost of the reprocurement. The absence of a remaining next bidder does not end liability. The traditional bid bond pays actual damages rather than an automatic full penal amount.

questions.question: A $5,000,000 contract with a 100 percent performance bond goes into default after $3,200,000 has been properly paid. Completing the work costs $2,300,000. The surety's liability is limited to:
questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that whatever completion method is used, the surety receives credit for the unpaid contract balance at default and owes only the excess cost to complete. The balance is $1,800,000, so the excess is $2,300,000 minus $1,800,000, or $500,000. The full completion cost, the balance itself, and the penal sum all ignore that credit.

questions.question: The owner's payments to the contractor were proper, but during construction the owner materially expanded the bonded work's scope without the surety's consent, and the contractor then defaulted. What relief may the surety claim on the owner's performance bond claim?

options.A: None, because the bond covers any changes the owner directs
options.B: Relief limited to any amount the owner overpaid the contractor
options.C: Relief for the increase in the contract sum over the original
options.D: A demand that the owner first pursue the A/E over the scope change

questions.explanation: Industry guidance explains that the performance bond protects against the contractor's default, not the owner's, and that a material scope increase without the surety's consent lets the surety claim relief for the amount by which the contract sum grew over the original. Relief for overpayment is the other example, but the owner's payments here were proper. The bond does not absorb unconsented owner changes, and the A/E is not a party the owner must pursue first.

questions.question: After a valid default claim, the surety's investigation finds the contractor's work fully satisfactory and its problems purely financial. Which course is suited to this situation?

options.A: Pay the owner the full penal amount and close out the bond
options.B: Have the owner finish the work and pay the full cost to complete
options.C: Arrange a completion contractor to work directly for the A/E
options.D: Finance the contractor, under careful supervision, to finish

questions.explanation: Industry guidance says that when the work is satisfactory and the trouble is only financial, the surety may finance the contractor to pay subcontractors, suppliers, and payroll so it can finish, doing so only under careful supervision. A completion contractor would work directly for the owner, not the A/E. Whatever completion method is used, the surety gets credit for the contract balance and owes only the excess cost to complete, so neither a full penal payout nor the full completion cost is its obligation.

questions.question: A sub-subcontractor on a bonded project has not been paid by the first-tier subcontractor. What notice do most payment bonds require of such a remote claimant?

options.A: Written notice to the contractor within 90 days of its last furnishing
options.B: Written notice to the owner within 90 days of substantial completion
options.C: Written notice to the surety within 30 days of its last furnishing
options.D: Written notice to the contractor within 90 days of final payment

questions.explanation: Industry guidance says most payment bonds require remote claimants to notify the contractor in writing within 90 days of the last date they furnished labor or material. The notice protects a contractor that already paid the first-tier subcontractor. The other options change the recipient, the period, or the triggering event.

questions.question: A supplier makes a payment bond claim for the unpaid purchase price of a crane that a subcontractor bought and now rotates among several of its jobs. How is the claim generally treated?

options.A: Covered, since the supplier furnished equipment to a bonded subcontractor
options.B: Covered, provided the supplier gave notice within the bond's time limit
options.C: Not covered; capital goods used across projects are outside the bond
options.D: Not covered, since payment bonds protect only first-tier subcontractors

questions.explanation: Industry guidance limits payment bond coverage to labor and material on the bonded project and states that the purchase price of capital goods or inventory usable on multiple projects is generally not a bond obligation. Timely notice does not convert an excluded item into a covered one. Coverage is not limited to first-tier parties, since sub-subcontractors and suppliers to subcontractors are generally covered.

questions.question: An owner wants a bid bond form under which it receives the bond's full face amount if the selected bidder fails to execute the agreement, even if that exceeds the gap to the next-lowest bid. Which form provides this?

options.A: EJCDC C-435, Bid Bond (Damages)
options.B: EJCDC C-430, Bid Bond (Penal Sum)
options.C: AIA Document A310, Bid Bond
options.D: ConsensusDocs 262, Bid Bond

questions.explanation: Industry guidance describes EJCDC C-430 as the penal-sum form, paying the owner the bond's face amount on the selected bidder's failure to execute, which can exceed the actual bid difference. EJCDC C-435 pays actual damages up to the bond sum, and industry guidance says AIA A310 and ConsensusDocs 262 follow that same traditional damages structure.

questions.question: A specifier wants evidence that the agent who signs a bond on the surety's behalf has authority to bind the surety. What should be required, and where?

options.A: A power of attorney filed with the bond, required in the instructions for procurement
options.B: A certificate of authority filed with the bid, required in the supplementary conditions
options.C: A surety rating letter filed with the bond, required in Division 01 general requirements
options.D: A notarized agent license filed at contract signing, required by the agreement form

questions.explanation: Industry guidance says authority to bind the surety is usually shown by a power of attorney naming the authorized agent, and the instructions for procurement should require a copy to be filed with the signed bond. A rating letter or certificate does not prove an agent's signing authority, and the supplementary conditions, Division 01, and the agreement are not where industry guidance puts this requirement.

questions.question: The bidding package for a project calls for performance and payment bonds but includes no bond form. What is the likely consequence, and how could it have been avoided?

options.A: The surety's standard form governs; specify a surety rated A- or better
options.B: The A/E must draft a form; add bond language to the general conditions
options.C: AIA forms apply by default; reference them in Division 01 requirements
options.D: The form becomes negotiable; include the forms in procurement documents

questions.explanation: Industry guidance warns that when no form is included, the bond form can become a matter for negotiation among the owner, contractor, and surety, and that including the required bond forms in the procurement documents avoids this. No form applies by default, and industry guidance does not shift drafting to the A/E; bond form choices carry significant legal consequences for the owner and its counsel.

questions.question: A first-time client asks the A/E to recommend the commercial general liability limits the contractor should carry. Who should be the source of that recommendation?

options.A: The A/E, drawing on limits used on similar past projects
options.B: The contractor's insurance broker, confirmed at bid time
options.C: The owner's legal counsel and the owner's insurance advisor
options.D: The specifier, using defaults stated in the general conditions

questions.explanation: Industry guidance assigns all recommendations on construction insurance to the owner's legal counsel and insurance advisor and says the A/E should neither act as an insurance advisor nor set or recommend limits. The contractor's broker serves the contractor rather than the owner, and the specifier, as part of the A/E team, is equally barred from determining limits.

questions.question: The A/E gives the owner AIA Document G612 or EJCDC C-052 to obtain the owner's insurance instructions. Where are the resulting insurance requirements incorporated?

options.A: The instructions for procurement
options.B: The supplementary conditions
options.C: Division 01 general requirements
options.D: The owner-contractor agreement

questions.explanation: Industry guidance describes G612 and C-052 as insurance information request forms used to get the owner's instructions for incorporating insurance requirements into the supplementary conditions. Procurement instructions, Division 01, and the agreement are not the destination industry guidance names for these instructions.

questions.question: What is the owner's first line of financial defense on a construction project?

options.A: A fully bonded contractor
options.B: An adequately insured contractor
options.C: The owner's builder's risk policy
options.D: Retainage held from progress payments

questions.explanation: Industry guidance calls an adequately insured contractor the owner's first line of financial defense, with the owner protected partly by requiring specific coverages at adequate limits. Bonds, owner-purchased policies, and retainage are other protections, but none is the item industry guidance gives that label.

questions.question: An owner assumes that the coverages it will require the contractor to carry make any insurance of its own unnecessary. How should the A/E respond?

options.A: Agree; required contractor coverage fully protects the owner
options.B: Agree, provided the owner is named on each certificate
options.C: Caution that contractor coverage may not meet all owner needs
options.D: Caution that contractor coverage protects only the contractor

questions.explanation: Industry guidance acknowledges that the contractor's required coverage supplies most of the protection both parties need but warns that it may not cover everything the owner needs, and that several policies exist for owners who want coverage beyond it. Contractor coverage does protect the owner and third parties to a degree, so saying it protects only the contractor overstates the limitation.

questions.question: The insurance that provides most of the protection both the owner and the contractor need during construction is the coverage required by which part of the documents?

options.A: Division 01 general requirements
options.B: The instructions for procurement
options.C: The individual specification sections
options.D: The conditions of the contract

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that the coverage required by the conditions of the contract supplies most of the protection the owner and contractor need during construction. Insurance requirements are contractual matters, so they are set in the general and supplementary conditions, not in Division 01, procurement instructions, or technical sections.

questions.question: The contractor's own excavator is damaged at the site, and the contractor submits the loss under its liability policy. How is the claim treated?

options.A: Not covered; it does not insure the insured's own equipment
options.B: Covered, because the loss occurred at the project site
options.C: Covered, because the contractor is the named insured
options.D: Not covered, because the policy applies only away from the site

questions.explanation: Industry guidance explains that liability policies protect the named insured against legal liability to others and do not cover damage to or loss of the insured's own products, machinery, or equipment. Being the named insured or having the loss occur on site does not change that. The off-site rationale is also wrong, since industry guidance says liability coverage is effective only at the project site.

questions.question: The AIA, EJCDC, and ConsensusDocs general conditions assign the duty to provide liability insurance to which party, and why?

options.A: The owner, because it holds title to the project property
options.B: The A/E, because it administers the construction contract
options.C: The contractor, because owners cannot purchase liability coverage
options.D: The contractor, because it is responsible for site activities

questions.explanation: Industry guidance notes that all three families of general conditions require the contractor to provide liability insurance because the contractor is responsible for what happens on the project site. Industry guidance ties the requirement to the contractor's control of site activities, not to any inability of owners to obtain coverage. The A/E's contract administration role does not make it the party providing this coverage.

questions.question: As industry guidance describes liability policies, which statement about their scope is accurate?

options.A: They pay the insured's own losses at the site, regardless of fault
options.B: They cover the insured's activities at any location it operates
options.C: They respond to others' claims arising from the insured's site work
options.D: They compensate for damage to covered property from insured perils

questions.explanation: Industry guidance describes liability policies as protecting the named insured from losses arising from legal liability to others for its activities, with coverage effective only at the project site. They do not pay the insured's own first-party losses, and compensating for damage to covered property from insured perils describes property insurance, not liability insurance.

questions.question: A specifier is editing the supplementary conditions for a project on which one small subcontractor is exempt from the state's workers' compensation law. What should the contract documents require of that subcontractor?

options.A: A copy of its state exemption certificate in lieu of any coverage
options.B: Additional insured status under the contractor's compensation policy
options.C: Voluntary workers' compensation insurance having the statutory effect
options.D: Employer's liability coverage only, without workers' compensation

questions.explanation: Industry guidance says contractors exempt from the statute should be made to carry voluntary workers' compensation insurance, which produces the same result as legally mandated coverage and keeps the owner protected from employee injury suits. An exemption certificate leaves that protection missing, employer's liability coverage fills gaps in non-comprehensive statutes rather than replacing workers' compensation, and this coverage is not extended through additional insured status.

questions.question: The state where a project is located has a compensation statute that does not reach every injury or every category of recoverable damages. Which policy covers the resulting immunity gap?

options.A: Employer's liability insurance
options.B: Umbrella excess liability insurance
options.C: Owner's protective liability insurance
options.D: Other states coverage

questions.explanation: When a state's compensation law leaves some injuries or categories of damages outside its reach, industry guidance says the resulting immunity gap is covered by employer's liability insurance, which the AIA, EJCDC, and ConsensusDocs general conditions require the contractor to carry. Umbrella coverage adds limits above other liability policies, owner's protective coverage addresses the owner's liability for the contractor's work, and other states coverage extends workers' compensation to additional states.

questions.question: A contractor's employees will fabricate subassemblies at its shop in one state and install them at a project site in another. Which term describes workers' compensation coverage that extends to every jurisdiction named in the policy's endorsement schedule?

options.A: Monopolistic fund coverage
options.B: Difference-in-conditions coverage
options.C: Broad form coverage
options.D: Other states coverage

questions.explanation: Industry guidance notes that compliance with state workers' compensation laws reaches subassemblies fabricated outside the project's state and that the contractor's insurance advisor should recommend coverage wherever employees work; coverage reaching all states in the endorsement schedule is called other states coverage. Monopolistic fund states require a compulsory state fund, difference-in-conditions fills builder's risk gaps, and broad form describes a type of hold-harmless clause.

questions.question: Site work for a new hospital requires rock blasting and deep excavation with temporary shoring next to an occupied building. To cover claims from the blasting and from structural failure when shoring is pulled, what change to the contractor's commercial general liability coverage should the owner require?

options.A: Conversion of the policy from an occurrence form to a claims-made form
options.B: Removal of the exclusion for explosion, collapse, and underground damage
options.C: Addition of an installation floater endorsement covering the temporary shoring
options.D: Modification of the general aggregate so that it applies only to this project

questions.explanation: Industry guidance explains that the basic CGL form carries the XCU exclusion (explosion, collapse, underground property damage) and that it must be removed to cover blasting, collapse from excavation or removal of shoring, and underground damage from mechanical excavation. A claims-made form weakens the owner's protection, an installation floater insures a subcontractor's materials during installation, and a per-project aggregate does not restore excluded perils.

questions.question: During construction of an addition, a subcontractor's incorrectly installed through-wall flashing lets water into the adjoining occupied building and damages a tenant's furnishings. How would the contractor's general liability policy typically respond?

options.A: It would cover the tenant's damaged furnishings but not the cost to redo the flashing
options.B: It would cover the cost to redo the flashing but not the tenant's damaged furnishings
options.C: It would cover both the flashing rework and the tenant's damaged furnishings in full
options.D: It would cover neither, since faulty workmanship is excluded from such policies

questions.explanation: Industry guidance stresses that a general liability policy pays for damage that results from defective work but not for repairing the defective work itself, so the tenant's furnishings are the covered loss while redoing the flashing remains the contractor's cost. The second option reverses that rule, the third ignores it, and the fourth overstates the exclusion, since industry guidance lists faulty workmanship among the damages these policies broadly address.

questions.question: An owner learns that its contractor carries one CGL policy for all of its jobs, so claims paid on other jobs during the policy year could erode the coverage shown on the certificate furnished for this work. What should the owner require?

options.A: A claims-made policy form so that each claim is tied to its own policy period
options.B: AIA Document G715 attached to the ACORD 25 certificate of liability insurance
options.C: A higher products and completed operations aggregate stated in Division 01
options.D: A per-project general aggregate, required in the supplementary conditions

questions.explanation: Industry guidance notes that the general aggregate caps everything the policy pays except products and completed operations claims, so claims already paid can leave less than the certificate shows; it recommends modifying the general aggregate to apply to each project and identifying that in the supplementary conditions. Claims-made forms weaken the owner's position, G715 adds subjects such as pollution liability, and the completed operations aggregate is separate from the general aggregate.

questions.question: The contractor's superintendent uses a personal pickup to run to a supplier for fasteners and causes an accident on the way. Which coverage should the specifications have required to address the contractor's liability exposure?

options.A: Owned-vehicle coverage under the contractor's general property and equipment policy
options.B: Non-owned, rented, or hired vehicle coverage within the contractor's auto insurance
options.C: Products and completed operations coverage under the contractor's general liability
options.D: Employer's liability coverage under the contractor's workers' compensation policy

questions.explanation: Industry guidance uses an employee running an errand in a personal car as its example of non-owned vehicle exposure and says non-owned, rented, or hired vehicle coverage should be required as part of the contractor's automobile insurance, secured through a business automobile coverage form. General property and equipment insurance covers tools and mobile equipment, completed operations relates to finished work, and employer's liability concerns injuries to the contractor's own employees.

questions.question: The contractor plans to use a leased helicopter to set rooftop skylights that are too heavy for the available crane. What should the owner require?

options.A: Nothing added, since hired vehicles fall under the business auto coverage form
options.B: Coverage under the contractor's general property and equipment insurance
options.C: Appropriate liability coverage for both owned and non-owned aircraft
options.D: Removal of the XCU exclusion from the contractor's general liability policy

questions.explanation: Automobile liability policies uniformly exclude aircraft and powerboats beyond set size and horsepower limits, so industry guidance says that when a project needs aircraft, such as a helicopter erecting skylights, the owner should require suitable liability coverage for both owned and non-owned aircraft. Relying on the auto form leaves the exclusion in place, general property and equipment insurance protects the contractor's own equipment rather than liability to others, and the XCU exclusion concerns explosion, collapse, and underground damage.

questions.question: A specifier is coordinating automobile liability requirements with the general conditions. On what basis do the AIA, EJCDC, and ConsensusDocs documents require that coverage to be written?

options.A: Per-occurrence (per-accident) basis
options.B: Claims-made basis
options.C: Reporting form basis tied to pay applications
options.D: Named-peril basis listing covered hazards

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that the AIA, EJCDC, and ConsensusDocs documents call for automobile coverage written on a per-occurrence (accident) basis for bodily injury or property damage arising from use of covered vehicles. Claims-made is a liability form industry guidance considers poorly suited to construction, the reporting form is a builder's risk valuation method, and named-peril describes a property insurance form.

questions.question: An owner's attorney notes that the supplementary conditions already name the owner as an additional insured on the contractor's liability policy and asks whether anything better is available. What is the correct response?

options.A: No; additional insured status is the most protection an owner can obtain
options.B: Yes; a broad form hold-harmless from the contractor offers stronger protection
options.C: Yes; an umbrella policy naming the owner supersedes additional insured status
options.D: Yes; owner's and contractor's protective insurance offers greater protection

questions.explanation: Industry guidance calls additional insured status under the supplementary conditions better protection for the owner but not the best, and says the owner's interests are better served by an OCP policy covering the same hazards as the contractor's liability insurance. A broad form hold-harmless is a contract clause rather than insurance and is unenforceable in a number of states, and an umbrella adds limits above the contractor's other liability coverage rather than replacing the owner's protective coverage.
questions.source: owner’s and contractor’s protective (OCP) liability insurance

questions.question: An owner on a ConsensusDocs 200 project selects the option for OCP insurance. Which party should obtain the policy, and why?

options.A: The owner, so that it can select a carrier already familiar with its risks
options.B: The contractor, to avoid conflict with the owner's existing liability policy
options.C: The A/E, because the coverage extends to its own design errors and omissions
options.D: The owner, since the policy insures the owner's role in the construction

questions.explanation: Industry guidance says the contractor typically obtains OCP insurance, which is the ConsensusDocs 200 default when that option is chosen, and that the contractor should provide it so that it does not conflict with the owner's existing liability policy. The owner's legal liability for its role explains why OCP is not duplicate coverage, not why the owner should buy it, and OCP does not cover the A/E's professional errors.
questions.source: owner’s and contractor’s protective (OCP) liability insurance

questions.question: An owner's risk manager objects that requiring OCP insurance would merely duplicate the contractor's own liability coverage. What is the basis for rejecting that objection?

options.A: OCP insures the contractor's tools and equipment, which liability coverage does not
options.B: OCP replaces builder's risk insurance, so total premiums stay about the same
options.C: The owner bears its own legal liability for its role in the construction process
options.D: OCP covers the owner's ordinary business operations away from the site

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that OCP insurance is not duplicate coverage because a legal liability exists for the owner's role in the construction process, even though OCP addresses the same hazards as the contractor's liability insurance. OCP is liability coverage tied to the construction work, so it neither insures the contractor's equipment, substitutes for builder's risk, nor covers the owner's unrelated operations.
questions.source: owner’s and contractor’s protective (OCP) liability insurance

questions.question: Which pair of reasons supports specifying a relatively high-limit umbrella excess liability policy for the contractor?

options.A: It replaces the primary policies and removes their standard exclusions
options.B: It covers the owner's own acts and the A/E's errors and omissions
options.C: It converts claims-made forms and fixes a per-project general aggregate
options.D: It economically raises limits and can broaden the underlying coverage

questions.explanation: Industry guidance gives two purposes: an umbrella is the most economical way to obtain limits above those customarily offered by general liability and automobile policies, and it can broaden the coverage those policies provide. It sits as a layer above the primary policies rather than replacing them, it does not cover the owner's or A/E's own acts, and aggregate or policy-form changes are made to the CGL itself.

questions.question: A specifier is comparing how standard documents handle umbrella liability. What does AIA Document A101 Exhibit A require?

options.A: Primary plus umbrella coverage at least equal to the stipulated primary coverage
options.B: Specific umbrella dollar limits entered in the supplementary conditions
options.C: An umbrella limit at least equal to the initial Contract Sum plus subsequent Modifications
options.D: Umbrella coverage written on a claims-made form with a stated extended reporting period

questions.explanation: Industry guidance says A101 Exhibit A addresses umbrella insurance only by requiring that the primary and umbrella policies together equal or exceed the coverage stipulated for the primary policies. Entering specific umbrella dollar amounts in the supplementary conditions is the EJCDC C-800 approach, and the Contract Sum plus Modifications measure is how the A101 exhibit sizes property insurance, not umbrella liability.

questions.question: On a project using EJCDC documents, the owner's insurance advisor has set umbrella limits. Which two umbrella values does EJCDC C-800 call for in the supplementary conditions?

options.A: Each occurrence limit and medical expense limit
options.B: Products-completed operations and personal injury limits
options.C: General aggregate and damage-to-rented-premises limits
options.D: General aggregate limit and each occurrence limit

questions.explanation: Industry guidance reports that EJCDC C-800 handles umbrella liability by having the supplementary conditions state dollar amounts for both the general aggregate and each occurrence. The other pairs mix in medical expense, products-completed operations, personal injury, and damage-to-rented-premises limits, which are separate CGL limits that industry guidance does not tie to the umbrella requirement.

questions.question: A specifier is distinguishing liability coverage from property insurance, which compensates insureds for damage to covered property caused by insured perils. Which policy is the cornerstone of a project's property insurance?

options.A: Equipment breakdown insurance
options.B: Builder's risk insurance
options.C: Installation floater
options.D: General property and equipment insurance

questions.explanation: Industry guidance defines property insurance as compensating insureds for damage to covered property from insured perils and names builder's risk insurance as the cornerstone of the project's property insurance. Equipment breakdown, installation floaters, and the contractor's general property and equipment insurance are narrower property coverages that supplement it.

questions.question: A university with several concurrent capital projects is starting a large, multiyear lab building whose insured value will climb steeply during the final phases. Which builder's risk form is likely most advantageous?

options.A: Completed value form, written for the anticipated completed value
options.B: Named peril form, limited to the perils listed in the policy
options.C: Difference-in-conditions form, maintained by the contractor
options.D: Reporting form, with premiums based on values at each update

questions.explanation: Industry guidance says the reporting form bases premiums on insured values at a given time, is most advantageous when values rise sharply late in construction, and suits large projects with lengthy schedules and owners handling many projects at once, provided the owner keeps up with the value reports. The completed value form fits inexperienced owners or a single project in progress, while named peril and difference-in-conditions are not builder's risk valuation forms.

questions.question: On an addition that ties into an existing building, the owner wants the builder's risk amount stated as the full cost of replacement at the time of loss, including existing structures. That wording comes from which standard document?

options.A: AIA A101 Exhibit A
options.B: EJCDC C-700
options.C: ConsensusDocs 200
options.D: AIA A201

questions.explanation: Industry guidance quotes three measures: A101 Exhibit A sets property insurance at no less than the initial Contract Sum plus later Modifications and work supplied by others; EJCDC C-700 uses the Work's full insurable replacement cost, subject to deductibles; and ConsensusDocs 200 uses replacement cost at the time of loss including existing structures. A201 is not the document industry guidance quotes for the amount.

questions.question: A transit authority will award three prime contracts for one station and will not purchase builder's risk insurance itself. What should the supplementary conditions do?

options.A: Name one prime contractor to insure the work, including the other primes' contract values
options.B: Require each prime contractor to carry a separate all-risk policy for its own contract
options.C: Require each prime contractor's subcontractors to purchase installation floaters instead
options.D: Require the primes to form a contractor-controlled insurance program for the station

questions.explanation: For multiple-prime work where the owner does not furnish builder's risk, industry guidance says the supplementary conditions should identify which prime contractor provides it, that contractor must include the value of the other prime contracts, and it should give the other primes proof of coverage. Separate policies for each prime duplicate premiums, which warns against, and all-risk coverage may not even be available on multiple-prime projects. Installation floaters supplement builder's risk rather than replace it, and a controlled insurance program would require significant changes to the standard forms.

questions.question: A mechanical subcontractor will install two large chillers. The project's builder's risk policy lists the subcontractor by name and broadly covers equipment once it is installed. Is a separate installation floater normally needed?

options.A: Yes; a floater is always required for generators, chillers, and similar items
options.B: No; that builder's risk coverage generally makes a floater unnecessary
options.C: Yes; builder's risk policies exclude equipment until the owner accepts the work
options.D: No; the contractor's property and equipment coverage protects the chillers instead

questions.explanation: Industry guidance says installation floaters, which insure a subcontractor's materials and work until the owner accepts the project, are generally required for expensive items such as generators or chillers, but are usually not required when the builder's risk policy names the subcontractor and broadly covers installed equipment. The stem rules out an equipment exclusion, and the contractor's general property and equipment insurance protects construction tools and mobile equipment, not installed systems.

questions.question: An owner wants to move staff into the completed first floor of a building while upper floors are still under construction. What must happen first regarding property insurance?

options.A: The A/E must certify the floor complete and notify the builder's risk carrier
options.B: The carrier must permit it, and under A101 Exhibit A give written notice of changes
options.C: The contractor must cancel builder's risk for that floor and add an OCP policy
options.D: The owner must purchase an installation floater covering the occupied area

questions.explanation: Industry guidance explains that partial occupancy changes the insurer's risk, so it should not begin without the carrier's permission, and A101 Exhibit A requires that the property insurer be contacted before occupancy and that written notice be received from it confirming the needed coverage changes. An A/E certification, cancelling coverage, or buying a floater does not meet that requirement, and floaters cover materials only during installation.

questions.question: A specifier who usually works with EJCDC documents takes on a project using AIA documents. How does responsibility for purchasing builder's risk insurance differ between the two families by default?

options.A: AIA: the contractor; EJCDC: the owner, transferable by agreement
options.B: Both: the contractor, with the owner named as an additional insured
options.C: Both: the owner, because it holds the insurable interest
options.D: AIA: the owner; EJCDC: the contractor, transferable to the owner

questions.explanation: Industry guidance notes that AIA documents place builder's risk on the owner because of its insurable interest, while EJCDC and ConsensusDocs place it on the contractor; the A101 exhibit allows transfer to the contractor, and EJCDC allows transfer to the owner through the supplementary conditions. One distractor reverses the two families, and the other two ignore that the families differ.

questions.question: While updating an older office master, a specifier finds a requirement for boiler and machinery insurance. What is this coverage now called?

options.A: Equipment breakdown insurance
options.B: Installation floater insurance
options.C: Inland marine insurance
options.D: Difference-in-conditions insurance

questions.explanation: Industry guidance identifies equipment breakdown insurance as the coverage formerly called boiler and machinery insurance, insuring against accidents to boilers, pressure vessels, machinery, electrical and HVAC equipment, and listed computer and communications equipment. An installation floater is the inland marine coverage for a subcontractor's equipment during installation, and difference-in-conditions coverage fills gaps left by an owner's builder's risk program; neither is the renamed boiler and machinery coverage.

questions.question: A specifier's master supplementary conditions still list a separate equipment breakdown policy as mandatory. How do the current AIA and EJCDC documents treat this coverage?

options.A: Both require it as a separate policy issued apart from builder's risk
options.B: AIA requires it in A101 Exhibit A, but EJCDC has dropped it
options.C: Both required it previously but no longer list it as a required type
options.D: EJCDC requires it in C-700, but AIA leaves it to the owner's option

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that AIA and EJCDC documents previously required equipment breakdown coverage but the current documents no longer specifically list it as a required insurance type. Industry guidance also notes that builder's risk policies usually include equipment coverage, negating the need for a separate policy. The other options wrongly keep it as a requirement in one or both document families.

questions.question: During construction, which loss falls within the scope of equipment breakdown insurance as industry guidance describes it?

options.A: A rented forklift damaged when it tips over in the laydown yard
options.B: A delivery truck damaged in a collision on the way to the site
options.C: A transformer that is damaged in an electrical accident
options.D: Owner-furnished casework stolen from an off-site warehouse

questions.explanation: Industry guidance says equipment breakdown insurance covers losses from accidents to boilers and pressure vessels, machinery, electrical equipment such as transformers and generators, HVAC equipment, and listed computer and communications equipment. A tipped forklift is mobile equipment protected by the contractor's general property and equipment insurance, a delivery truck falls under automobile coverage, and stolen stored materials are a property insurance question for the party holding title.

questions.question: A contractor's crawler crane is damaged in a work accident on the site. Which insurance is intended to cover this asset?

options.A: Contractor's general property and equipment insurance
options.B: Contractor's business automobile liability coverage form
options.C: Project builder's risk insurance, all-risk form
options.D: Equipment breakdown insurance on the project
