questions.question: For an owner-build (force-account) project, is there a need to develop procurement requirements?

options.A: No, because the owner provides its own construction services, removing the need
options.B: Yes, because owner-build still requires the same procurement requirements as DBB
options.C: No, because the architect/engineer assumes the owner's construction role here
options.D: Yes, but only the bid-bond and performance-bond forms must be developed for it

questions.explanation: Because the owner supplies its own construction services in owner-build, there is no outside construction to procure, so procurement requirements are not needed.

questions.question: For an indoor swimming pool room, which is the LEAST significant product-evaluation consideration relative to the others?

options.A: Noise control, given the hard wet surfaces that amplify the reverberation
options.B: Resistance to fading, given the limited and indirect daylight in the room
options.C: Humidity control, given the constant moisture load of a natatorium space
options.D: Safety, given the wet floors and the slip hazards around the pool deck

questions.explanation: For a natatorium, humidity control, noise control, and safety are all major concerns, while resistance to fading matters comparatively little — making fading the least significant of the four.

questions.question: On the Gulf Coast office building, the contractor's most appropriate initial sequencing consideration is to:

options.A: Construct the brick masonry exterior walls fully before any roofing is set
options.B: Perform some activities out of sequence to finish the project as fast as possible
options.C: Finish the second-floor mechanical and electrical work before any roofing
options.D: Get framing, sheathing, and roof membrane in place to dry-in for interior work

questions.explanation: The key early sequencing move is to dry the building in — get the framing up, sheathing on, and roof membrane installed as the schedule allows — so that interior work is protected from the weather.

questions.question: Which consideration is NOT necessary for product-selection decisions on a Gulf Coast (southeastern) office building?

options.A: Severity of the winter, given the mild winters typical of the Gulf Coast region
options.B: Risk of storm surges, given the building's proximity to coastal water bodies
options.C: Hurricanes, given the building's exposure to the high-velocity coastal wind events
options.D: Amount of sunlight, given the heat gain driving Gulf Coast cooling loads

questions.explanation: On the Gulf Coast, hurricanes, storm-surge risk, and intense sunlight all bear on product selection, but winter severity does not — mild winters make it the unnecessary consideration here.

questions.question: Which set of exterior conditions should an A/E evaluate when selecting site-suitable products?

options.A: Reverberation time, sound path length, and the conditioned interior air quality
options.B: MasterFormat division titles, section arrangement, and assignment of trade work
options.C: Heating, cooling, ventilation, and the interior lighting levels of the building
options.D: Weather severity, event frequency, groundwater, seismicity, and water proximity

questions.explanation: Exterior-condition evaluation considers factors such as weather severity; how often major events like tornadoes, hail, or hurricanes occur; groundwater levels; seismic activity; and how close the site is to a body of water.

questions.question: A specifier is evaluating a proposed rainscreen cladding system. Beyond the design intent, industry guidance names several criteria against which proposed systems are evaluated. Which group consists entirely of criteria from that list?

options.A: Code requirements, contractor means and methods, quality, and cost
options.B: Climate conditions, warranty length, reference standards, and cost
options.C: Code requirements, climate conditions, constructability, and quality
options.D: Constructability, installer availability, reference standards, and quality

questions.explanation: Industry guidance says that, in addition to design intent, proposed systems are checked against code requirements, climate conditions, constructability, reference standards, quality, and cost. Only the keyed group draws every item from that list. The other groups each slip in an item industry guidance does not name here: contractor means and methods, warranty length, or installer availability.

questions.question: A specifier on a wastewater treatment upgrade has limited time to analyze the products proposed for the project. Which kinds of products does industry guidance single out as especially needing the specifier's analysis to confirm they suit the project?

options.A: Finish materials chosen mainly for their appearance
options.B: Products specified solely by reference standard
options.C: Owner-furnished items installed by the contractor
options.D: Complex equipment and new technologies

questions.explanation: The product evaluation overview states that the specifier analyzes products to confirm they fit the project, with particular emphasis on complex equipment and new technologies. Finish materials chosen for appearance, products specified by reference standard, and owner-furnished items are not the categories industry guidance singles out for this extra scrutiny.

questions.question: In summarizing the specifier's role in product evaluation, industry guidance states that the evaluation of systems, assemblies, and materials is driven primarily by which of the following?

options.A: The owner's needs and requirements
options.B: The contractor's preferred installation methods
options.C: The manufacturers' published performance data
options.D: The A/E firm's office master specifications

questions.explanation: Industry guidance sums up the specifier's role by saying the owner's needs and requirements are what the specifier uses to evaluate systems, assemblies, and materials. Manufacturer data and office masters are tools in the process, not the basis of the evaluation. The contractor's preferred methods are not the driver of design-phase product evaluation.

questions.question: An A/E must select a building's HVAC system as well as the diffusers, dampers, and controls that connect to it. How should the A/E order these evaluations to make the selection process efficient?

options.A: Evaluate the components first, then fit a system around them
options.B: Evaluate the major system first, then the components for compatibility
options.C: Evaluate system and components together, resolving conflicts at submittals
options.D: Evaluate the system only, leaving components to contractor submittals

questions.explanation: Because some products affect the performance of others and later selections, industry guidance directs the A/E to evaluate major systems and subsystems first and then judge smaller components on quality, performance, and compatibility with the earlier choices. Starting with components reverses that order. Deferring components, or their conflicts, to contractor submittals abandons the A/E's evaluation role.

questions.question: What is the primary goal of evaluating systems, assemblies, and materials during design?

options.A: To identify the least costly product that still satisfies minimum code
options.B: To establish a list of acceptable manufacturers before bidding begins
options.C: To determine product applicability and compatibility for the project
options.D: To confirm that installers hold the required trade qualifications

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that the primary goal is to determine whether available products are applicable and whether different products and systems are compatible in meeting the project requirements. Cost savings are mentioned only as a possible side benefit of competition, not the goal. Manufacturer lists and installer qualifications are not what industry guidance identifies as the purpose of the evaluation.

questions.question: An A/E's checklist for a proposed curtain wall covers three of the four standard product evaluation components: requirements and design intent, code requirements, and constructability and construction sequence. Which component is missing from the checklist?

options.A: Availability from multiple local suppliers
options.B: Conformance with the schedule of values
options.C: Consistency with the project drawings
options.D: Acceptance by the owner's maintenance staff

questions.explanation: Industry guidance lists four components for evaluating systems, assemblies, and materials: compliance with project requirements and design intent, consistency with the project drawings, compliance with code requirements, and compatibility with desired constructability and sequence. The missing one is consistency with the drawings. Supplier availability, the schedule of values, and maintenance staff acceptance are not on the list.

questions.question: An owner asks when the A/E will begin evaluating products for a new clinic. Under the progressive evaluation industry guidance describes, in which phase does product evaluation begin?

options.A: Schematic design
options.B: Design development
options.C: Construction documents
options.D: Procurement

questions.explanation: Industry guidance describes a progressive evaluation that starts in schematic design, when the A/E or owner makes conceptual decisions on primary products to define functional requirements. Design development is when detailed product information is gathered and reviewed, and when regulatory review is refined. Construction documents and procurement come after products have already been evaluated.
questions.source: evaluating products for compliance with project requirements and design intent

questions.question: Which pairing correctly describes the roles in establishing and checking the requirements that drive product selection?

options.A: The A/E sets the requirements; the owner checks products against them
options.B: The owner sets the requirements; the A/E evaluates products for compliance
options.C: The A/E sets the requirements; the contractor verifies them during submittals
options.D: The owner sets the requirements; the contractor evaluates products for compliance

questions.explanation: The owner establishes the requirements for the project's details and design, and those requirements shape product selection. The A/E then evaluates products for compliance with the owner's requirements. Reversing the roles, or shifting the compliance evaluation to the contractor at submittals, misstates who does what during design.
questions.source: evaluating products for compliance with project requirements and design intent

questions.question: During design development, an A/E collects detailed manufacturer data on three candidate roofing systems. Under a progressive evaluation approach, what must be established before the A/E develops the specifications and drawings for the roofing products?

options.A: That contractor pricing has been obtained for each candidate system
options.B: That the owner has signed an acceptance of each listed manufacturer
options.C: That the installing subcontractor has completed a constructability review
options.D: That the selected items comply with the project's requirements

questions.explanation: Industry guidance says the A/E prepares specifications and drawings for selected products only after determining that those products comply with the project requirements. Contractor pricing and subcontractor constructability reviews are not prerequisites industry guidance names for this step. Owner sign-off on each manufacturer is likewise not the gate; the gate is the A/E's compliance determination.
questions.source: evaluating products for compliance with project requirements and design intent

questions.question: While reviewing regulatory requirements, an A/E finds that two different standards each define functional requirements for the same type of product, and their requirements differ substantially. What does this redundancy make especially important?

options.A: Specifying whichever of the two standards was published most recently
options.B: Knowing what the compliance evaluation covers and which standard is cited
options.C: Leaving the choice of governing standard to the AHJ at plan review
options.D: Citing both standards and letting the contractor choose either one

questions.explanation: Industry guidance notes that overlapping codes and standards can impose very different requirements on the same product, so it is critical to know which product aspects the code compliance evaluation covers and which standard the specifications reference. Picking the newest edition or deferring to the AHJ does not address that. Letting the contractor choose between standards would invite the lesser requirement.
questions.source: evaluating products for compliance with code requirements

questions.question: Late in design development, an A/E finds that a light fixture the owner favors for its appearance fails to comply with a safety standard specified for the project. What is the best course of action?

options.A: Include it, provided the owner accepts the risk in writing
options.B: Include it and require the contractor to seek an AHJ variance
options.C: Exclude it from the products selected for the work
options.D: List it as an approved substitution for the specified fixture

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states plainly that a product failing an applicable code, safety rule, or other specified standard should not be included in the project. Owner acceptance of risk, a contractor-sought variance, or listing it as a substitution would all still put a noncompliant product into the work. Code compliance is the screen that removes products creating unreasonable hazards.
questions.source: evaluating products for compliance with code requirements

questions.question: In the recommended approach to evaluating products for constructability and sequencing, which two inputs does the constructability evaluation use to develop the dates and milestones that feed the sequence evaluation?

options.A: The schedule of values and the submittal register
options.B: The bid tabulation and the list of proposed subcontractors
options.C: The drawing index and the project manual table of contents
options.D: The overall project schedule and a list of major equipment

questions.explanation: Industry guidance says the constructability evaluation draws on the overall project schedule and a list of major equipment to set dates and milestones for the sequence evaluation. Procurement dates and supplier delivery requirements are then checked against that sequence. The schedule of values, bid tabulation, and drawing index are construction-phase or document-control tools, not the inputs industry guidance names.
questions.source: evaluating products for constructability and sequencing

questions.question: A pump station design includes six identical pumps that each require factory start-up and testing. When evaluating design and construction sequencing, which approach does industry guidance direct the A/E to take?

options.A: Group the similar pump work and integrate commissioning into the schedule
options.B: Stagger each pump installation across separate phases to level the workforce
options.C: Defer commissioning considerations until the work reaches substantial completion
options.D: Assign each pump to a separate subcontractor so the work proceeds in parallel

questions.explanation: Industry guidance advises sequencing similar activities together on projects with multiple pieces of the same equipment to gain efficiency from repetition. It also has the A/E evaluate commissioning and start-up needs so they are integrated with design and construction sequencing in the overall schedule. Staggering or splitting identical work loses those efficiencies, and deferring commissioning defeats the integration industry guidance calls for.
questions.source: evaluating products for constructability and sequencing

questions.question: A school renovation must be completed over one summer, and the specified switchgear has a long manufacturing lead time. Which action does industry guidance identify as a way to reduce the schedule impact of such materials?

options.A: Procure the long-lead item early in the project schedule
options.B: Wait to order it until the contractor's schedule is approved
options.C: Replace it with field-assembled equipment built on site
options.D: Extend the contract time by change order after award

questions.explanation: Industry guidance gives early procurement of long-lead materials as a way to limit their effect on the overall schedule, and it stresses that the schedule must allow enough time to procure specified materials. Waiting for the contractor's schedule pushes the order later. Field assembly and a time extension do not address the lead-time problem industry guidance describes.
questions.source: impact of project conditions on materials and methods

questions.question: An owner's project has a very short construction timeframe, and the lowest-cost source of a key product cannot deliver in time. Which trade-off may be appropriate?

options.A: Splitting the order among several lower-cost suppliers
options.B: Employing a more expensive manufacturer to save time
options.C: Relaxing the reference standards to widen product availability
options.D: Replacing the manufactured product with site-built construction

questions.explanation: Industry guidance notes that on projects with short schedules, more expensive manufacturers may be used to save time in the product's schedule and lessen the effect on the overall schedule. Splitting the order among cheaper suppliers, relaxing reference standards, or switching to site-built work are not the trade-off industry guidance describes, and relaxing standards would sacrifice quality.
questions.source: impact of project conditions on materials and methods

questions.question: An A/E is comparing a factory-built pump skid with field assembly of the same components. Industry guidance notes that using a shop-fabricated item, where working conditions can be better controlled, is often beneficial to the owner on what assumption?

options.A: That the fabricator is located in the same state as the site
options.B: That the AHJ inspects the work at the fabrication facility
options.C: That the contractor waives the right to propose substitutions
options.D: That the product can be shipped to the site after fabrication

questions.explanation: Industry guidance says shop work under better-controlled conditions is often to the owner's benefit, provided the product can actually be shipped to the site once fabricated. Project conditions determine whether off-site assembly yields cost or schedule benefits. Fabricator location, off-site AHJ inspection, and substitution waivers are not the condition industry guidance states.
questions.source: impact of project conditions on materials and methods

questions.question: When selecting products for interior conditions, which group consists entirely of components that industry guidance lists for evaluation?

options.A: Building air quality, ventilation, lighting, and noise
options.B: Heating, ventilation, lighting, and occupant security
options.C: Air quality, noise, lighting, and fire separation
options.D: Heating, noise, ventilation, and space planning

questions.explanation: Industry guidance names building air quality, heating, ventilation, lighting, and noise as interior components to evaluate when selecting products. Occupant security, fire separation, and space planning are not among the components industry guidance lists, so only the keyed group stays entirely within that list.

questions.question: To keep interior materials in a busy school from needing frequent replacement and becoming costly maintenance items, industry guidance directs particular attention to durability for which materials?

options.A: Materials concealed within wall and ceiling cavities
options.B: Materials selected for appearance, such as wall coverings
options.C: Materials subject to heavy wear, such as flooring
options.D: Materials with long lead times, such as custom casework

questions.explanation: Industry guidance asks the A/E to evaluate durability within the interior conditions, especially for materials that take a lot of wear, with flooring as its example. Concealed materials, appearance-driven finishes, and long-lead items are not the emphasis of this interior durability guidance.

questions.question: An A/E evaluates products that improve a building's energy efficiency and interior conditions. This is mainly accomplished by efficiently reducing the energy needed for which uses?

options.A: Cooling, plumbing, and vertical transportation
options.B: Heating, ventilation, and stormwater pumping
options.C: Heating, lighting, and equipment operation
options.D: Lighting, elevators, and domestic hot water

questions.explanation: Industry guidance ties energy-efficient product selection mainly to reducing the energy used for heating, lighting, and equipment operation. Ventilation appears in the list of interior components to evaluate, not in this energy statement, and stormwater pumping is a site concern. Cooling, plumbing, elevators, and hot water are not the uses industry guidance names.

questions.question: A national developer wants to build its southwestern stucco-wall, flat-roof house prototype unchanged in a Midwest subdivision. Besides the colder climate, what does industry guidance say materials and methods must also be compatible with?

options.A: The developer's national brand and marketing standards
options.B: Regional and local cultural and aesthetic conditions
options.C: The original prototype's referenced standard editions
options.D: Nationally available manufacturer warranty programs

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that materials and methods must suit specific regional and local cultural and aesthetic conditions, contrasting southwestern stucco and flat roofs with Midwest wood framing, vinyl siding, and pitched roofs. A national brand standard or warranty program does not override local conditions. Carrying over the prototype's standard editions does nothing to address regional fit.

questions.question: For a site that experiences frequent wet weather events and intense storms, which design response does industry guidance identify as becoming more important?

options.A: Specifying products suited to mild climates with humidity swings
options.B: Assembling components off-site under controlled shop conditions
options.C: Selecting stucco walls and flat roofs typical of arid regions
options.D: Directing stormwater away from the site and controlling its release

questions.explanation: Industry guidance links frequent wet weather and intense storms to a greater need to direct stormwater away from the site and control its release, or to pick products suited to wetter climates. Products for mild, humidity-swinging climates answer a different condition. Off-site assembly concerns shop control and schedule, and stucco with flat roofs is the example of an arid regional style.

questions.question: Among the types of reference standards, ASTM E2112, Standard Practice for Installation of Exterior Windows, Doors and Skylights, is given as an example of which type?

options.A: Installation standard
options.B: Performance standard
options.C: Workmanship standard
options.D: Test method standard

questions.explanation: Industry guidance lists ASTM E2112 as its example of a workmanship standard, despite the word installation in its title. The installation standard example is NFPA 13 for sprinkler systems. ASTM F1487 illustrates performance standards and ASTM E119 illustrates test method standards.

questions.question: Industry guidance classifies each of its example reference standards by type. Under which type does it list ACI 318, Building Code Requirements for Structural Concrete?

options.A: Code
options.B: Product standard
options.C: Basic material standard
options.D: Design standard

questions.explanation: Although its title mentions building code requirements, industry guidance lists ACI 318 as the example of a design standard. The code example is ANSI/ASME A17.1 for elevators and escalators. APA PS-1 illustrates product standards and ASTM B211 illustrates basic material standards.

questions.question: A specification section cites a referenced standard only by its designation and title. The contractor argues that the standard's provisions are not binding because their text does not appear in the project manual. How do the referenced provisions apply?

options.A: Only provisions restated in Part 2 of the section are binding
options.B: They become binding only when the local AHJ adopts the standard
options.C: They become part of the specifications as if included in full
options.D: They serve as guidance unless repeated in Division 01 sections

questions.explanation: Industry guidance explains that standards cited by number, title, or other designation become part of the specifications just as though their full text were included. That is what saves the A/E from writing lengthy text. Restating provisions in Part 2 or Division 01 is not required, and AHJ adoption governs code status, not whether a cited standard binds the contract.

questions.question: An A/E is choosing between two reference standards for a fire-resistive joint system and wants to ensure acceptance by the authority having jurisdiction. Where applicable, what does industry guidance recommend?

options.A: Use the standards listed in the model or local codes
options.B: Use the more recent of the two standards' editions
options.C: Use whichever standard the manufacturer certifies to
options.D: Use the standard with the most demanding requirements

questions.explanation: Industry guidance advises using standards listed in the model or local codes, where applicable, to secure acceptability with the AHJ; depending on how a code lists it, the standard may act as a code requirement or as a guideline for acceptance. Edition date, manufacturer certification, and stringency do not by themselves establish AHJ acceptance.

questions.question: While reviewing a reference standard before citing it, an A/E finds that several of its provisions conflict with other parts of the project. What choice must the A/E make?

options.A: Cite it with a precedence clause, or let the AHJ resolve the conflicts
options.B: Cite it with stated exceptions, or write original requirements instead
options.C: Omit it and let the contractor propose an equivalent standard instead
options.D: Cite it unchanged and resolve the conflicts through submittal review

questions.explanation: When a standard is not compatible with other project requirements or contains duplications and contradictions, industry guidance says the A/E must either reference it while defining exceptions or write original requirements into the specifications. Precedence clauses, AHJ resolution, contractor-proposed equivalents, and submittal review all leave the contradiction in the documents.

questions.question: A small A/E firm finds that keeping a current library of every reference standard it might cite is expensive and difficult. What does industry guidance advise as the minimum?

options.A: Rely on manufacturers' summaries of the cited standards
options.B: Obtain each standard only when a contractor requests it
options.C: Cite only standards that the AHJ keeps on file locally
options.D: Obtain at least the commonly referenced standards

questions.explanation: Industry guidance says the A/E should have access to the standards it proposes to cite and, while a complete current library is costly, should at a minimum obtain the commonly referenced ones. Manufacturer summaries are not access to the standard itself. Waiting for contractor requests or limiting citations to what the AHJ holds does not meet the advice.

questions.question: A specifier intends to cite a newly revised ASTM standard that she has not yet read, planning to check its content during submittal review. What is wrong with this plan?

options.A: It should be reviewed and understood in full before it is incorporated
options.B: Revised standards may not be cited until the AHJ formally adopts them
options.C: Submittal review of standards is the responsibility of the contractor
options.D: Newly revised standards must be referenced by title without a date

questions.explanation: Industry guidance requires that a reference standard be reviewed and its content and purpose thoroughly understood before it is written into the specifications. Checking it during submittals is too late to catch incompatibilities or contradictions. Industry guidance sets no AHJ-adoption prerequisite here, and omitting the date would weaken, not satisfy, a proper citation.

questions.question: To deal with overlaps between referenced standards, a specifier adds a statement that the more stringent requirement governs whenever a standard conflicts with the specifications or another standard. How should this statement be viewed?

options.A: It resolves every conflict, so duplications need not be identified
options.B: It cannot cover every conflict; duplications must still be resolved
options.C: It is improper because it shifts design responsibility to the contractor
options.D: It belongs in the owner-contractor agreement, not in Division 01

questions.explanation: Industry guidance allows the A/E to state that the more stringent requirement applies, but warns that such a statement cannot be relied on for every possible conflict. The A/E still has to identify duplications and modify the references in the specifications to remove contradictions. Industry guidance neither prohibits the statement nor relocates it to the agreement.

questions.question: Industry guidance cites one reference standard that covers numerous contractor-owner and contractor-subcontractor relationships and uses the terms owner and contract documents in a different sense than the general conditions do. Which standard is it?

options.A: AISC Code of Standard Practice
options.B: AISC Specification for Structural Steel Buildings
options.C: NFPA 13 Standard for Installation of Sprinkler Systems
options.D: ACI 318 Building Code Requirements for Structural Concrete

questions.explanation: Industry guidance uses the AISC Code of Standard Practice as its example of a standard whose relationship provisions and use of the terms owner and contract documents differ from the general conditions, inviting misunderstandings. The AISC structural steel specification is the example for multiple nested standards, not this problem. ACI 318 and NFPA 13 appear as examples of design and installation standards.

questions.question: A specifier cites a standard because one of its provisions appears to be a mandatory, permanent part of the standard, and does not restate that provision in the section. What risk does this create?

options.A: A footnote or later paragraph may void it unless the specs state it
options.B: The provision binds only the subcontractor that the standard names
options.C: The provision lapses once the related submittals have been approved
options.D: The general conditions automatically override the cited provision

questions.explanation: Industry guidance warns that some provisions seem to be an irrevocable part of a standard, yet a footnote or subsequent paragraph can void them unless the specifications state them explicitly. Subcontractor references are a separate concern industry guidance says to avoid. Submittal approval does not cancel provisions, and industry guidance does not say the general conditions automatically override them.

questions.question: Which situation in a draft specification illustrates what industry guidance calls an embedded option in a reference standard?

options.A: A cited standard that refers in turn to several other standards
options.B: A cited standard whose minimums nearly any product can meet
options.C: A cited standard that assigns work to a particular trade
options.D: A cited standard offering several classes that must be selected

questions.explanation: Industry guidance defines embedded options as the categories, classes, or groups within a standard from which applicable properties must be chosen, and says they must be identified and modified to avoid discrepancies. A standard citing other standards is the multiple-standards problem. Overly liberal minimums concern level of requirements, and trade references are the trades and subcontracts issue.

questions.question: Industry guidance illustrates the problem of multiple standards with a structural steel document that refers to several ASTM standards, which in turn refer to still other ASTM standards. Which document does it use?

options.A: AISC Code of Standard Practice for Steel Buildings and Bridges
options.B: AISC Specifications for Design, Fabrication, and Erection of Structural Steel
options.C: AWS D1.1, Structural Welding Code, Steel
options.D: ACI 318, Building Code Requirements for Structural Concrete

questions.explanation: Industry guidance uses the AISC document on design, fabrication, and erection of structural steel for buildings, which cites ASTM standards that cite still others. The AISC Code of Standard Practice is the example of conflicting contractual terminology. AWS D1.1 is not the example, and ACI 318 is its design standard example.

questions.question: A section cites a primary standard that in turn lists several secondary standards. How do these nested standards affect the specification?

options.A: They take precedence over the primary standard wherever they differ
options.B: They can create conflicts and multiple choices, as a single reference can
options.C: They eliminate any embedded options found in the primary standard
options.D: They apply to the fabricator but not to the prime contractor

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that standards referenced within other standards create conflicts of information and multiple choices in the same way a single reference standard does. Industry guidance gives them no precedence over the primary standard. They add options rather than removing them, and nothing in industry guidance limits them to the fabricator.

questions.question: An A/E is concerned that standards nested within a cited AISC document may carry qualifications that contradict the project specifications. What does industry guidance identify as the only real solution?

options.A: Adding a clause stating that the latest edition of each standard governs
options.B: Deleting every secondary reference contained in the cited primary standard
options.C: Knowing and understanding the content of the additional referenced material
options.D: Requiring the contractor to certify compliance with each nested standard listed

questions.explanation: Industry guidance says nested standards must not carry qualifications that contradict other referenced standards or the project specifications, and that there is no easy fix other than knowing and understanding the additional referenced material. An edition-governs clause or contractor certification leaves contradictions undetected. Deleting secondary references from a published standard is not something the specifier can do.

questions.question: A referenced roofing standard states that the roofing subcontractor shall perform certain field tests. Why should such a subcontractor reference be avoided in the project specifications?

options.A: MasterFormat sections are organized to assign work to specific trades
options.B: Construction contracts are usually written for one contractor
options.C: The owner normally selects and contracts with each subcontractor
options.D: Subcontractor duties may be defined only in Division 01 sections

questions.explanation: Industry guidance notes that reference standards may name a trade or subcontractor, but because construction contracts are usually written with one contractor, such references should be avoided. MasterFormat is expressly not intended to assign work to trades. The owner does not normally contract with subcontractors, and industry guidance sets no rule confining subcontractor duties to Division 01.

questions.question: A specifier finds that the minimum requirements in a reference standard are so liberal that nearly any product on the market can meet them. What is the appropriate response?

options.A: Cite the standard unchanged because its minimums govern
options.B: Leave the quality level to the contractor's product submittals
options.C: Ask the AHJ to amend the standard before it is cited
options.D: Make exceptions to the standard within the specifications

questions.explanation: Industry guidance notes that reference standards often set minimum requirements that can be either so restrictive they exclude most available materials or so liberal that almost anything qualifies, and that exceptions may be made to avoid those extremes. Citing it unchanged accepts the low bar. Deferring to submittals or asking the AHJ to amend the standard does not fix the specification.

questions.question: A specifier is sorting the warranty requirements in a project manual using the two basic warranty types that industry guidance identifies. Which pair matches those categories?

options.A: Construction warranties covering products and workmanship, and product-only warranties
options.B: Express warranties stated in writing, and implied warranties arising from a sale
options.C: Full warranties with all UCC remedies, and limited warranties with reduced remedies
options.D: Contractor correction-period obligations, and manufacturer extended warranties

questions.explanation: Industry guidance divides warranties into construction warranties or guaranties, which cover both products and workmanship, and warranties that cover products alone. Express versus implied is the UCC classification of purchasing warranties, and full versus limited describes the breadth of remedies. The correction period is a contractual obligation, not one of the two warranty types.

questions.question: An owner building identical facilities in two states asks why its counsel warns that the same manufacturer's product warranty might be interpreted differently at each site. Which explanation is consistent with industry guidance?

options.A: The UCC is a federal statute, but each state's building code modifies its warranty terms
options.B: Each state separately adopted the UCC as its own law, and the enactments vary somewhat by state
options.C: Product warranties are governed by the general conditions, which each state amends by statute
options.D: The UCC applies only to consumer goods, so state common law governs construction products

questions.explanation: Warranties on goods arise from a sales transaction and are governed by the UCC, other applicable state law, and the warranty's own terms. Because every state enacted the UCC individually, the law is largely uniform but differs in places from state to state. The UCC is not a federal statute, and industry guidance does not name building codes or the general conditions as the source of these differences.

questions.question: Construction warranties, which cover both products and workmanship, are usually which of the following?

options.A: Third-party guaranties furnished through a surety company
options.B: One-year warranties set by the standard general conditions
options.C: Implied warranties attached by law to the sale of goods
options.D: Extended warranties specified in various specification sections

questions.explanation: Industry guidance characterizes construction warranties as usually being extended warranties written into the individual specification sections. The one-year obligation in standard general conditions is a correction period rather than an extended warranty, and implied warranties come from the UCC rather than the specifications. A surety-backed guaranty is a separate three-party arrangement.

questions.question: Industry guidance cites Black's Law Dictionary to explain that guaranty and warranty are etymologically the same word. What basis does it give?

options.A: The Old German letter w was rendered as g in Middle English law
options.B: Both derive from a Latin legal term for a promise made under seal
options.C: Both entered American usage through the drafters of the UCC
options.D: The Norman French letter g is interchangeable with the English w

questions.explanation: Black's Law Dictionary traces both words to one root, noting that the Norman French g corresponds to the English w. The Latin, UCC, and Old German origins in the other choices are not what industry guidance gives. Despite the shared root, the law assigns the two words slightly different meanings.

questions.question: A surety company signs a separate contract agreeing to step in if a roofing contractor does not perform its obligations to the owner. Using the legal meanings industry guidance gives, this arrangement is best described as a:

options.A: Warranty, because it assures stipulated responsibilities for completed work
options.B: Guaranty, because a third party assumes responsibility if the principal defaults
options.C: Warranty, because the surety becomes the principal for the roofing work
options.D: Guaranty, because the principal itself assures performance of its own completed work

questions.explanation: Legally, a guaranty is a separate contract by a third party, much like a surety bond, that applies if the principal fails to perform. A warranty is the principal's own assurance that it will carry stipulated responsibilities for completed work. The warranty choices misapply that definition, and the last choice attaches the warranty's defining feature to a guaranty.

questions.question: A contractor installs a manufacturer's storefront system. Using the strict legal meanings industry guidance assigns to guaranty and warranty, which statement correctly describes the parties' assurances for the storefront?

options.A: The manufacturer warrants the material; the contractor warrants both that material and its installation
options.B: The manufacturer guarantees the material; the contractor warrants both that material and its installation
options.C: The manufacturer warrants the material; the contractor guarantees that material and warrants its installation
options.D: The manufacturer guarantees the material; the contractor guarantees both that material and its own installation

questions.explanation: Industry guidance explains that a manufacturer warrants its own material, while the contractor gives a third-party guaranty for that same material and a warranty for its own installation work. The contractor is a third party with respect to the manufacturer's product, so in the strict legal sense its assurance on the material is a guaranty, even though everyday contract language often says the contractor warrants materials. The manufacturer is the principal for its product, so it warrants rather than guarantees.

questions.question: A pump section requires a five-year manufacturer's warranty. At closeout, the contractor states that this warranty begins only when the one-year correction period expires. How do specified warranties relate to the contractor's general warranty and correction period?

options.A: They replace the general warranty for the specified equipment
options.B: They follow the correction period and begin when it expires
options.C: They are in addition to them and run concurrently with them
options.D: They govern over the general warranty when durations conflict

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that warranties specified for materials and equipment are additional to the contractor's general warranty and guaranty and the correction period, and they run at the same time rather than in sequence. The five-year term therefore does not wait for the correction period to end. The specified warranty also does not displace or override the general warranty; both apply.

questions.question: Industry guidance cautions that warranties are as technical and confusing as another subject, one that it says most A/Es have learned to avoid specifying. Which subject?

options.A: Project insurance requirements
options.B: Performance and payment bonds
options.C: Testing and inspection services
options.D: Product substitution procedures

questions.explanation: Industry guidance compares warranties to insurance and observes that although most A/Es have learned not to write insurance requirements, specifying warranties is still common. Bonds are a related risk-transfer topic but are not the comparison industry guidance makes. Testing services and substitution procedures are routinely specified and are not described this way.

questions.question: A specifier routinely copies warranty durations from manufacturers' literature into PART 1 without reviewing the warranty terms, reasoning that product research is the real job. Which course of action reflects recommended practice?

options.A: Stop specifying warranties and rely on the general conditions' correction period
options.B: Keep the durations and require submittal of each manufacturer's standard warranty
options.C: Transfer warranty review to the contractor through the closeout submittal process
options.D: Understand warranty terms as thoroughly as the products' physical properties

questions.explanation: Industry guidance says anyone specifying warranties for the owner must know them as well as the physical properties and materials of the products specified. Requiring only the manufacturer's standard warranty can let the manufacturer limit its responsibility unreasonably, and shifting review to the contractor removes the A/E's evaluation. Industry guidance acknowledges that A/Es commonly specify warranties and does not tell them to stop.

questions.question: A roofing manufacturer's warranty states adequate maintenance by the owner as a condition rather than an exclusion. The owner skips the required inspections, and the membrane later fails from a manufacturing defect unrelated to maintenance. What is the likely result?

options.A: Only damage traceable to the missed maintenance is removed from the warranty coverage
options.B: The warranty still applies, because the failure is unrelated to the missed maintenance
options.C: Liability may be disclaimed, since the unmet requirement voids the warranty
options.D: The contractor's correction-period obligations shift the claim to the roofing installer

questions.explanation: Industry guidance distinguishes an exclusion, which narrows what a warranty covers, from a condition, which must be satisfied for the warranty to be effective at all. If a condition such as adequate maintenance is not met, the warranty is null and void, and the manufacturer may refuse liability even for an unrelated failure. Removing only maintenance-related damage describes how an exclusion operates, not a condition.

questions.question: A firm's master specifications include a one-year warranty article in every section, and its project manuals place the 20-year roofing warranty in Division 01. The project uses AIA general conditions. Which revision aligns with industry guidance?

options.A: Keep the one-year articles and move the roofing warranty into the supplementary conditions
options.B: Delete the one-year articles and specify the roofing warranty in PART 1 of the roofing section
options.C: Delete the one-year articles and specify the roofing warranty in PART 3 of the roofing section
options.D: Keep the one-year articles and leave the roofing warranty in Division 01 for coordination

questions.explanation: With AIA, EJCDC, or similar standard general conditions, specifying one-year warranties is unnecessary. Those general conditions do not provide extended warranties, so industry guidance says extended warranties belong in PART 1—GENERAL of the product section. PART 3 addresses execution, and neither the supplementary conditions nor Division 01 is the location industry guidance names.

questions.question: Industry guidance notes that the general warranty and the one-year correction period are not always distinguished, and that some contracts actually cap the contractor's warranty obligations at one year. Which contracts does it cite as the most notable example?

options.A: Public works contracts using EJCDC general conditions
options.B: Private contracts using ConsensusDocs general conditions
options.C: Design-build contracts using AIA general conditions
options.D: Federal contracts written using language from the FAR

questions.explanation: Industry guidance explains that the one-year correction period in standard general conditions is a specific obligation and owner remedy that is not meant to limit warranties. It singles out federal construction contracts using FAR warranty language as ones that actually restrict the contractor's warranty obligations to one year. It notes that the warranties in AIA, EJCDC, and ConsensusDocs general conditions carry no time limitation.

questions.question: An owner's main concern on a hospital project is being able to pursue the insulating glass fabricator directly if seals fail; the fabricator was engaged by the glazing subcontractor, not by the owner. Which purpose of construction warranties listed in industry guidance addresses this concern?

options.A: Extending the manufacturer's responsibility beyond the end of the correction period
options.B: Protecting the owner against failures despite technical compliance with the contract
options.C: Giving the owner recourse against parties outside a direct contractual relationship
options.D: Allowing the owner a remedy beyond the normal statute of limitations

questions.explanation: One reason industry guidance lists for construction warranties is to give the owner recourse against manufacturers, subcontractors, and suppliers that have no direct contract with the owner, which is this owner's concern. The other choices are also listed purposes, but they address latent failures in compliant work or timing (the correction period and the statute of limitations) rather than reaching a remote party.

questions.question: An owner insists on 10-year extended warranties for all rooftop compressors after a bad experience on a prior project. What should guide the A/E's decision whether to specify them?

options.A: Whether the general conditions already include a correction period
options.B: Whether competing manufacturers offer warranties of equal duration
options.C: Whether the warranty duration matches the expected service life
options.D: Whether the benefit to the owner justifies the warranty's cost

questions.explanation: Industry guidance recognizes that owners often insist on extended warranties for products such as compressors, roofing, and insulating glass because performance and replacement cost are unpredictable, but it tells the A/E to weigh the decision on cost-benefit to the owner. Matching competitors' durations or service life is not the test industry guidance gives, and the correction period exists whether or not an extended warranty is specified.

questions.question: Industry guidance recounts that the built-up roofing industry once offered a third-party roof bond that was considered of little value. What led that industry to begin offering extended warranties instead?

options.A: Single-ply systems entered the market with extended warranties
options.B: Model building codes began requiring extended warranties on roof systems
options.C: Owners began rejecting the one-year correction period as insufficient
options.D: Federal agencies began requiring roof warranties under the FAR

questions.explanation: Industry guidance uses built-up roofing as an example of warranties driven by market conditions: once single-ply systems arrived with extended warranties, built-up roofing manufacturers matched them to stay competitive. No code mandate, owner rejection of the correction period, or federal requirement is cited. Industry guidance adds that when two products perform similarly, the available warranty may decide the purchase.

questions.question: Two roofing manufacturers offer identical 20-year extended warranties. Which of the following is a prerequisite for anyone to benefit from either warranty?

options.A: The installer must be certified by the manufacturer before bidding
options.B: The manufacturer must be financially secure enough to cover its liabilities
options.C: The owner must register and sign the warranty at substantial completion
options.D: The warranty term must equal the roof system's expected service life

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that no one benefits from an extended warranty unless the manufacturer is financially able to cover its liabilities. Installer qualification is one of the benefits a sound extended warranty brings, not the precondition. Industry guidance treats a signing requirement as a warning sign and cautions against equating warranty length with service life.

questions.question: Industry guidance identifies immediate benefits that an equitable extended warranty can provide, which could make it worth the owner's cost. Which set matches its list?

options.A: Installer qualification by the manufacturer, manufacturer involvement in construction, and insurance against failure
options.B: Installer qualification by the manufacturer, longer system service life, and reduced owner maintenance costs
options.C: Manufacturer involvement in construction, longer system service life, and transfer of design liability to the manufacturer
options.D: Insurance against failure, reduced owner maintenance costs, and transfer of design liability to the manufacturer

questions.explanation: Industry guidance names three immediate benefits: the manufacturer qualifies the installer, the manufacturer becomes involved in construction, and the warranty serves as insurance against failure. Each other set includes one listed benefit alongside items industry guidance does not claim here, such as longer service life, reduced maintenance costs, or transfer of design liability. Industry guidance also warns against assuming that warranty length predicts service life.

questions.question: On a prior project, an A/E specified a built-up roof with a short warranty and learned the roofer had become an approved installer with a single phone call. To obtain manufacturer prequalification of the installer and involvement during construction, what does industry guidance recommend?

options.A: Extend the contractor's correction period to match the manufacturer's warranty term
options.B: Keep the shorter warranty but require a third-party roof bond from the installer
options.C: Require the owner to register the warranty with the manufacturer before installation
options.D: Specify the manufacturer's best system, often a 20-year system with full warranty

questions.explanation: Industry guidance recommends specifying the manufacturer's best system, which for built-up roofing is often a 20-year system carrying a full workmanship and materials warranty. With that commitment, most manufacturers prequalify the installer and take part in construction because they have a stake in long-term performance. A bond, early registration, or a longer correction period does not produce that manufacturer involvement.

questions.question: A below-grade waterproofing membrane sold with no stipulated warranty limitations fails, flooding finished spaces below. Under a full warranty as industry guidance describes it per the UCC, what may the remedy include?

options.A: Refund or replacement plus labor, but excluding any damage to furnishings or adjacent construction
options.B: Refund or replacement of the product only, prorated for the years of service already provided
options.C: Refund or replacement, labor to repair or replace, and consequential and incidental damages
options.D: Labor to repair the product only, capped at the original installed cost of the waterproofing

questions.explanation: Unless otherwise stipulated, materials are sold under a full warranty, which under the UCC covers refund or replacement, the labor to repair or replace, and consequential and incidental damages such as harm to furnishings and adjacent work. Excluding labor or consequential damages, prorating, and capping repairs at original cost are features of limited warranties, not full ones.

questions.question: An A/E is concerned that manufacturers will submit warranties with exclusions that strip the owner's protection. Which specification approach does industry guidance recommend for controlling unwanted exclusions?

options.A: List acceptable exclusions and make A/E approval of others a condition of acceptance
options.B: Require the manufacturer's standard warranty and rely on the UCC to void unfair exclusions
options.C: Specify only the warranty duration so that exclusions can be negotiated during submittals
options.D: Require the owner to sign each warranty so that exclusions are enforceable only by consent

questions.explanation: Industry guidance advises listing the exclusions that are acceptable and making the A/E's approval of any additional exclusion a condition of accepting the product or its warranty. Accepting the standard warranty can let a manufacturer limit its responsibility unreasonably, and specifying only duration leaves no basis to reject a deficient warranty. A signature requirement is something industry guidance flags as a warning sign.

questions.question: Six years into a 15-year roofing warranty, the owner sells the building. The warranty expressly prohibits assignment. What is the new owner's position?

options.A: Covered for the remaining term, but only for materials and not for labor
options.B: Covered, because the law assumes a warranty transfers with the facility
options.C: Not covered, because the warranty's terms bar its transfer to a buyer
options.D: Not covered, because warranties never transfer when a facility is sold

questions.explanation: Industry guidance notes that the law generally presumes a warranty is transferable when a facility is sold before the warranty expires, which makes the second choice tempting. When the warranty specifically prohibits assignment, however, the new owner has no coverage. Saying warranties never transfer overstates the rule, since transfer is the default absent such a prohibition.

questions.question: A sealant manufacturer's 10-year warranty begins on the date the contractor installs the product, about 14 months before the project is complete. What effect does this start date have on the owner's protection?

options.A: More protection, because coverage begins earlier in the construction project
options.B: Less protection than if the warranty began at substantial completion
options.C: Equal protection, because the warranty term is the same length
options.D: No effect, because the term restarts automatically at substantial completion

questions.explanation: Industry guidance points out that a product warranty beginning when the contractor buys or installs the product gives the owner less protection than one starting at substantial completion, because part of the term is used up before the owner takes over. An equal term length does not mean equal coverage for the owner, and industry guidance gives no rule that restarts such a term at substantial completion; the A/E must study the warranty's terms.

questions.question: A manufacturer offers a no-dollar-limit roof warranty that eliminates prorated coverage. What specific requirement does the manufacturer impose in exchange for paying full replacement costs?

options.A: Owner acceptance of the warranty as the sole and exclusive remedy
options.B: Installation exclusively by the manufacturer's own field crews and inspectors
options.C: A performance bond from the installer covering the full warranty term
options.D: Use of all or almost all of its own products within the warranted system

questions.explanation: Industry guidance explains that manufacturers who remove exclusions usually add other costs or conditions; for no-dollar-limit roof warranties, prorating disappears but the system must consist of all or nearly all of the manufacturer's products. Installation by factory crews, installer bonds, and exclusive-remedy clauses are not the trade-off industry guidance describes for this warranty type.

questions.question: Two extended warranties for a waterproofing system are being compared. Which features are the most essential features of a warranty?

options.A: Its duration and the start date of its term
options.B: The nature of its remedies and their limitations
options.C: The registration fee and the claim procedure
options.D: The products and components it lists as being covered

questions.explanation: Industry guidance notes that the UCC lets manufacturers disclaim implied warranties in writing and limit both duration and remedies, and it calls the nature of the remedies and their limits the most essential features of a warranty. Duration is the term most often compared, but industry guidance says it may be among the least important. Covered components and claim procedures matter but are not ranked as most essential.

questions.question: A specification section states only: Submit manufacturer's standard warranty. What risk does this create for the owner?

options.A: The manufacturer may limit its responsibility to an unreasonable level
options.B: The correction period is shortened to match the manufacturer's warranty term
options.C: The implied warranties are automatically converted into express warranties
options.D: The A/E becomes liable for gaps between the warranty and UCC remedies

questions.explanation: Industry guidance warns that asking only for the manufacturer's standard warranty lets the manufacturer set limits that may be unreasonable from the owner's standpoint, to the point that the owner could be better off without any warranty. A specified warranty does not shorten the correction period, and the requirement neither converts implied warranties nor shifts liability to the A/E.

questions.question: A roof leaks at a large owner's facility, and the firm that installed the roof makes repairs immediately, before obtaining the manufacturer's approval under its warranty claim procedure. What is the risk?

options.A: The A/E must certify the repairs before the manufacturer can reimburse them
options.B: The owner forfeits the rest of the warranty because the repair was unauthorized
options.C: The repairs restart the warranty term as of the date the repair work was done
options.D: The manufacturer may decline to pay for those repairs

questions.explanation: Industry guidance notes that most manufacturers have a procedure contractors must follow to be paid for warranty repairs, and repairs made without waiting for approval may go uncompensated. The contractor is caught in a bind because a slow response can damage its relationship with a large owner. Because the installing contractor did the work, the concern about repairs by other parties invalidating the warranty does not apply.

questions.question: An air barrier assembly includes membrane, transition flashing, and sealant from three manufacturers, each offering its own warranty. To keep the owner from having to resort to litigation to sort out who is at fault after a failure, what does industry guidance recommend?

options.A: Require separate warranties from each manufacturer with matching durations
options.B: Specify a warranted system whose manufacturer accepts system responsibility
options.C: Require the contractor to extend its correction period to cover all components
options.D: Specify prorated component warranties that run concurrently with one another

questions.explanation: For multicomponent systems, industry guidance says the A/E should require the warranting manufacturer to accept responsibility for the whole system and should specify a warranted system rather than individually warranted components. Matching durations or concurrent component warranties still leave the owner to prove which party caused a failure. Extending the correction period does not create single-source manufacturer responsibility.

questions.question: A sealant section says only: Provide 15-year manufacturer's warranty. The submitted warranty runs 15 years but excludes labor and limits remedies to replacement material. What is the A/E's position?

options.A: The A/E may reject it, since a limited warranty violates the implied full warranty
options.B: The A/E has no basis to reject it, since the specified duration was met
options.C: The A/E may reject it, since the UCC requires labor in every product warranty
options.D: The A/E has no basis to reject it, since warranties are outside the A/E's review

questions.explanation: Industry guidance cautions that when only a duration is specified, the A/E has nothing on which to reject a warranty that meets that duration but is otherwise unacceptable. The UCC permits buyer and seller to agree to limited warranties with reduced remedies, so the two rejection choices are wrong. Warranty forms are properly reviewed with other submittals, so the last choice misstates the A/E's role.

questions.question: An owner needs a concealed below-slab vapor retarder to perform for the life of the building. A newly introduced product carries a 30-year warranty; an established product carries 15 years. What should the A/E do before specifying?

options.A: Specify the established product only if its manufacturer will extend to 30 years
options.B: Select the 30-year product, since its warranty covers the longer performance period
options.C: Verify each product's performance history and the testing that supports its term
options.D: Specify either product, since warranty duration reflects expected service life

questions.explanation: Industry guidance notes that warranty time limits often bear no direct relationship to expected service life, so where performance duration is critical the A/E should check the product's performance history and the manufacturer's testing behind the stated period. Choosing by warranty length or treating duration as a proxy for service life is exactly what industry guidance cautions against.

questions.question: An owner directs the specifier to name a single brand of submersible pump, overriding the supplier's recommendation for the application. Under the UCC as industry guidance explains it, which warranty does the buyer give up by demanding one named brand?

options.A: Express warranty created by the product description
options.B: Implied warranty of merchantability
options.C: Warranty of clear title free of any security interests
options.D: Implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose

questions.explanation: The implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose depends on the buyer relying on the seller's skill and judgment to choose suitable goods. A buyer who demands a particular brand is relying on its own judgment, so industry guidance says no fitness warranty arises. Industry guidance ties only the fitness warranty to this kind of reliance on the seller.

questions.question: One specification calls for a pump; another calls for a submersible pump. The assurance that the second pump will operate under water comes from which warranty?

options.A: Express warranty based on a sample or model of the pump
options.B: Implied warranty of merchantability
options.C: Warranty of clear title to the goods
options.D: Implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose

questions.explanation: Industry guidance contrasts a generic pump, whose seller impliedly warrants it is merchantable for ordinary pump uses, with a submersible pump, whose seller may also warrant fitness for the particular purpose of working under water. Merchantability covers only ordinary purposes, title concerns ownership free of security interests, and no sample or model is involved in the illustration.

questions.question: A manufacturer's product data sheet makes a written performance claim, while fine print elsewhere in the same document disclaims that claim. Under the UCC as described, how is the conflict resolved?

options.A: Warranty language takes precedence over the conflicting disclaimer
options.B: The disclaimer controls, because it is the more specific language
options.C: Both are void, so only the implied warranties remain in effect
options.D: The disclaimer controls if it uses the words as is, with all faults

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that express warranties are disclaimed in the same manner they are created, but where warranty and disclaimer language conflict, the warranty language governs. The phrase as is, with all faults is a recognized way to disclaim implied warranties, not a way to override a conflicting express warranty. Neither specificity nor mutual voiding is the rule industry guidance gives.

questions.question: Industry guidance, citing a business law text, explains what the term merchantable means under the implied warranty of merchantability. Which quality level does it give?

options.A: Goods of fair, average, medium quality
options.B: Highest commercially available quality
options.C: Quality matching the approved sample
options.D: Quality suited to the buyer's specific use

questions.explanation: Industry guidance quotes Smith and Roberson's Business Law for the meaning of merchantable as fair, average, medium quality, meaning goods reasonably fit for the general purpose for which they are sold. Fitness for a buyer's specific use is the separate implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose, and conformance to a sample is a form of express warranty. Nothing in the definition calls for the highest available quality.

questions.question: Before starting the project manual, an A/E needs the owner's decisions on the construction contract and bidding procedures. Which document does industry guidance identify for obtaining this information?

options.A: AIA Document B101, Owner-Architect Agreement
options.B: AIA Document A701, Instructions to Bidders
options.C: AIA Document G612, Owner's Instructions to the Architect
options.D: AIA Document A201, General Conditions of the Contract for Construction

questions.explanation: Industry guidance notes that the owner typically supplies information about contract procedures and points to AIA G612, Owner's Instructions to the Architect, which has parts addressing the construction contract and bidding procedures. A701 and A201 are documents those decisions later feed into, and B101 sets out the A/E's services rather than collecting the owner's procurement decisions.
questions.source: aligning the specifications with project delivery methods and schedules

questions.question: A specifier preparing documents for a multiple-prime project with no construction manager looks for guidance. Under which delivery method or option are multiple-prime contracts normally discussed?

options.A: The construction manager as advisor/agent option
options.B: The negotiated option of the design-bid-build method
options.C: The construction manager at risk method
options.D: The design-build project delivery method

questions.explanation: Industry guidance acknowledges that multiple-prime contracts can be used without construction management but places its discussion of them under the CM as advisor/agent option in Section 10.4. The negotiated option, CMAR, and design-build are treated elsewhere and are not where industry guidance takes up multiple-prime contracting.
questions.source: aligning the specifications with project delivery methods and schedules

questions.question: An A/E moving from competitive-bid work to a project delivered under a different method asks what will shape the documents. Which may determine both the type of documents required and the methods of specifying used?

options.A: The A/E's office master specification system
options.B: The procurement and contracting procedures used
options.C: The size and complexity of the drawing set
options.D: The permit process of the authority having jurisdiction

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that procurement and contracting procedures may determine which documents are needed and how the work is specified, which is why the owner's input on contract procedures is gathered early. Office masters, drawing size, and permitting affect content but are not what industry guidance identifies as driving document type and specifying method.
questions.source: aligning the specifications with project delivery methods and schedules

questions.question: Which three options fall under the design-bid-build delivery method, and which one is treated as the baseline?

options.A: Competitive bid, competitive proposal, and negotiation; negotiation is the baseline
options.B: Competitive bid, qualifications-based selection, and negotiation; competitive bid is the baseline
options.C: Competitive bid, competitive proposal, and negotiation; competitive bid is the baseline
options.D: Competitive bid, qualifications-based selection, and negotiation; negotiation is the baseline

questions.explanation: Industry guidance lists competitive bid, competitive proposal, and negotiation as the three design-bid-build options and uses the competitive bid option as its baseline, which is why Section 10.2 concentrates on the other two. Qualifications-based selection is not one of the listed options, and the negotiated option is discussed as a variation from the baseline, not as the baseline itself.
questions.source: document variations for the Design-Bid-Build project delivery method

questions.question: A public owner uses the competitive proposal option of design-bid-build. What chiefly distinguishes it from the competitive bid option?

options.A: Proposers submit added documents used to evaluate the best-qualified contractor
options.B: The project manual is completed after negotiations begin during the early design phases
options.C: Pricing is based on outline specifications leading toward a guaranteed maximum price
options.D: The A/E shares project manual decisions with the owner and the selected contractor

questions.explanation: The competitive proposal option resembles competitive bidding except that proposers submit added documents, which the owner uses to evaluate them and pick the best-qualified contractor. Completing the project manual after negotiations start, pricing from outline specifications toward a GMP, and shared decision-making are characteristics industry guidance attributes to the negotiated option.
questions.source: document variations for the Design-Bid-Build project delivery method

questions.question: An owner selects a contractor early in design under the negotiated option of design-bid-build. What are the negotiations frequently based on?

options.A: Schematic design drawings and a preliminary description leading to unit prices
options.B: Bidding documents and a complete project manual leading to a stipulated sum
options.C: Outline specifications and design development documents leading to a GMP
options.D: Construction documents and addenda leading to cost-plus-fee without a maximum

questions.explanation: For the negotiated option, industry guidance says negotiations often rest on outline specifications and design development documents and lead to a cost-of-the-work agreement with a guaranteed maximum price. The project manual is completed afterward to finalize the design, obtain permits, and get actual prices, so a finished project manual or addenda would not be the basis. Unit prices and an open-ended fee are not what industry guidance describes.
questions.source: document variations for the Design-Bid-Build project delivery method

questions.question: On a design-bid-build project using the negotiated option, industry guidance notes the A/E will not necessarily be the sole decision-maker on items normally within its responsibility. With whom are those decisions often shared?

options.A: The owner and the construction manager
options.B: The owner and the contractor
options.C: The contractor and its major subcontractors
options.D: The owner and its cost consultant

questions.explanation: Under the negotiated option, industry guidance says other team members, especially the owner and the contractor, often share decisions the A/E would usually make alone. Sharing with the owner and a construction manager is the parallel statement industry guidance makes for CMAR projects. Subcontractors and cost consultants are not the parties industry guidance names here.

questions.question: A design-bid-build project is switched from the competitive bid option to the negotiated option. Which portion of the project manual is expected to change the most?

options.A: Division 01
options.B: Division 00
options.C: Divisions 02 through 49
options.D: PART 1 of each product section

questions.explanation: Industry guidance singles out Division 00 as the part of the project manual that changes most when a design-bid-build project moves to the competitive proposal or negotiated option, because bid forms are swapped or dropped. Division 01 needs coordination of negotiated procedures, and product sections in Divisions 02 through 49 are described as not significantly different, so neither is the area of greatest change.

questions.question: An owner intends to negotiate a design-bid-build contract directly with one contractor it trusts. The specifier is adapting the office's competitive-bid Division 00 master. What does industry guidance indicate about the procurement portion?

options.A: Each bid form should be replaced with a proposal form
options.B: The full set of bidding documents should be retained
options.C: Its requirements should be relocated into Division 01
options.D: Many of its forms and documents will be unnecessary

questions.explanation: For the negotiated option, industry guidance notes that many procurement forms and documents are not needed, since the price is reached by negotiation rather than competition. Replacing bid forms with equivalent proposal forms describes the competitive proposal option, and nothing in industry guidance calls for keeping a full bidding package or moving procurement requirements into Division 01.

questions.question: A specifier preparing Division 00 for a design-bid-build project procured by competitive proposal deletes most procurement documents, reasoning that no bids will be received. What is wrong with this approach?

options.A: The set should resemble the bid documents, with proposal forms replacing bid forms
options.B: Nothing; most procurement documents are unnecessary under the competitive proposal option
options.C: The deleted documents belong in Division 01 rather than being removed from the manual
options.D: Only the bid form should have been removed; other bidding documents stay as written

questions.explanation: Under the competitive proposal option, industry guidance describes Division 00 as much like the competitive-bid version, except that proposal forms and documents take the place of the bidding forms. Dropping most procurement documents is the pattern for the negotiated option, not competitive proposals, and industry guidance gives no basis for moving them into Division 01 or keeping the bid documents unchanged.
