questions.question: A specifier must decide where to describe site-built assemblies and site-manufactured systems within a SectionFormat section. Which part includes them?

options.A: PART 3—EXECUTION, with installation or application
options.B: PART 2—PRODUCTS, with fabrications and mixes
options.C: PART 1—GENERAL, with the section's temporary requirements
options.D: PART 2—PRODUCTS, with systems and assemblies

questions.explanation: Industry guidance places site-built assemblies and site-manufactured products and systems in PART 3—EXECUTION, along with installation or application, preparatory actions, and post-installation cleaning and protection. PART 2 covers products, fabrications, mixes, systems, and assemblies for incorporation into the project, and PART 1 covers administrative, procedural, and temporary requirements.

questions.question: To make each section 'complete,' a specifier copies the full submittal procedures from Division 01 into PART 1 of every section. What is the best course of action?

options.A: Retain the copies, since sections are meant to stand alone in bidding
options.B: Retain the copies, but add an order-of-precedence clause in Division 01
options.C: Move the procedures from Division 01 into PART 3 of each affected section
options.D: Delete the copies; add only items that supplement Division 01

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that sections are not intended to stand alone and that PART 1 should not duplicate statements in Division 01; each PART 1 article should supplement and coordinate with Division 01 to avoid repetition or conflict. Keeping the copies invites conflicting requirements, and PART 3 covers execution, not administrative procedures.

questions.question: A specifier must address a temporary requirement that applies only to the work of one section and is not covered in Division 01. Where is it described?

options.A: PART 3—EXECUTION, with preparatory actions
options.B: PART 1—GENERAL, as an extension of Division 01
options.C: PART 2—PRODUCTS, with the materials it needs
options.D: Division 01, in the temporary facilities and controls section

questions.explanation: Industry guidance says PART 1—GENERAL describes the administrative, procedural, and temporary requirements unique to the section and is an extension of subjects covered in Division 01. Division 01 covers temporary facilities and controls for the project as a whole, PART 3 covers installation and preparatory actions, and PART 2 covers products.

questions.question: A specifications manager argues that adopting CSI PageFormat in the office master is purely cosmetic because SectionFormat already governs content. Which benefit does industry guidance attribute specifically to PageFormat's uniform arrangement of text on the page?

options.A: It eases preparation, review, and publication and saves users time searching for information
options.B: It establishes the three-part structure that organizes text consistently within each section
options.C: It assigns the numbers and titles that locate each section within the project manual
options.D: It fixes the sequence of standard article titles under PART 1, PART 2, and PART 3

questions.explanation: A consistent page layout makes the document easier to prepare, check, and publish, and it helps readers locate information more quickly. Organizing text into three parts and ordering the standard article titles are handled by SectionFormat, while section numbers and titles come from MasterFormat rather than PageFormat.

questions.question: A specifier requires the flooring installer to test the in-place concrete slab for moisture vapor emission and alkalinity immediately before installing sheet vinyl. Following the SectionFormat outline, where does this preinstallation testing requirement belong?

options.A: PART 1, under the Quality Assurance article with Preconstruction Testing
options.B: PART 1, under the Administrative Requirements article with Preinstallation Meetings
options.C: PART 3, under the Examination article with Verification of Conditions
options.D: PART 3, under the Preparation article with Surface Preparation

questions.explanation: SectionFormat places Preinstallation Testing in PART 3 under EXAMINATION, with Verification of Conditions and Evaluation and Assessment, and the SectionFormat appendix uses slab vapor emission and alkalinity testing before floor finishes as its example. Preconstruction Testing under PART 1 Quality Assurance qualifies products before procurement, Preinstallation Meetings fall under PART 1 Administrative Requirements, and Surface Preparation under PART 3 Preparation covers readying the substrate, not testing it.

questions.question: A specification requires concrete proportioned at four parts coarse aggregate, two parts fine aggregate, and one part cement with a 0.5 water-cement ratio. The contractor supplies concrete exactly as proportioned, but it does not withstand a 3000 psi load. Who is responsible for the shortfall?

options.A: The contractor, because 3000 psi strength is implied by the specified mix
options.B: The A/E, because it assumes the burden of performance under this method
options.C: The concrete supplier, because it furnished the mix that failed to perform
options.D: The contractor and A/E jointly, because the strength was implied but unstated

questions.explanation: Industry guidance uses this mix-design case to illustrate descriptive specifying: the 3000 psi strength is only implied by the proportions, never stated, so the contractor who followed the mix cannot be held to it. Under a descriptive specification the A/E carries responsibility for how the product performs. Neither the contractor nor the supplier is bound by an unstated strength, and industry guidance does not describe any joint responsibility.

questions.question: A state agency's enabling statute prohibits naming manufacturers in its construction specifications, and no adequate industry reference standard exists for a custom-fabricated lobby screen. Which specifying method may be the only logical choice?

options.A: Reference standard specifying, citing the nearest related industry standard
options.B: Open proprietary specifying, naming three products followed by 'or equal'
options.C: Closed proprietary specifying, naming the single product that suits the design
options.D: Descriptive specifying, detailing the required properties and workmanship

questions.explanation: Industry guidance notes that a descriptive specification may be the only sensible option when the law bars naming products and no suitable reference standard is available. Both proprietary methods name products, which the statute prohibits, and reference standard specifying fails here because no adequate standard exists.

questions.question: A senior specifier notes that her firm now writes far fewer descriptive specifications than it did 30 years ago. Which explanation for this trend does industry guidance give?

options.A: Projects have become more complex, and better reference standards are now available
options.B: Public owners now prohibit descriptive text, and proprietary names are now preferred
options.C: Descriptive text shifts performance risk to contractors, who now decline to accept it
options.D: Building codes now mandate performance criteria for most products and assemblies

questions.explanation: Industry guidance notes the once widely preferred descriptive method is used less often as projects become more complex and better reference standards become available. Descriptive specifying places the performance burden on the A/E, not the contractor, and industry guidance cites it as the logical choice where proprietary names are prohibited, so the public-owner and contractor-risk options invert recommended practice. Codes are said to be moving toward performance criteria, not mandating them.

questions.question: While preparing a descriptive specification for a commodity shelf bracket, a specifier finds that catalog information fully describes the product and that a manufacturer's product certification covers every required property. Following the fifth step in preparing descriptive specifications, which submittal and testing requirements should the section include?

options.A: Shop drawings and a product certification, with no laboratory tests
options.B: Product data and a product certification, with no shop drawings or tests
options.C: Product data and independent laboratory tests, with no shop drawings
options.D: Shop drawings, product data, and independent laboratory tests of each property

questions.explanation: Step 5 says to specify only the submittals, testing, and procedures necessary to ensure acceptable products are provided. Industry guidance adds that extensive shop drawings should not be required if catalog information is adequate, and tests should not be required if a product certification suffices. Catalog data and a certification cover everything here, so any option adding shop drawings or independent tests goes beyond step 5.

questions.question: Drafting a descriptive specification for a door closer, a specifier combines the slimmest arm profile from one manufacturer, the highest cycle rating from a second, and the widest backcheck adjustment from a third. Which risk does industry guidance warn this practice creates?

options.A: The section becomes proprietary because three manufacturers are implied
options.B: The section may describe a product that does not actually exist
options.C: The A/E shifts the burden of performance onto the hardware supplier
options.D: The section may require tests where a product certification would suffice

questions.explanation: Industry guidance cautions in step 4 that picking the best individual features from several manufacturers can produce a description that matches no real product. Under descriptive specifying the A/E keeps the burden of performance, and implying multiple sources does not turn a section proprietary. Excessive testing is a separate step 5 issue, not a consequence of combining features.

questions.question: A specifier writes a descriptive specification for a shelf support assembly. Which information would be shown on the drawings rather than in the specification?

options.A: Finish of the standards and the type of mounting screws
options.B: Maximum spacing of mounting screws and slot spacing
options.C: Bracket depth at the butt and at the tip
options.D: Location, length, and spacing of the supports

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that location, length, and spacing of the supports would be shown on the drawings, consistent with step 3 of deciding which features are best specified and which are best shown. The specification itself covers the standards' finish, screw type and maximum screw spacing, slot spacing, and bracket depths at butt and tip, so those belong in the specification.

questions.question: A performance specification for an operable partition states the required sound transmission class but provides no means to measure, test, or evaluate whether the installed partition achieves it. Which element of a complete performance specification is deficient?

options.A: A statement of the required results
options.B: Freedom from unnecessary limitations on methods
options.C: Criteria for verifying compliance
options.D: A description of the means of achieving results

questions.explanation: Industry guidance defines a performance specification as a statement of required results, with criteria for verifying compliance, without unnecessary limitations on methods. The verification element requires criteria capable of measurement, test, evaluation, or other acceptable assurances, which is what is missing here. The required result (the STC rating) is stated, nothing limits methods, and describing the means is contrary to performance specifying.

questions.question: A design-build RFP's performance specification for a building envelope omits several of the end results the owner actually expects. What is the principal risk of this incomplete statement of required results?

options.A: Requirements that no manufacturer can meet, making the work unachievable
options.B: Loss of quality control over materials, equipment, and workmanship
options.C: Transfer of the burden of performance from the contractor back to the A/E
options.D: Restriction of competition to the single product that the A/E had in mind

questions.explanation: Industry guidance says desired end results must be spelled out, and an incomplete performance specification may lead to a significant loss of quality control over materials, equipment, and workmanship. Unachievable requirements result from criteria no manufacturer can meet, a different error, and burden shifting and restricted competition are not the consequences industry guidance ties to omitted results.

questions.question: A performance specification for a curtain wall requires that water penetration resistance be verified after the building has been occupied through one full rainy season. A reviewer objects that performance criteria must be verified before installation. How should the specifier respond?

options.A: Keep it; measurement and testing may occur after a period of service
options.B: Revise it; measurement and testing must occur before production
options.C: Revise it; measurement and testing must occur at the time of production
options.D: Keep it, but only if testing is also performed in place at the site

questions.explanation: Industry guidance allows verification of performance at several stages: ahead of production, during production, in place on site, or once the work has been in service for a while. Testing after a rainy season of occupancy is therefore acceptable by itself. The revise options incorrectly restrict verification to a single stage, and industry guidance does not require it to be paired with on-site testing.

questions.question: A specifier knows exactly which ceiling-hanger wire she wants and plans to write a full set of performance criteria derived from that wire's properties so that bidders will provide it. What is the better course?

options.A: Write the criteria anyway, since performance language invites innovation
options.B: Delete the product name and list its catalog properties as the criteria
options.C: Use a systems approach and leave the hanger design to the contractor
options.D: Describe the wire directly, stating its gage, coating, and annealing

questions.explanation: Industry guidance says that working backward from a known item to performance criteria takes much more time and effort and secures nothing better than descriptive or proprietary specifying. It notes it is much easier to ask for 10-gage galvanized, annealed steel wire. Copying catalog properties without a name is the closed proprietary pattern industry guidance criticizes elsewhere, and a systems approach abandons the known product.

questions.question: An owner intends to make performance specifying the primary mode of design and contracting for a new transit maintenance facility. What should the project team anticipate?

options.A: Standard contract documents, with simpler procedures and fewer participants
options.B: Specialized contract documents, with complex procedures and many participants
options.C: Standard contract documents, with complex procedures and many participants
options.D: Specialized contract documents, with simpler procedures and fewer participants

questions.explanation: Industry guidance explains that when performance specifying drives design and contracting, the project often needs specialized contract documents, and its procedures become more complex and typically involve many different parties. Each distractor is wrong on at least one count, predicting standard documents, simpler procedures, or fewer participants.

questions.question: Who should determine a project's suitability for performance specifying, and at what point?

options.A: The A/E alone, during the construction documents phase
options.B: The owner and the A/E, early in the planning process
options.C: The owner and the contractor, during the procurement phase
options.D: The A/E and the AHJ, during design development review

questions.explanation: Industry guidance assigns this decision to the owner and the A/E together, and it should be made at the start of planning. Deferring it to the construction documents or procurement phase is too late, and industry guidance does not name the contractor or the AHJ as participants in the decision.

questions.question: An owner's main concern is speed: a data center must open within 14 months. The owner wants proposers to offer any proven, commercially available modular power system that meets stated capacities. Which owner need listed in industry guidance as a reason for performance specifying does this best reflect?

options.A: To utilize technology not yet standardized within the industry
options.B: To develop new technology through the project's procurement
options.C: To expedite construction and access a wide range of existing options
options.D: To delegate technical design responsibility to industry specialists

questions.explanation: Industry guidance lists expediting construction and accessing a wide range of options using existing technology and systems techniques as one owner need that makes performance specifying feasible. The scenario's schedule pressure and proven, commercially available systems match that need. Unstandardized or new technology does not fit proven products, and the owner is choosing among existing systems rather than delegating design.

questions.question: A design architect tells the owner that performance specifying is all-or-nothing: either every section is performance-based or none is. Which statement corrects this?

options.A: Performance specifying is limited to complete systems and never single attributes
options.B: Performance specifying applies only where codes have adopted performance criteria
options.C: Performance specifying is reserved for projects using design-build delivery
options.D: Performance specifying can extend from a single attribute to an entire project

questions.explanation: Industry guidance describes performance specifying as scalable, ranging anywhere from one attribute up to a whole project, with many variations between those extremes. It does not confine the method to complete systems, to criteria already adopted by codes, or to design-build delivery; it simply observes that codes and standards are trending toward performance criteria.

questions.question: A specifier cites an industry-accepted standard for gypsum board rather than writing detailed product requirements. What does referencing the standard establish, and what does it provide?

options.A: Minimum requirements, giving greater confidence in the outcome of its use
options.B: Maximum requirements, limiting the contractor's liability to the standard
options.C: Exact requirements, eliminating the need to review related submittals
options.D: Recommended practices, which the contractor may adopt at its option

questions.explanation: Industry guidance explains that citing a standard sets minimum requirements, which gives the specifier greater assurance about how the product will perform on the project. Reference standards establish minimums rather than maximums or exact limits, submittals still need review to enforce them, and a cited standard is mandatory, not optional for the contractor.

questions.question: A specifier is deciding whether to cite an industry-accepted standard for vinyl composition tile or to write out detailed product requirements in the section. Which observation about reference standard specifying supports citing the standard?

options.A: Reference standards set maximum values, which limits the contractor's liability
options.B: Citing a standard avoids duplication and contradiction with other documents
options.C: Many manufacturers know the standards that shape their products' development
options.D: AHJs enforce the same edition of each standard, which simplifies compliance

questions.explanation: Industry guidance notes that many product manufacturers are familiar with the reference standards that shape and steer product development, and that referencing a standard to set minimum requirements gives the specifier more confidence in the outcome. Standards generally set minimums, not maximums; industry guidance cautions that they can create duplication and contradiction; and AHJs may enforce different editions of the same standard.

questions.question: A section's References article lists 'ASTM International (ASTM) C150/C150M, Standard Specification for Portland Cement,' and the entire standard applies to the work. Judged against the elements of a complete reference standard designation, what is missing?

options.A: A citation of the applicable requirements within the standard
options.B: The website address where the standard may be purchased
options.C: The mailing address of the issuing organization
options.D: The date of issue of the standard

questions.explanation: Industry guidance lists the elements of a complete designation as the issuing organization's name, number, title, date of issue, and citation of applicable requirements unless the entire standard is required. Because the whole standard applies, no citation is needed, so only the date of issue is missing. Websites and organization addresses are optional additions, not designation elements.

questions.question: Rather than spelling out each standards-issuing organization's name at first mention in every section, a specifier wants one central place in the project manual that defines those abbreviations and can also list the organizations' addresses. Where does this belong?

options.A: Division 01, Section 01 42 00—References
options.B: Division 01, Section 01 41 00—Regulatory Requirements
options.C: Division 01, Section 01 43 00—Quality Assurance
options.D: Division 00, Document 00 21 13—Instructions to Bidders

questions.explanation: The second approach places the definitions of all standards-organization abbreviations in Section 01 42 00 in Division 01, and that section can also list the organizations' addresses. The first approach instead writes out the full name with its initials the first time it appears in each section. Industry guidance does not put these definitions in regulatory requirements, quality assurance, or the instructions to bidders.

questions.question: While updating the office master, a specifier uses the standards organizations' current catalogs to replace each dated reference with the year of the latest edition. What must the A/E also do before changing these publication dates?

options.A: Obtain the contractor's agreement to cite the newer editions
options.B: Obtain the owner's written approval of each newer edition
options.C: Move the dated designations from PART 1 into Division 01
options.D: Review the changes made to each standard in the new edition

questions.explanation: Industry guidance cautions that the A/E should not simply update a publication year without first studying what changed in the newer edition; when dates are listed, identifying the correct edition is the A/E's job. Contractor agreement and owner approval play no part in this step, and the dated-designation approach keeps them in the PART 1 References article.

questions.question: A project manual lists reference standards without dates. To avoid contradictions among editions, a statement in Section 01 42 00 is recommended that fixes the governing date as the one in effect as of:

options.A: The date of the owner-contractor agreement, or as adopted by the AHJs
options.B: The date of the notice to proceed, or as accepted by the A/E
options.C: The date of receipt of bids, or as adopted by the AHJs
options.D: The date the specifications were issued, or the latest edition

questions.explanation: The recommended Section 01 42 00 statement ties the standard's date to the date of receipt of bids or as adopted by the AHJs. The agreement date, notice to proceed, and specification issue date are near-miss milestones that do not appear in the statement, and the A/E's acceptance is not part of it.

questions.question: Under the two approaches to dating reference standards, who determines the applicable edition when dates are listed, and who becomes responsible for checking compliance when standards are undated and Section 01 42 00 carries the recommended statement?

options.A: The A/E when dates are listed; the contractor when undated
options.B: The contractor when dates are listed; the A/E when undated
options.C: The A/E when dates are listed; the AHJ when undated
options.D: The AHJ when dates are listed; the contractor when undated

questions.explanation: Listing dates makes the A/E responsible for identifying the applicable or most recent edition. If dates are left out and Section 01 42 00 includes the recommended statement, responsibility for verifying compliance shifts to the contractor. An AHJ may adopt particular editions, but industry guidance assigns neither duty to it.

questions.question: A specifier wants to cite a tentative standard for a new anchor test method because it reflects the sponsoring organization's latest practice. What is the principal concern with doing so?

options.A: It has not yet been approved by the sponsoring organization
options.B: It is unofficial, and AHJs usually do not accept it
options.C: It reflects practices the final standard will likely supersede
options.D: It must be quoted in full because it is not yet published

questions.explanation: Industry guidance says tentative draft standards are usually not accepted by AHJs and that A/Es should use them with caution because of their unofficial status. They have already been approved by the sponsoring organization but await final approval by its membership or other stakeholders, and they usually represent its latest thinking rather than outdated practice. Industry guidance says nothing about quoting them in full.

questions.question: A specifier references ASTM C1193 for sealant joints and is deciding how to handle the portions of that standard that matter most on this project. Which approach follows industry guidance?

options.A: Quote the clauses most pertinent to the work so bidders see them
options.B: Cite specific clauses that bidders commonly overlook, for emphasis
options.C: Cite a specific clause only where the specification modifies that clause
options.D: Reproduce pertinent clauses verbatim so bidders need not buy the standard

questions.explanation: Industry guidance advises citing an individual clause of a standard only when the specification changes what that clause requires. It discourages referencing a standard and then quoting selected passages, since the quotation may be inaccurate and readers may conclude that only the quoted text applies. Singling out clauses just for emphasis creates the same misunderstanding.

questions.question: Once reference standards are specified, the usual methods of ensuring conformance include checking shop drawings, samples, manufacturers' literature, test reports, and other required submittals, plus periodic on-site observations by:

options.A: Field representatives sent by the standards-issuing organizations
options.B: Building inspectors employed by the authorities having jurisdiction
options.C: The contractor's quality control manager and independent testing agency
options.D: Construction contract administrators or knowledgeable design team members

questions.explanation: Industry guidance lists submittal checking plus periodic on-site observations by construction contract administrators or knowledgeable design team members as the usual means of enforcing referenced standards. Standards organizations do not observe projects, and industry guidance does not assign this enforcement role to AHJ inspectors or the contractor's own quality control staff.
questions.source: enforce the requirements of the standard

questions.question: A section names three acceptable manufacturers for a fire alarm control panel and states that no other products will be considered and that bids must be based on one of those named. How does industry guidance classify this specification?

options.A: Closed proprietary, because substitutions are not allowed
options.B: Open proprietary, because more than one product is named
options.C: Non-restrictive, because at least three products are named
options.D: Open proprietary, because bidders may choose among products

questions.explanation: Industry guidance says the fundamental distinction between closed and open proprietary specifications is how they handle substitutions. A closed specification may name one product or several as options, but substitutions are not allowed. Naming several products does not make it open, and naming three without accepting equals is not non-restrictive.

questions.question: An owner's project manager asks why the A/E chose to proprietary-specify the curtain wall system. Which reason does industry guidance list as an advantage of proprietary specifications?

options.A: The contractor's prior experience with the named product is assured
options.B: The named product's continued availability through construction is assured
options.C: More detailed drawings can be prepared from the manufacturer's precise data
options.D: Errors in model and product designations are eliminated from the documents

questions.explanation: Among the listed advantages is that more detailed and complete drawings can be prepared from precise information obtained from the selected manufacturer's data. The other choices contradict listed disadvantages: the contractor may have had little or negative experience, the product may no longer be available, and errors may occur in model or product designations.

questions.question: On a closed proprietary specification naming optional products, how does industry guidance say control of products and substitutions is accomplished?

options.A: By the instructions for procurement, cross-referencing Section 01 42 00
options.B: By the instructions for procurement, cross-referencing Section 01 25 13
options.C: By the supplementary conditions, cross-referencing Section 01 25 13
options.D: By the supplementary conditions, cross-referencing Section 01 42 00

questions.explanation: Industry guidance explains that products and substitutions are controlled through a cross-reference from the instructions for procurement to Section 01 25 13, Product Substitution Procedures. Section 01 42 00 addresses references rather than substitutions, and industry guidance does not assign this control to the supplementary conditions.

questions.question: A closed proprietary specification names four acceptable manufacturers for toilet compartments, and no substitutes will be considered. The A/E wants to know promptly which of the four products the successful bidder priced. What may the specifications require?

options.A: A substitution request identifying the product within 10 days of award
options.B: A product selection list at bid time or within a few days after opening
options.C: Identification of the product in the first shop drawing submittal after award
options.D: A/E selection among the named products at the preconstruction conference

questions.explanation: Under the optional product approach, industry guidance says the successful contractor may be required to submit a product selection list when bids are received or within a few days after bid opening. A substitution request does not apply because no substitutes are considered. Waiting for shop drawings or having the A/E choose at a conference is not the mechanism industry guidance describes.

questions.question: On a project using controlled substitutions, the A/E sets the deadline for bidders' substitution requests and will issue written acceptances to all bidders by addendum. At least how much time should be allowed between that deadline and publication of the addendum?

options.A: Three days
options.B: Five days
options.C: Seven days
options.D: Ten days

questions.explanation: Industry guidance recommends allowing a minimum of three days between the request deadline and issuing the addendum so requests can be properly evaluated, and the A/E decides the deadline itself. Ten days is a distractor drawn from the sample instruction asking that requests arrive at least 10 days before bids are due, which is a different interval.

questions.question: During bidding, (1) a roofer asks to replace the specified membrane with another manufacturer's product, and (2) the bid form requests an added price for a named upgraded membrane. Using standard terminology, what are items (1) and (2)?

options.A: (1) an alternate; (2) a substitute
options.B: (1) an alternate; (2) an alternate
options.C: (1) a substitute; (2) a substitute
options.D: (1) a substitute; (2) an alternate

questions.explanation: Industry guidance notes the terms are often misused: an alternate is something named for which alternative pricing is requested, and a substitute is something requested to replace a specified item. The roofer's request to replace the membrane is a substitute, and the named upgrade priced on the bid form is an alternate.

questions.question: For a hospital's emergency power transfer switches, the owner values assured performance far above competitive pricing. Which proprietary approach best fits this item?

options.A: Open proprietary with controlled substitutions under Section 01 25 13
options.B: Closed proprietary that prohibits substitutions entirely
options.C: Open proprietary that invites proposed substitutions with bid prices
options.D: Three named products, each followed by 'or equal' to admit equals

questions.explanation: Industry guidance says accepting substitutions opens the project to unknown and perhaps inferior products, and if the item is part of a vital system, a proprietary specification prohibiting substitutions entirely may be called for. Controlled substitutions, proposed substitutions, and 'or equal' language all admit other products, which suits projects where keen competition and low cost outweigh assured performance, the opposite of this owner's priority.

questions.question: A firm on a compressed design schedule wants to minimize its own design and specifying effort for interior finishes. Which method is best from that standpoint, and why?

options.A: Open proprietary, because bidders carry the burden of proving comparability
options.B: Open proprietary, because A/E workload falls as bidders' choices increase
options.C: Closed proprietary, because one named product speeds the documents
options.D: Descriptive, because no product research is needed before writing

questions.explanation: Industry guidance says the closed proprietary method is best for reducing design and specifying effort, because naming one product per application lets drawings and specifications be completed quickly and precisely. Open specifications increase A/E workload in direct proportion to the bidders' degree of choice, and descriptive specifying begins with researching available products.

questions.question: An owner insists that substitutions be allowed on a school project to get the lowest material costs. The A/E worries that apparent savings may be lost to high maintenance and replacement costs. What should the A/E do?

options.A: Word the procurement documents to give a definite, controllable review method
options.B: Prohibit all substitutions, since cost must never outweigh assured performance
options.C: Append 'or equal' after every product name to signal substitutions are allowed
options.D: Let the contractor approve substitutions to speed the procurement process

questions.explanation: Industry guidance notes that permitting substitutions lowers material costs but invites lesser products whose savings can be lost to maintenance and replacement. Its answer is for the A/E to carefully word the procurement documents to provide a definite, controllable method for review and approval. Industry guidance allows substitutions where competition and low cost are more critical, calls repeated 'or equal' awkward, and keeps approval with the A/E.

questions.question: For a public project, a specifier deletes a manufacturer's name and lists that product's salient qualities verbatim from its literature as the requirements, giving no ranges. How does industry guidance characterize the result?

options.A: A non-restrictive performance specification, since no name appears
options.B: An open proprietary specification, since substitutions are not barred
options.C: A fully proprietary, closed specification despite the missing name
options.D: A descriptive specification that is suitable for most public work

questions.explanation: Industry guidance calls this a proprietary specification masquerading as a performance specification. Because no ranges of characteristics or performance are given, it results in a fully proprietary, closed specification unsuitable for a non-restrictive project. Removing the name does not make it non-restrictive, open, or an acceptable descriptive specification.

questions.question: To convert a closed proprietary specification into a non-restrictive one for a public agency, what does industry guidance say such agencies usually require?

options.A: At least three brand names plus 'or equal,' with salient characteristics described
options.B: At least two brand names plus 'or equal,' with salient characteristics described
options.C: At least three brand names plus 'or equal,' with an applicable reference standard cited
options.D: At least two brand names plus 'or equal,' with an applicable reference standard cited

questions.explanation: Industry guidance says public agencies usually require a minimum of three brand names followed by 'or equal,' along with descriptions of the salient characteristics of the item to provide a basis for judging equality. Two names is a near-miss count, and a cited reference standard is not the basis industry guidance names for judging equality.

questions.question: On a federally assisted project, a specifier writes a performance specification for laboratory casework that names no manufacturer, but only one manufacturer's product can meet the combined criteria. How should this specification be characterized?

options.A: Non-restrictive, because no proprietary name appears in it
options.B: Non-restrictive, because performance methods are inherently open
options.C: Open proprietary, because other products may still be proposed
options.D: Restrictive, even though no proprietary name appears in it

questions.explanation: Industry guidance says descriptive and performance specifications can easily be used for non-restrictive specifications, but care must be taken that several manufacturers or suppliers can meet the requirements. Failure to do so makes the specifications restrictive even though no proprietary name has been used. Omitting names or using performance language does not by itself make a specification non-restrictive.

questions.question: An owner's representative believes performance specifying suits only whole-building design-build procurements. What are the narrowest and broadest scales to which performance specifying can be extended?

options.A: From a single product up to a complete system or assembly
options.B: From a single attribute up to an entire project
options.C: From a single component up to one complete specification section
options.D: From one specification section up to an entire division

questions.explanation: Industry guidance describes performance specifying as scalable: it can extend from a single attribute to an entire project, with many variations between those extremes. The other options set the wrong endpoints (a product, component, or section at the narrow end; an assembly, a section, or a division at the broad end), and whole-building design-build use is only the broad extreme of the range.

questions.question: A specifier wants bidders to be free to offer different solutions, provided each one meets the same requirements. Which feature of performance specifying provides this flexibility?

options.A: Allowing substitution requests after the contract is awarded
options.B: Naming several acceptable manufacturers for each product
options.C: Incorporating a recognized industry standard by reference
options.D: Defining the end result that the work must achieve

questions.explanation: Because performance specifying states the end result rather than the means, it allows optional solutions as long as each satisfies the same requirements. Substitution procedures, multiple named manufacturers, and reference standards are separate devices, not the feature of performance specifying that industry guidance credits with this flexibility.

questions.question: A firm's newest specifier has read about performance specifying and is about to write a complete performance-based section. Which caution applies to this step?

options.A: Putting it into an entire section can be hard for those with little experience
options.B: Describing it is the hard part; putting it into a section is straightforward
options.C: It can be applied to individual attributes but never to an entire section
options.D: A complete performance section may be written only for a design-build contract

questions.explanation: Industry guidance observes that performance specifying is easy to describe but can be hard to apply in a real document, such as a whole specification section, for someone with little experience in it. The second option reverses that point, the third conflicts with the statement that it can extend to an entire project, and industry guidance places no design-build-only limit on writing a performance section.

questions.question: When performance specifying is used for complete construction systems and assemblies, what does industry guidance identify as a primary advantage?

options.A: Attracting research-and-development expertise and resources to create new products
options.B: Delegating final design and construction tasks to a design-builder entity
options.C: Using available products and systems for conventional project requirements
options.D: Describing emerging systems the A/E is not familiar enough with to detail

questions.explanation: Industry guidance names the use of available products and systems to meet conventional project requirements as a primary advantage of performance specifying. Attracting R&D expertise is the advantage cited for developing new technology, delegating to a design-builder belongs to delegating responsibilities, and unfamiliar emerging systems are the non-standard technologies context.

questions.question: A school district planning a modest classroom addition wants to performance specify the roofing and HVAC using readily available systems, but its board believes performance specifying is reserved for large programs. Which response is consistent with industry guidance?

options.A: Relying on existing technology makes it practical even for smaller projects
options.B: It is generally limited to large public agencies with high construction volume
options.C: It is practical for a small project only when the entire project is included
options.D: It is practical for a small project only under design-build project delivery

questions.explanation: Industry guidance explains that because it draws on existing technology, performance specifying is practical even for smaller projects and may cover all or part of a project. The large-owner limitation applies to using performance specifications to develop new technology, not to available systems, and industry guidance imposes no whole-project or design-build condition for small projects.

questions.question: A specifier intends to performance specify an entire building enclosure assembly that will require specialized engineering and performance-based criteria. What does industry guidance note about this level of performance specifying?

options.A: It must be limited to portions of a project, not complete assemblies
options.B: It requires the owner to fund prototype tests before solicitation
options.C: It is feasible only for owners with in-house engineering departments
options.D: It may be subject to licensure and regulation by the AHJs

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that entire systems and assemblies may require specialized engineering and performance-based criteria, and that this level of performance specifying may be subject to licensure and regulation by AHJs. Industry guidance says performance specifying can apply to complete systems and assemblies; prototype-test expense is a disadvantage of developing new technology; and in-house departments are not stated as a prerequisite.

questions.question: An A/E must specify a building monitoring system. The system is not entirely new, but it has not yet evolved into settled configurations, and no alternatives are similar enough to describe without excluding other variations. Under which performance specifying context does this fall?

options.A: Developing new technology
options.B: Utilizing non-standard technologies
options.C: Construction systems and assemblies
options.D: Delegating responsibilities

questions.explanation: Industry guidance covers products that emerge from research and development and are not entirely new, but whose development leaves no alternatives similar enough to specify descriptively; building monitoring systems are one of its examples. Developing new technology applies where existing products do not suit the owner's needs and innovation must be encouraged, and the other two contexts concern available systems and design-build delegation.

questions.question: Industry guidance notes that sustainable design certifications are increasing the need for alternative solutions to traditional construction. It cites LEED for structures; which certification does it cite for infrastructures?

options.A: Green Globes
options.B: WELL Building Standard
options.C: Envision
options.D: Living Building Challenge

questions.explanation: Industry guidance names Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design (LEED) for structures and Envision for infrastructures as certifications that make alternative solutions to traditional construction necessary. The other rating systems are not the infrastructure certification industry guidance cites.

questions.question: Which group does industry guidance give as examples of products and systems whose stage of development may leave no alternatives similar enough to specify descriptively?

options.A: Alternative energy, environmental control, building monitoring, and data systems
options.B: Wood or metal trusses, precast concrete, and certain types of foundation systems
options.C: New materials made from recycled pre-consumer and post-consumer waste streams
options.D: Fire sprinkler systems, curtain walls, and sophisticated exterior cladding systems

questions.explanation: Industry guidance lists alternative energy systems, environmental control systems, building monitoring systems, and data and communication systems as examples of non-standard technologies. Trusses, precast concrete, and foundations are the examples of design transfer to engineered elements, and recycled-content materials are cited under developing new technology.

questions.question: A specifier's office master roofing section was written for conventional membrane roofs, but the project now includes a green roof to support a LEED goal. What point does the green roof example illustrate?

options.A: Green roofs are entirely new technology that must be prototype tested first
options.B: Green roofs must be specified descriptively in order to qualify for LEED
options.C: Green roofs shift roof design responsibility to the roofing system manufacturer
options.D: Non-traditional roofing calls for rethinking traditional roofing requirements

questions.explanation: Industry guidance cites green roofs as an example of non-traditional roofing that requires reconsideration of traditional roofing requirements. Industry guidance does not call them entirely new technology needing prototype tests, does not require descriptive specifying for LEED, and does not tie them to a transfer of design responsibility.

questions.question: The owner of a single small office building wants to use performance specifications to spur development of a new exterior wall technology that no manufacturer currently produces. Which advice best reflects industry guidance?

options.A: Proceed, since performance specifying is practical even for smaller projects
options.B: Reconsider, since this use is generally limited to large, high-volume owners
options.C: Proceed, provided the AHJ agrees to issue a contingent building permit
options.D: Reconsider, since new materials cannot be described by salient characteristics

questions.explanation: Industry guidance says using performance specifications to develop new technology is generally feasible only for large corporate owners or public agencies that build in high volume, given the time, expense, and need for economies of scale. Practicality for smaller projects applies to existing technology, not development of new products, and a contingent permit does not address the owner's cost and risk.

questions.question: Shortcomings in available technology that lead an owner to encourage innovation may relate to which factors?

options.A: Aesthetic quality, long-term durability, or warranty duration
options.B: Code compliance, design licensure, or permit timing
options.C: Technical capabilities, construction cost, or expediency
options.D: Product availability, bidder competition, or labor participation

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that shortcomings in available technology may relate to technical capabilities, construction cost, or expediency. The other lists borrow terms from neighboring topics, such as licensure, competition, and labor participation, that industry guidance does not give as these shortcomings.

questions.question: A specifier wants to allow a newly developed panel product made from recycled pre-consumer and post-consumer waste. How can such new materials be utilized?

options.A: By stating performance requirements that describe their salient characteristics
options.B: By naming the developing manufacturer and excluding unproven alternatives
options.C: By referencing the industry standard that governs the conventional product
options.D: By deferring their use to substitution procedures after the contract award

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that new materials consisting of recycled pre-consumer and post-consumer waste can be utilized by providing performance requirements describing the salient characteristics. Naming a single manufacturer, borrowing the conventional product's standard, or deferring to substitutions are not the means industry guidance describes.

questions.question: A public agency plans to use performance specifications to obtain a unique modular wall system for one building, with no plan to use the system again. Which concern applies most directly?

options.A: The system must be limited to products that manufacturers already produce
options.B: Performance specifying gives no access to industry research and development
options.C: The new system must first be described by detailed prescriptive requirements
options.D: The requirements must gain economies of scale to offset the production expense

questions.explanation: Industry guidance cautions that requirements for newly developed technology must achieve economies of scale, since producing a one-of-a-kind product, system, or assembly can be very costly. Industry guidance presents attracting R&D expertise as an advantage of this approach, and it neither limits the work to existing products nor requires prescriptive descriptions first.

questions.question: A national retail chain with an extensive, ongoing construction program maintains its own architectural department but does not want to assume full design or construction responsibilities. To whom may such owners pass those responsibilities?

options.A: The construction manager as advisor
options.B: The supplier
options.C: The authority having jurisdiction
options.D: The owner's facility manager

questions.explanation: Industry guidance notes that many owners with large, continuing construction programs keep in-house architectural or engineering departments yet choose not to take on full design or construction responsibility, passing it instead to the supplier. Industry guidance does not assign these responsibilities to a CM-advisor, an AHJ, or the owner's facility manager.

questions.question: An owner intends to use performance specifying to establish its project requirements and then hand off the remaining design and construction work. Which project delivery method does industry guidance associate with this approach?

options.A: Design-bid-build
options.B: Construction manager as advisor/agent
options.C: Construction manager as constructor
options.D: Design-build

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that an owner can use performance specifying to establish its requirements for a project using the design-build project delivery method. Design-bid-build and the construction manager methods are not the delivery method industry guidance ties to this delegation.

questions.question: When responsibilities are delegated through performance specifying, which allocation of tasks is correct?

options.A: Owner sets requirements by performance criteria; design-builder does final design and construction
options.B: Design-builder sets the performance criteria; owner completes final design before construction begins
options.C: Owner completes the final design; design-builder writes the performance criteria for construction
options.D: Owner's A/E does final design; design-builder only verifies compliance with the performance criteria

questions.explanation: Industry guidance describes the owner using performance criteria to hand off final design and construction to the design-builder, relying on well-developed performance specifications to make sure its needs are met. The other options reverse who sets the criteria or leave final design with the owner or its A/E.

questions.question: A project team member argues that moving some packages to performance-oriented procurement and contracting will not change anyone's role. Which statement reflects industry guidance?

options.A: Roles stay unchanged, because only the method of specifying is different
options.B: All design responsibility then transfers from the A/E to the contractor
options.C: Some customary roles and responsibilities of participants may be altered
options.D: Roles may shift, but only on projects using design-build delivery

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that performance-oriented design, documentation, procurement, and contracting may change some of the roles and responsibilities participants traditionally assume. It does not say roles are unchanged, that all design moves to the contractor, or that the changes are confined to design-build; industry guidance also discusses multiple-prime and CM-advisor/agent settings.

questions.question: An owner wants to issue performance criteria for a new laboratory but also expects to reject any compliant solution it finds unappealing. What should the A/E advise, consistent with industry guidance?

options.A: The owner may still reject any compliant solution during submittal review
options.B: The owner keeps full control because it alone writes the criteria
options.C: The owner should have the contractor write the criteria to share that risk
options.D: The owner gives up some control and must accept results meeting the criteria

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that by using performance criteria the owner relinquishes some control over the solution and must be willing to accept the results of the criteria. That is why the owner must be able to communicate the criteria thoroughly; rejecting compliant solutions, claiming full control, or handing criteria writing to the contractor conflict with this.

questions.question: An owner begins a project by defining its requirements as performance criteria and intends to use design-build delivery. The criteria might then be used to prepare which document?

options.A: An invitation to bid
options.B: A request for proposals
options.C: The instructions to bidders
options.D: A bid form and supplements

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that the owner may define project requirements via performance criteria, which might then be used to prepare a request for proposals using the design-build delivery method. Invitations to bid, instructions to bidders, and bid forms are bidding documents, not the document industry guidance names for this purpose.

questions.question: An owner's facilities director asks how relying on performance criteria might change the owner's own work during planning. Which effect does industry guidance describe?

options.A: It may prompt a more comprehensive analysis of needs than usual
options.B: It reduces the need to communicate the criteria in full detail
options.C: It increases the owner's control over the selected final solution
options.D: It shifts the burden of analyzing needs to the design-builder

questions.explanation: Industry guidance says this feature of performance specifying may encourage the owner to perform a more comprehensive analysis of needs than in a traditional relationship. Industry guidance also says the owner must communicate criteria thoroughly and relinquishes some control, which rules out the second and third options.

questions.question: Industry guidance notes that performance specifying may also be a form of design transfer. Which element does it list as one where this is frequently the case?

options.A: Building monitoring systems
options.B: Green roof assemblies
options.C: Precast concrete
options.D: Data and communication systems

questions.explanation: Industry guidance says performance specifying can amount to design transfer, which often occurs with engineered elements like wood or metal trusses, precast concrete, and some foundations. Building monitoring and data and communication systems are the examples of non-standard technologies, and green roofs illustrate non-traditional roofing.

questions.question: An A/E plans to performance specify metal trusses so that the fabricator's engineer completes the truss design. What regulatory caution does industry guidance raise for this situation?

options.A: AHJs will not issue any permit until the truss design is complete
options.B: Some states may limit the transfer of design from the A/E of record
options.C: Design transfer is allowed only under design-build project delivery
options.D: The truss manufacturer must also provide its specialized installation

questions.explanation: Industry guidance cautions that regulations in some states may restrict transferring design away from the A/E of record. Industry guidance does not bar permits until design is complete, does not restrict design transfer to design-build, and does not require the manufacturer to install.

questions.question: In the traditional design role, an A/E decides that certain elements will be performance specified. What must the A/E know?

options.A: Levels that yield a satisfactory solution, plus standards, tests, and verification methods
options.B: The specific products that each bidder will propose, and each such product's installed cost
options.C: The construction means, methods, and sequences the contractor will use for each element
options.D: The research history and prototype test results of every candidate system and assembly

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that the A/E must know what performance levels result in a satisfactory solution and must know standards, tests, and verification methods. The A/E need not know bidders' products or costs, the contractor's means and methods, or prototype test histories to performance specify an element.

questions.question: An owner with a facility manager on staff has retained an A/E of record and a construction manager as advisor/agent, and has let several prime contracts, including a general trades contract; some are for performance-specified systems and others for descriptively specified work. Which participant might assume the task of coordinating these multiple-prime contracts?

options.A: The A/E of record
options.B: The general trades prime contractor
options.C: The CM-advisor/agent
options.D: The owner's facility manager

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that when a construction manager as advisor/agent is involved, the CM-advisor/agent might assume the task of coordinating multiple-prime contracts. The A/E coordinates with the CM on design matters, and industry guidance assigns this coordination to neither a prime contractor nor a facility manager.

questions.question: Why does industry guidance say the CM-advisor/agent becomes involved in handling performance items and interfacing them with traditionally designed items?

options.A: AHJs require a single party to sign each permit application
options.B: The A/E is barred from involvement once documents go out for procurement
options.C: Manufacturers submit compliance proof only through the CM-advisor/agent
options.D: Details of some items may not be known before release for procurement

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that details of some items may not be known before releasing the documents for procurement, so the CM-advisor/agent administers procurement of performance items and interfaces them with traditionally designed items. Industry guidance has the CM coordinating with the A/E rather than replacing it, and manufacturers submit proof through contractual lines.

questions.question: On a multiple-prime project that includes performance-specified packages, which activity does industry guidance describe as part of the CM-advisor/agent's involvement?

options.A: Coordinating with the A/E on design matters
options.B: Completing traditional detailing after contract award
options.C: Submitting proof of compliance through contractual lines
options.D: Reviewing performance specifications for code conformance

questions.explanation: Industry guidance lists administering procurement of performance items, interfacing them with traditionally designed items, and coordinating with the A/E on design matters as the CM-advisor/agent's involvement. Completing traditional detailing after award is the successful contractor's task, submitting compliance proof is the manufacturer's, and code-conformance review belongs to AHJs.

questions.question: A mechanical firm wins one of several prime contracts, bidding only on a performance-specified system. Interfaces with other systems were unknown at bid time. How are these details resolved?

options.A: The A/E resolves them by issuing an addendum before bids are received
options.B: The contractor resolves them after award through traditional detailing
options.C: The owner resolves them by issuing change orders once construction starts
options.D: The AHJ resolves them while reviewing the definitive materials for permit

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that when a contractor bids on only a specific system as one of multiple-prime contracts, the successful contractor is responsible for resolving unknown interface details after award and completing traditional detailing. Industry guidance does not place this on the A/E by addendum, the owner by change order, or the AHJ.

questions.question: A trade union representative asks whether a shift to performance-based requirements will reduce the work available to its members. Which response is consistent with industry guidance?

options.A: Yes; the overall amount of work decreases when performance criteria are used
options.B: Yes; manufacturers' own crews will perform all erection and installation
options.C: Generally no, except possibly with extensive use of factory-prefabricated systems
options.D: Generally no, except on projects where design-build delivery is used instead

questions.explanation: Industry guidance says performance-based requirements generally will not significantly affect labor participation, naming as a possible exception the extensive use of prefabricated systems built mostly in a factory. The overall amount of work is essentially unchanged, manufacturers' erection crews must be coordinated with other work rather than replacing it, and industry guidance ties no exception to design-build delivery.

questions.question: A general contractor with no in-house design staff is considering joining a design-build entity that will respond to an owner's performance criteria. What does generating solutions within those criteria require?

options.A: Only traditional detailing, because the owner's criteria already fix the design
options.B: Design and engineering capability, perhaps with closer manufacturer collaboration
options.C: Licensure of the contractor by the AHJ before any proposal can be submitted
options.D: Reliance on the owner's A/E to develop the needed solutions after contract award

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that the contractor or design-builder must generate solutions within the bounds of performance criteria, which requires design and engineering capabilities and may require closer collaboration with suppliers and manufacturers. Performance criteria do not fix the design, and industry guidance imposes no AHJ licensure step or reliance on the owner's A/E for this.

questions.question: A manufacturer whose product was selected to meet a performance-specified requirement wants to send its compliance test data straight to the owner. How should the manufacturer submit proof of compliance?

options.A: Directly to the owner, which must accept compliant results
options.B: Through the owner's independent testing agency for review
options.C: Directly to the AHJ along with the permit application
options.D: Through the contractual lines of the project

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that manufacturers are responsible for submitting proof of compliance with the specified performance criteria through contractual lines. Sending data straight to the owner or the AHJ, or routing it through an owner's testing agency, bypasses that chain and is not what industry guidance describes.

questions.question: A manufacturer's sales director asks how products are chosen on projects whose specifications state required results rather than naming products. On what basis is a product's use then decided?

options.A: Its performance measured against the specified criteria
options.B: The owner's preference among the products proposed
options.C: The A/E's familiarity with the product from prior projects
options.D: The strength of its advertising and brand recognition

questions.explanation: Industry guidance explains that performance specifications put competing products on the common ground of performance, so a product's use rests on performance rather than on an effective advertising campaign. The owner relinquishes some control and must accept compliant results, and neither A/E familiarity nor brand recognition is the basis industry guidance gives.

questions.question: Which additional assistance does industry guidance say a manufacturer might provide on a performance-specified project?

options.A: Coordinating its work under the multiple-prime contracts
options.B: Determining which of the project elements will be performance specified
options.C: Engineering to size its products to meet specific criteria or codes
options.D: Reviewing the performance specifications for code conformance

questions.explanation: Industry guidance says manufacturers might provide additional assistance such as design services, for example engineering to size their products to meet specific criteria or codes, and in some cases specialized installation. Coordinating multiple-prime contracts is a CM-advisor/agent task, deciding which elements to performance specify is the A/E's, and code-conformance review is the AHJ's.

questions.question: A design-build team applies for a building permit while final documentation is still incomplete. What do AHJs review for code conformance in such cases?

options.A: The complete construction documents prepared by the A/E of record
options.B: The available definitive materials and the performance specifications
options.C: The contractor's shop drawings and product data for all trades
options.D: The owner's program statement and the approved project budget

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that AHJs generally do not have complete construction documents at permit application in performance-based procurement, so they review the available definitive materials and the performance specifications for code conformance. Complete documents do not yet exist, and shop drawings and owner program documents are not what industry guidance says AHJs review.

questions.question: After reviewing the available materials on a performance-based project, the AHJ finds no conflicts in evidence. What may the AHJ be asked to issue?

options.A: A temporary certificate of occupancy pending final review
options.B: Permits contingent on successful prototype testing of each system
options.C: A conditional variance from the applicable code requirements
options.D: Permits contingent on inspection and final documentation approval

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that if no conflicts are in evidence, AHJs may be asked to issue permits contingent on inspection and final documentation approval. Prototype testing is a development-stage cost, not a permit condition in recommended practice, and a certificate of occupancy or code variance is not what is requested at this stage.

questions.question: On a project procured on a performance basis, when does industry guidance indicate final documentation is often completed?

options.A: Before permit application, so that code review can occur
options.B: After contract award but before construction has begun
options.C: Sometime after award, once construction has already begun
options.D: Before the contract is awarded, while proposals are being reviewed

questions.explanation: Industry guidance notes that on performance-based procurement, final documentation often is not finished until some time after award, once construction is under way. That is why AHJs lack complete documents at permit application, which rules out completion before permit, before award, or before construction starts.

questions.question: An owner and A/E are deciding how to apply performance specifying on a new laboratory building. Determining the extent of a performance specification involves which two interdependent decisions?

options.A: Which delivery method to use, and which bidders can respond to the performance criteria
options.B: Which attributes to evaluate, and which tests will verify compliance with each criterion
options.C: Which elements to performance specify, and how far each of them is performance specified
options.D: Which organizational format to use, and which drawings will accompany the specifications

questions.explanation: Industry guidance treats setting the extent of performance specifying as two linked choices: picking which project elements (from individual parts up to whole systems) will be written in performance terms, and deciding how far each of those elements is taken. Bidder capability only influences the level selected, while attributes and verification tests are worked out after the extent is fixed, so neither of those pairs defines the extent.

questions.question: On a mid-rise office project, the owner wants only the curtain wall and HVAC system written as performance criteria, with descriptive methods for everything else. A consultant objects that performance specifying must cover the whole building or none of it. Which response is correct?

options.A: Selected subsystems may be performance specified, with other approaches used for the remainder
options.B: Selected subsystems may be performance specified only when the contract is design-build
options.C: Performance specifying applies to individual components and cannot address complete subsystems
options.D: Performance specifying must cover the entire structure so a single entity designs all interfaces

questions.explanation: Industry guidance notes that entire structures can be performance specified, but some projects have only selected subsystems specified in performance terms while other specifying methods better suit the remainder. Industry guidance places no design-build condition on this partial use, and performance specifying is not limited to components or to whole structures.

questions.question: An owner asks the A/E when they must decide how much of a new transit facility will be performance specified. When should this extent be determined?

options.A: During construction documents, once drawings are substantially complete
options.B: During procurement, after the capabilities of likely bidders are confirmed
options.C: After award, when the contractor makes final product selections
options.D: Early in the project life cycle, to suit the owner's needs

questions.explanation: The owner and A/E should settle how much of the project to performance specify at the outset of the project life cycle, choosing the extent that fits the owner's needs. Putting the decision off to construction documents, procurement, or post-award product selection delays a choice industry guidance expects to be made at the start.

questions.question: An A/E is evaluating four building elements for possible performance specifying. Which element's circumstances most favor performance specifications?

options.A: A storefront for which the owner has standardized on one recognized system as the exclusive choice
options.B: An exterior wall forming a large share of the work, with several reasonably cost-competitive solutions
options.C: A roof system for which one solution costs far less than every other acceptable option available
options.D: A small trim element whose configuration must exactly match the existing historic profile in every detail

questions.explanation: Where a range of options exists, industry guidance lists conditions favoring performance specifications: no single solution is recognized as an exclusive choice, costs of options are reasonably competitive, and the system is a substantial portion of the project not requiring a configuration that precludes options. The storefront has an exclusive choice, the roof options are not cost-competitive, and the trim demands a fixed configuration.

questions.question: The first determination in performance specifying project elements is which elements, if any, should be specified in performance terms. Which question frames that determination, and at what scale does it apply?

options.A: Which elements offer a range of options whose competition yields optimum solutions; at any scale from part to system
options.B: Which elements carry the greatest design liability for the A/E; at any scale from part to system
options.C: Which elements offer a range of options whose competition yields optimum solutions; at the system and assembly scales
options.D: Which elements can be verified by independent testing; at the system and assembly scales

questions.explanation: Industry guidance frames the first decision around whether an element has a range of available options whose competition will produce the best solution, and it applies that question at every scale, from a single part or component through assemblies and full systems. A/E design liability and independent testing are not the stated criterion, and restricting the question to systems and assemblies wrongly leaves out parts and components.

questions.question: An owner needs a blast-resistant glazing assembly with properties that no product currently on the market can deliver. How does this circumstance bear on the choice of specifying method?

options.A: It weighs against performance specifications, since no standard solution exists to set criteria from
options.B: It favors a proprietary specification naming the manufacturer most likely to develop the product
options.C: It favors performance specifications, as one of the conditions under which they offer advantages
options.D: It favors a descriptive specification, since the A/E must define the new configuration in detail

questions.explanation: Industry guidance lists conditions under which performance specifications may offer advantages, including when nothing on the market satisfies the owner's needs and when development beyond the current state-of-the-art is required. Lack of a standard solution is a reason to use performance criteria, not to avoid them, and a proprietary or descriptive specification presumes a known product or an A/E-defined solution that does not yet exist.

questions.question: To speed production, a specifier proposes writing the building envelope sections in UniFormat order and the interior finishes sections in MasterFormat order, bound together in one volume. What is the correct guidance?

options.A: Combine them, provided each section title carries both the MasterFormat and UniFormat numbers
options.B: Combine them, provided overall performance requirements are collected in Section 01 80 00
options.C: Combine them only in design-build contracts using the broadest levels, H and J
options.D: Do not combine the two formats in a single project manual

questions.explanation: Industry guidance advises against mixing MasterFormat-based and UniFormat-based specifications within one project manual. Section 01 80 00 is available for stating overall performance requirements, but that does not permit combining formats, and industry guidance makes no exception for dual-numbered section titles or for design-build projects.

questions.question: Using typical sample performance criteria, a curtain wall's metal framing will support a plastered surface. When tested per ASTM E330, what deflection limit normal to the wall plane applies?

options.A: 1/175 of clear span
options.B: 1/480 of span
options.C: 1/360 of span
options.D: 1/240 of span

questions.explanation: The curtain wall criterion limits framing deflection to 1/175 of clear span or 3/4 inch, whichever is less, except that 1/360 of span applies where a plastered surface is affected. The l/480 (plaster and stucco) and l/240 (other finishes) limits belong to the broader exterior vertical enclosure example based on ASCE/SEI 7.
questions.source: establishing the level of performance specifying

questions.question: An A/E's UniFormat-based performance specification currently describes B20—Exterior Vertical Enclosures. The owner now wants only curtain walls, framed in aluminum or steel. How should the A/E revise the specification?

options.A: Narrow B20 to B2010.40—Curtain Wall Assemblies and list acceptable or unacceptable framing
options.B: Keep B20 and add an l/240 deflection limit so non-curtain-wall systems cannot comply
options.C: Keep B20 and rely on proposal evaluation to reject any bronze, timber, and fiberglass framing
options.D: Abandon performance specifying and name one curtain wall manufacturer's system
