questions.explanation: The example narrows B20—Exterior Vertical Enclosures to curtain walls by specifying B2010.40—Curtain Wall Assemblies, and limits framing by listing acceptable materials (aluminum, steel) or unacceptable ones (bronze, timber, fiberglass). A deflection limit does not restrict the system type, exclusions never stated in the criteria cannot fairly be applied in evaluation, and naming one manufacturer gives up performance specifying rather than narrowing it.
questions.source: establishing the level of performance specifying

questions.question: An A/E who wants to retain greater control over a performance-specified element's configuration should take which approach?

options.A: Use a broad degree, describing the subsystem in general terms with broad functional criteria
options.B: Use a broad degree, organizing the elements under UniFormat to integrate related subsystems
options.C: Use a narrow degree, naming a specific manufacturer and basing criteria on its published product data
options.D: Use a narrow degree, identifying the type of component and basing criteria on its intrinsic traits

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that greater control over configuration is retained with a narrow degree of performance specifying, in which the particular type of component (such as aluminum curtain wall) is identified and criteria rest on characteristics intrinsic to that type. A broad degree, including broad UniFormat descriptions, grants greater latitude rather than control, and naming a manufacturer is proprietary rather than performance specifying.
questions.source: establishing the level of performance specifying

questions.question: An A/E proposes a broad level of performance specifying for a school in a rural market where few local contractors have design or engineering capability. What is the best course of action?

options.A: Keep the broad level and require each bidder to perform all design services in-house
options.B: Set the level according to the local construction community's capabilities to respond
options.C: Keep the broad level, since its advantages do not depend on the number of participants
options.D: Defer setting the level until bids are opened and actual participation is known

questions.explanation: Industry guidance requires considering the local construction community's likely response: enough bidders must be capable and willing, and insufficient participation can negate the advantages of performance specifying. The level must therefore be established according to the community's capabilities. Bidders may retain services rather than keep them in-house, and the level cannot wait until bids are opened.

questions.question: A general contractor with no engineers on staff asks whether it can respond to a performance-based solicitation that requires design of the specified systems. How may bidders or proposers furnish the necessary services?

options.A: In-house, because design responsibility cannot be delegated to outside firms
options.B: Through the A/E of record, under an amendment to its agreement with the owner
options.C: In-house, or by retaining them on a project-by-project basis as needed
options.D: Through the system manufacturer, as part of its standard product warranty

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that bidders or proposers may provide the necessary services in-house or retain them on a project-by-project basis as needed. Industry guidance does not restrict these services to in-house staff, the A/E of record, or the manufacturer.

questions.question: Which set of activities does a performance-based solicitation require of participating bidders or proposers?

options.A: Administering contracts, designing items, acquiring systems products, coordinating installation
options.B: Writing performance criteria, selecting test methods, evaluating proposals, awarding contracts
options.C: Preparing the program, securing financing, approving the budget, obtaining the building permit
options.D: Reviewing submittals, certifying payments, issuing change orders, accepting the completed work

questions.explanation: A performance-based solicitation asks bidders or proposers to take on contract administration, design and engineering of the performance-specified items, procurement of suitable systems products, and coordination of installation where needed. Drafting criteria, choosing tests, and evaluating proposals fall to the owner and A/E, and the other sets describe owner duties or routine contract administration.

questions.question: A state agency's procurement rules require that every proposal be judged strictly on a complies/does-not-comply basis, with no negotiation. Which level of performance specifying may be best?

options.A: A broader level, because objective evaluation reduces the A/E's design effort
options.B: The broadest levels, H and J, because objective scoring suits systems proposals
options.C: Any level, because the evaluation method does not affect the level chosen
options.D: A narrower level, because absolute objectivity in evaluation is demanded

questions.explanation: Industry guidance indicates that when evaluation must be strictly objective, judged only as complying or not complying, a narrower level of performance specifying is likely the better fit. Broader levels depend on subjective judgment and the freedom to accept, reject, or negotiate, so the evaluation method does drive the level chosen, and objective scoring does not favor the broadest levels.

questions.question: An owner's representative argues against broad-level performance specifying because it will necessarily lengthen proposal development and complicate evaluation. Which statement is accurate?

options.A: Both effects necessarily follow, so broad levels suit only negotiated procurements
options.B: Neither necessarily follows, though the broad level does demand more A/E design time
options.C: Neither necessarily follows, and the broad level also reduces the A/E's design time
options.D: Only longer development follows, since evaluation time is fixed by the owner's rules

questions.explanation: Choosing a broad level does not automatically make proposal preparation longer or evaluation more complex. What it does add is A/E time to design proposed solutions that rely on the performance specification to achieve the design intent. The remaining choices either claim a necessary consequence industry guidance denies or get the effect on A/E time backward.

questions.question: A contractor that regularly uses systems building components is reviewing two solicitations, one with broad-level and one with narrow-level performance specifications. What risk does the narrow-level approach carry?

options.A: It may demand highly developed design and manufacturing capability
options.B: It may permit only a subjective evaluation of each proposal
options.C: It may serve only to exclude otherwise acceptable options
options.D: It may require drawings that are diagrammatic in content

questions.explanation: Industry guidance notes that a contractor who regularly uses systems building components may readily respond to broad-level performance specifications, whereas narrow-level specifications may serve only to exclude otherwise acceptable options. Demanding design capability, subjective evaluation, and diagrammatic drawings are associated with broad levels, not narrow ones.

questions.question: A specifier's performance section for cast-in-place concrete states required mix proportions and also a minimum 28-day compressive strength. What problem may result?

options.A: The bidder might have the option of complying only with the lesser requirement
options.B: The bidder must comply with whichever requirement is more stringent in each case
options.C: The mix proportions automatically govern, and the strength becomes advisory only
options.D: The section converts to a reference standard specification by default

questions.explanation: Industry guidance warns against specifying the same item in both descriptive and performance terms, citing concrete specified by mix proportions as well as strength as a potential conflict. The bidder or proposer might then have the option of complying only with the lesser requirement. Industry guidance states no rule that the stricter or the descriptive requirement governs.

questions.question: A specifier wants to cite a test method that was originally developed for one material to evaluate a different material in a performance specification. Which statement is correct?

options.A: It should not be used, since tests developed for one material never apply to others
options.B: It may have valid application, but its validity and applicability must be verified
options.C: It may be cited for information only, since criteria cannot rely on material-specific tests
options.D: It may be used as is, since any published standard test is inherently performance oriented

questions.explanation: Industry guidance cautions that many standards and tests were developed for a specific material and conditions, yet other material-oriented tests may have valid applications to other materials despite their origins. Familiarity with the test is vital to ensure its validity, applicability, and usefulness. Industry guidance also requires referenced tests to be performance oriented, so a published test is not automatically suitable, and material-specific origin alone does not bar its use.

questions.question: To appear thorough, a specifier adds several referenced standards to a performance specification that have no real utility for the project conditions. What is the effect of this overspecifying?

options.A: It lowers the owner's risk by expanding the basis for rejecting proposals
options.B: It shifts design liability from the A/E to the referenced testing agency
options.C: It turns the performance specification into a reference standard method
options.D: It raises costs by placing an unnecessary burden on the bidder or proposer

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that specified standards or tests should reflect project conditions and that requiring standards with no real utility serves no purpose. Such overspecifying increases costs by placing an unnecessary burden on the bidder or proposer. Industry guidance does not describe it as reducing risk, shifting liability, or changing the specifying method.

questions.question: Midway through design, the A/E decides to narrow the level of performance specifying for an exterior wall system from broad to narrow. How should the accompanying drawings change?

options.A: They should become more diagrammatic in composition and content
options.B: They should be omitted, leaving the written criteria to govern
options.C: They should become more definitive in composition and content
options.D: They should be reduced to existing condition drawings only

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that a broad level of performance specifying dictates diagrammatic drawings, while a narrower level requires more definitive drawings. Most performance specifications are accompanied by drawings that supplement the written criteria, and existing-condition-only drawings belong to the broadest levels.

questions.question: Drawings for a performance-specified sunshade system show an illustrative blade layout, but the A/E does not intend to require strict adherence to that configuration. What should the A/E do?

options.A: Note that the layout represents only a suggested definition
options.B: Delete the layout, since drawings cannot accompany performance criteria
options.C: Leave the layout un-noted, since written criteria always govern graphics
options.D: Restate the layout as a descriptive requirement in the section text

questions.explanation: Industry guidance says any drawings representing only a suggested definition, without requiring strict adherence to a configuration, should be noted, and contradictions between written and graphic material must be avoided. Performance specifications are normally accompanied by drawings, and restating the layout descriptively would specify the same item in two ways.

questions.question: On a project with several performance-specified systems, the owner asks where it will be made clear which party is responsible for coordinating the design once the final performance product characteristics are known. Which documents clarify this?

options.A: The design development drawings
options.B: The procurement documents
options.C: The project record documents
options.D: The preliminary project description

questions.explanation: Industry guidance assigns this to the procurement documents, which make clear which party coordinates the design once the final performance product characteristics are established. Design development drawings and the preliminary project description are earlier design-phase tools, and record documents are assembled after construction, too late to allocate the responsibility.

questions.question: A turnkey project is procured at the broadest level of performance specifying. What do the drawings furnished to proposers consist of?

options.A: Structural layout and foundation drawings fixed by the A/E
options.B: Definitive drawings with blanks at performance-specified items
options.C: Site drawings plus fully detailed elevations and sections
options.D: Existing condition drawings only

questions.explanation: For the broadest level of performance specifying, as in turnkey or design-build delivery, industry guidance says the drawings furnished are limited to existing conditions, and the design criteria carry most of the design direction. Definitive drawings with blanks, A/E-fixed structural layouts, and fully detailed elevations are features of narrower levels, where the A/E still draws much of the work.

questions.question: Separate prime contracts are awarded for a performance-specified curtain wall and a performance-specified skylight system that meet at a common edge. When are the details at that interface coordinated?

options.A: Before bidding, by the A/E on its definitive construction drawings
options.B: During bidding, as each bidder details its interface with the other system
options.C: After each of the interfacing systems has been selected
options.D: After the first system is selected, by that system's successful bidder

questions.explanation: Under multiple-prime contracts for performance-specified systems, industry guidance says the A/E draws descriptive items definitively and shows performance-specified items only generically. Where multiple performance-based elements interface, those details are coordinated after each interfacing system has been selected, not by the A/E before bidding, by bidders during bidding, or once only the first system is chosen.

questions.question: A performance-specified rooftop mechanical system appears on the bid drawings only as an outline without detail. What must the A/E still show definitively?

options.A: The elements with which the system must interface
options.B: The configuration and dimensions of the system itself
options.C: The manufacturer and model the design is based on
options.D: The routing of every duct and pipe within the system

questions.explanation: Industry guidance permits a performance-specified element to be shown as an undetailed outline, but the A/E must still clearly identify the elements the system or component has to interface with. The bidder or proposer then prepares detailed drawings of its proposed item and how it relates to adjacent work, so configuration, internal routing, and product selection are left to the proposer.

questions.question: An owner awards a separate prime contract for each of several systems that will be assembled before delivery. When does the A/E begin developing definitive construction drawings that integrate those systems?

options.A: Before bidding, so each bidder can price against fixed details
options.B: Not until the final selection of each system has been made
options.C: During bidding, as addenda answering bidders' questions
options.D: After the first system is selected, ahead of the others

questions.explanation: For systems assembled before delivery under separate prime contracts, industry guidance says no definitive drawings accompany the performance specifications; the A/E provides only a schematic design and bidders submit definitive drawings for their systems. The A/E begins definitive construction drawings integrating the systems only after the final selection of each system.

questions.question: A broad-level performance specification uses UniFormat as the organizational format for the project manual. How is each section titled?

options.A: With the MasterFormat number and title, adding the UniFormat number in the footer
options.B: With both MasterFormat and UniFormat numbers, separated by a slash in the title
options.C: With a descriptive title only, numbering being assigned in the table of contents
options.D: With the UniFormat number and title in place of a MasterFormat number and title

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that for broad-level performance specifying that uses UniFormat to organize the project manual, the section title includes the applicable UniFormat number and title in place of a MasterFormat number and title. Retaining MasterFormat numbering, dual numbering, or dropping numbers altogether is not what industry guidance describes.

questions.question: A specifier preparing a broad-level performance specification organized by UniFormat assumes CSI's PageFormat no longer applies to the page layout. Which statement is correct?

options.A: PageFormat can be used for narrow-level performance specifying only
options.B: PageFormat applies only when sections carry MasterFormat numbers and titles
options.C: PageFormat can be used for either narrow- or broad-level performance specifying
options.D: PageFormat is replaced by a UniFormat page layout for broad-level work

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that PageFormat can be used for either narrow- or broad-level performance specifying. Only the section number and title change when UniFormat organizes the manual; there is no separate UniFormat page layout and no restriction to narrow-level work.

questions.question: When the three-part SectionFormat is adapted for use in performance specifications, how are its article headings typically changed?

options.A: It omits some article headings, adds one broad article title, and adds several narrow ones
options.B: It keeps every standard heading unchanged and adds a separate fourth part for performance criteria
options.C: It omits PART 3—EXECUTION, since the contractor determines the installation methods
options.D: It adds several broad article titles and omits all of the narrow article titles

questions.explanation: The adapted format leaves out article headings that typically would not apply to performance specifications, adds one broad article title, and adds several narrow article titles. This reflects the concept that all article titles are optional, while the three-part structure, including PART 3, is retained for consistency and flexibility.

questions.question: In a performance specification for a curtain wall, the specifier must define how the system interfaces with the structural frame and roofing specified in other sections. Which PART 1 article should be used?

options.A: References
options.B: Summary
options.C: Quality Assurance
options.D: Project or Site Conditions

questions.explanation: The Summary article is where the specifier defines how the system connects with systems or products covered in other sections. References carries definitions and cited standards, Quality Assurance carries qualifications, and Project or Site Conditions covers environmental conditions and field measurements, so none of them is the place for interface requirements.

questions.question: A specifier wants test reports and design data for a performance-specified skylight system submitted with the proposal, and a colleague insists submittals cannot be required before award. At which points in time may performance submittals be requested?

options.A: With bid, after award, before fabrication, during installation, at substantial completion
options.B: After award, before delivery, before installation, after installation, at final payment
options.C: Before bid, after award, before fabrication, after installation, after final acceptance
options.D: Before bid, with bid, before fabrication, before installation, before final acceptance

questions.explanation: Industry guidance identifies five times when performance submittals may be called for: ahead of the bid or proposal, along with it, prior to fabrication, prior to installation, and prior to final acceptance. Requiring data with the proposal is therefore allowed, and the other lists include points such as after award or substantial completion that industry guidance does not list.

questions.question: The submittals required in a performance specification can be separated into which two groups, and with provisions intended to ensure what?

options.A: Action and informational, ensuring timely and consistent review by the A/E
options.B: Prebid and postbid, ensuring fair and open competition among all proposers
options.C: Quality assurance and quality control, ensuring correct design liability
options.D: Product and closeout, ensuring complete and accurate project record documents

questions.explanation: Industry guidance divides performance submittals into quality assurance and quality control groups, with provisions meant to place design liability with the correct party. Although industry guidance also separates submittals requiring review and approval from those furnished only as documentation or information, that distinction is not the one linked to design liability, and the other pairings are not the grouping.

questions.question: For a performance-specified precast cladding system, which entities does industry guidance say the Quality Assurance article's qualification requirements must cover with credentials, possibly including engineering licensure by AHJs?

options.A: Manufacturer, contractor, designer, installer, and testing agency
options.B: Owner, A/E of record, contractor, installer, and testing agency
options.C: Manufacturer, supplier, installer, surety, and building official
options.D: Contractor, subcontractors, installer, inspector, and A/E of record

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that under the broad Quality Assurance article, qualification requirements must include credentials for the manufacturer, contractor, designer, installer, and testing agency, and these may require engineering expertise and AHJ licensure. The owner, A/E of record, surety, and building official are not entities whose credentials the performance specification sets.

questions.question: Within the Performance/Design Criteria article, industry guidance relates attributes, requirements, criteria, and tests. Which describes the role of a criterion?

options.A: A statement of the discrete need or expected result for an attribute
options.B: A statement that sets limits or gives standards bounding a requirement
options.C: The procedure by which the element's performance is evaluated
options.D: A characteristic of the element, such as fire resistance or deflection

questions.explanation: Industry guidance explains that the article lists each element's performance attribute and states discrete needs or expected results (requirements), which are limited by criteria statements that set limits or give standards. A test, related to each criterion, is how performance is evaluated. The distractors describe a requirement, a test, and an attribute.

questions.question: A specifier is converting a descriptive section to a performance specification. Which group of PART 2 article titles is seldom used, because those decisions are typically left to the manufacturer, fabricator, supplier, or contractor?

options.A: Performance/Design Criteria, Components, and Finishes
options.B: Components, Finishes, and Source Quality Control
options.C: Manufacturers, Performance/Design Criteria, and Mixes
options.D: Materials, Mixes, and Fabrication

questions.explanation: Because end results rather than means are specified, industry guidance says titles such as Manufacturers, Materials, Manufactured Units, Equipment, Mixes, and Fabrication are seldom used, though they can narrow products to acceptable or unacceptable ones. Performance/Design Criteria, Components, Finishes, and Source Quality Control appear among the PART 2 articles in a performance-adapted SectionFormat.

questions.question: On a small clinic, the A/E's performance criteria for a daylighting system would require advancing the current state-of-the-art technology. What response should the A/E anticipate?

options.A: A limited response unless the volume of work supports research and development costs
options.B: A broad response, because performance criteria invite innovation from many suppliers
options.C: A broad response, because state-of-the-art requirements lower proposers' design costs
options.D: A limited response unless the criteria are restated as proprietary product requirements

questions.explanation: Industry guidance warns that criteria requiring the element's technology to move beyond the current state of the art can draw few responses unless the amount of work is large enough to justify research and development spending. It also notes that an A/E pursuing the most economical solution with existing technology should avoid overspecifying, and it does not offer proprietary restatement as a remedy.

questions.question: A performance specification for an integrated ceiling needs distinct attributes, requirements, criteria, and tests for the grid, the acoustical panels, and the light fixtures. How should PART 2 be organized?

options.A: List all of them together within a single Performance/Design Criteria article
options.B: Provide a separate article for each one, which may carry that item's actual name
options.C: Specify each one under a Manufactured Units article with its own model number
options.D: Move each one into its own section and cross-reference it under the Summary

questions.explanation: Industry guidance explains that complex systems may define attributes of major components as well as the total system, using the generic Components article or the component's actual name, such as Suspension Grid, Acoustical Panels, and Luminaires. Each component gets a separate article with its own attributes, requirements, criteria, and tests. Manufactured Units is seldom used in performance specifications.

questions.question: A specifier drafting a performance specification section for an exterior wall system states the required air-infiltration rate in PART 2. A consultant then adds a PART 3 paragraph prescribing the sealant sequence and anchor spacing the installer must use to reach that rate. What is the main concern with this draft?

options.A: PART 3 of a performance section may not contain an installation article of any kind
options.B: Specifying the PART 2 result and a PART 3 method to achieve it can cause conflicts
options.C: The prescribed method belongs in Section 01 80 00 rather than in PART 3 of the section
options.D: Installation methods for performance sections belong in PART 1 under Quality Assurance

questions.explanation: Industry guidance cautions that conflicts arise when a section states the PART 2 performance requirement and also prescribes, in PART 3, a way to achieve it. The installation article in a performance section may or may not be included, so an outright prohibition overstates the rule. Section 01 80 00 supplies numbers and titles for performance requirements of building elements, not installation methods, and industry guidance does not move installation into PART 1.

questions.question: A performance specification section for a roofing system will accept several manufacturers' systems, each with its own application, and the installer may choose among options. What may be all that is necessary in the PART 3 installation article?

options.A: A detailed installation procedure written around the basis-of-design system
options.B: A cross-reference to Section 01 80 00 for each element's installation method
options.C: No PART 3 content, because execution articles do not apply to performance sections
options.D: A statement requiring compliance with the manufacturer's installation instructions

questions.explanation: Industry guidance notes that several products may satisfy a performance specification, each with its own application, so sometimes a single statement requiring the installer to follow the manufacturer's instructions is all that is needed. Writing the procedure around one system ignores that installation may depend on the product a manufacturer develops for the project. Industry guidance says PART 3 articles generally apply to performance specifying, and Section 01 80 00 addresses performance requirements, not installation methods.

questions.question: A design-build owner wants the project manual to establish end-result requirements for broad-scope building elements without referencing specific products. Which numbering approach suits this broad level of performance specifying?

options.A: UniFormat Level 1 and 2 numbers and titles for the element sections
options.B: Section 01 80 00 Level 2 and 3 numbers and titles for each element
options.C: UniFormat Level 3 and 4 numbers and titles for each specific product
options.D: Section 01 80 00 and UniFormat numbers combined in one project manual

questions.explanation: Industry guidance says broad performance specifying with UniFormat can use its Level 1 and 2 numbers and titles for sections covering broad-scope element requirements. Section 01 80 00's Level 2 and 3 numbers and titles serve a narrow level of performance specifying. Industry guidance states that 01 80 00 and UniFormat both suit design-build but not together in the same project manual, and product-level numbering contradicts the no-specific-products approach.

questions.question: A specifier's section title list will be distributed to the owner and other design team members early in design. What is it preferable to add to the list, and what can the list ultimately become?

options.A: Article and page numbers for each section; the master for all cross-references
options.B: Cost estimates for each section's scope; the basis for the schedule of values
options.C: Other documents and forms in the project manual; the manual's table of contents
options.D: Names of the consultants writing each section; the drawing coordination checklist

questions.explanation: Because the section title list is usually distributed to the owner and other design team members, industry guidance says it is preferable to list other documents and forms included in the project manual; in final form the list can become the table of contents. Industry guidance directs references to section numbers only, not article or page numbers, which may change with revisions. Cost estimates and consultant assignments are not purposes industry guidance gives for the list.

questions.question: Working from an office master guide specification, a specifier renumbers several master sections to suit a project. Why should this be done with care?

options.A: MasterFormat does not permit project-specific changes to section numbers
options.B: Renumbered sections lose their SectionFormat article structure
options.C: Cross-references to the original numbers may exist in other sections
options.D: The owner must approve each change made to the section title list

questions.explanation: Industry guidance warns that renumbering sections taken from a master guide specification requires care, because other sections of the master may contain cross-references to them. Industry guidance states no MasterFormat prohibition, no effect on SectionFormat structure, and no owner-approval requirement for renumbering. The related rule is to reference section numbers only, never article or page numbers.

questions.question: When a master guide specification system is used, industry guidance says the proposed section title list should be compared with the master system's contents. What should that comparison identify?

options.A: Sections that can be edited from guide text versus those to be custom-prepared
options.B: Sections to be prepared by consultants versus those prepared by the A/E
options.C: Sections belonging in Division 01 versus those in Divisions 02 through 49
options.D: Sections to be specified descriptively versus those to be specified by performance

questions.explanation: Industry guidance says the list of proposed section titles should be compared with the master's contents and should indicate which sections can be developed or edited from the master guide text and which must be custom-prepared. Attention should also go to products or work that might be specified in more than one section. Consultant assignment, Division placement, and specifying method are not what industry guidance says this comparison indicates.

questions.question: A specifier includes product illustrations within several specification sections. Where may text that clarifies the status of the graphics within the documents be included?

options.A: In the instructions to bidders, under the bidders' representations
options.B: In the supplementary conditions, under definitions of contract documents
options.C: In Division 01, under the submittal procedures for product data sheets
options.D: In the owner-contractor agreement, under the enumeration of documents

questions.explanation: Industry guidance says graphics should be used only with text that clarifies their status within the documents, and that such text may be included in the supplementary conditions under definitions of contract documents. The instructions to bidders, Division 01 submittal procedures, and the agreement's enumeration are not where industry guidance places this clarifying text.

questions.question: A specifier wants to include a manufacturer's data sheet to illustrate the basis-of-design product in a section. Besides referencing the data sheet in the section, where does industry guidance note SectionFormat suggests inserting it?

options.A: In an appendix placed after the last section of Division 49
options.B: On a supplementary sheet issued with the contract drawings
options.C: In PART 2 of the section, under the article naming manufacturers
options.D: In the project manual immediately following the individual section

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that manufacturers' data sheets illustrating basis-of-design products can be referenced in the individual section or, as SectionFormat suggests, inserted in the project manual following the individual section. An end-of-manual appendix, a drawing sheet, or embedding within a PART 2 article are not the placement industry guidance attributes to SectionFormat.

questions.question: A specifier plans to paste a photograph of a lighting fixture, copied from a manufacturer's catalog, into a lighting section. What should the specifier consider before doing so?

options.A: Photographs belong only on the contract drawings, so the image must be moved there
options.B: Copyright release may be needed, and a patented design may imply added requirements
options.C: Only isometric views are permitted, so the photograph must be redrawn as one
options.D: A photograph makes the section a closed proprietary specification requiring owner approval

questions.explanation: Industry guidance says illustrations, graphics, and photographs may require permission or copyright release from the graphics owner, and that proprietary or patented designs could imply additional specification requirements. Industry guidance expressly allows illustrations, including photographs and isometric views, within specifications, and it lists lighting fixtures among items that benefit from them. Nothing in the subsection converts a photograph into a closed proprietary specification.

questions.question: A firm's specification style guide must state the three qualities industry guidance says characterize good specification writing style. Which three should it list?

options.A: Clarity, correctness, and completeness
options.B: Accuracy, brevity, and clarity
options.C: Brevity, consistency, and precision
options.D: Accuracy, conciseness, and completeness

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that a good writing style is characterized by accuracy, brevity, and clarity. Clarity, correctness, and completeness are drawn from the separate four Cs of effective communication (clear, concise, correct, complete), not the writing-style triad. Consistency and precision are not named as the three characterizing qualities.

questions.question: A consultant's section is written in long sentences that attach several qualifying clauses to each requirement. Under recommended specification writing style, in what form should sentence structure be maintained?

options.A: Simple statements in declarative or imperative form
options.B: Narrative statements explaining each requirement's intent
options.C: Compound statements that group related requirements
options.D: Conditional statements that state any exceptions first

questions.explanation: Among the writing style rules is keeping sentence structure to simple declarative or imperative statements. Narrative explanations of intent, compound groupings, and conditional constructions each add the length and complexity that the companion rule to use simple sentences is meant to prevent.

questions.question: A draft section contains one long sentence that combines products, installation locations, and exceptions in several clauses. Under recommended specification writing style, what is the specific risk of such complicated sentences?

options.A: The sentence cannot be converted to the imperative mood without rewriting
options.B: Reviewers outside the design team may not understand trade terminology
options.C: Complex sentences increase page count and reproduction costs of the manual
options.D: Inadvertent omission or insertion of punctuation could change the meaning

questions.explanation: The writing style rules warn against complicated sentences, because accidentally dropping or adding a punctuation mark could alter the meaning or make it ambiguous. Mood conversion, unfamiliar trade terminology, and page count are not the risk industry guidance ties to complicated sentences; word choice is addressed by a separate rule to use simple, clearly understood terms.

questions.question: Applying the rule that the shorter of two equally correct spellings is preferred, a specifier changes every 'through' in the project manual to 'thru.' How does recommended spelling practice treat this change?

options.A: Acceptable, because shorter spellings are preferred in contract documents
options.B: Acceptable, if the change is applied consistently in every section
options.C: Unacceptable, because spellings created for brevity should be avoided
options.D: Unacceptable, unless 'thru' appears in the office supplemental term list

questions.explanation: Industry guidance prefers the shorter of two equally correct spellings (facia, gage, molding, catalog) but says unacceptable spellings produced by attempts at brevity or simplification should be avoided, citing thru instead of through. The shorter-spelling rule applies only when both spellings are equally correct, and consistency or a supplemental list does not make thru acceptable.

questions.question: Two specifiers in the same firm disagree on how to spell several words. What should spelling in the specifications be based on?

options.A: The spellings used in the reference standards cited in each section
options.B: An office-standard dictionary, with a supplemental list of technical terms
options.C: The spellings preferred by the manufacturer of each basis-of-design product
options.D: The MasterFormat titles and keywords index published for each section

questions.explanation: Industry guidance bases correct, consistent spelling on one dictionary that the office designates as its standard, plus a supplemental list for technical terms that dictionary lacks. Reference standards, manufacturers' literature, and MasterFormat titles are not the basis industry guidance designates for spelling.

questions.question: Compare 'Install equipment plumb and level' with 'The Contractor shall install equipment plumb and level.' Per industry guidance, these illustrate the two basic grammatical sentence moods for specifications. Which moods are they, in order?

options.A: Indicative mood, then imperative mood
options.B: Imperative mood, then indicative mood
options.C: Imperative mood, then subjunctive mood
options.D: Declarative mood, then indicative mood

questions.explanation: Industry guidance names the imperative and indicative moods as the two basic moods for conveying requirements. The imperative places the action verb first, as in 'Install equipment plumb and level,' while the indicative typically uses shall or will. Reversing the order mislabels the examples, and subjunctive and declarative are not the moods industry guidance names.

questions.question: A paragraph reads 'Provide the following accessories' and is followed by three subparagraphs that list the items. How should that introductory paragraph end?

options.A: With a semicolon, showing that the list continues the sentence
options.B: With no punctuation, since the subparagraphs complete it
options.C: With a period, since every paragraph must end in a period
options.D: With a colon, so that the subparagraphs are linked to it

questions.explanation: Industry guidance says a parent paragraph ends with a colon when its subparagraphs must be linked to it. Paragraphs end with either a period or a colon, so a period is not mandatory for every paragraph, and semicolons or no punctuation are not the terminations industry guidance allows.

questions.question: A draft sentence begins 'One of the elongated central fasteners are to be placed...' What grammatical error does it contain?

options.A: The singular subject 'one' is paired with the plural verb 'are'
options.B: The plural subject 'fasteners' is paired with a singular verb
options.C: The modifier 'elongated central' has no noun for it to modify
options.D: The passive verb 'to be placed' does not name the responsible party

questions.explanation: Industry guidance explains that the incorrect example pairs the singular subject 'one' with the plural verb 'are,' showing how a singular subject can be confused with a plural modifier. 'Fasteners' belongs to the plural modifier, not the subject, and industry guidance does not identify a dangling modifier or a missing party as the error.

questions.question: For the same fastener requirement, industry guidance gives an incorrect, a correct, and a preferred version. Which is the preferred version?

options.A: Place one elongated central fastener around eye of panel and bolt.
options.B: One of the elongated central fasteners is to be placed around panel eye and bolted.
options.C: Bolt one elongated central fastener to panel eye.
options.D: Panel eye shall receive one bolted central fastener.

questions.explanation: Industry guidance labels 'Bolt one elongated central fastener to panel eye' as preferred because it has number agreement and is a simple, direct instruction. 'Place one... and bolt' is the grammatically correct but lengthier version. The remaining options use a passive or a shall construction rather than a direct imperative.

questions.question: A mechanical section's scope paragraph lists 'Heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning.' Applying the rules of parallel construction and punctuation, how should this series read?

options.A: Heat, ventilation, and air-conditioning
options.B: Heating, ventilation and air-conditioning
options.C: Heating, ventilating, and air-conditioning
options.D: Heating, ventilating and air-conditioning

questions.explanation: Industry guidance gives 'Heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning' as incorrect and 'Heating, ventilating, and air-conditioning' as correct and preferred, because items in a series should share an identical grammatical structure. Options without the comma before 'and' also violate the Oxford comma rule, and 'Heat, ventilation' does not fix the parallelism.

questions.question: Good grammar requires identical grammatical structure in both parts of a compound subject or predicate. For which other construction does industry guidance also recommend an identical grammatical structure?

options.A: A parent paragraph and each of its subparagraphs
options.B: A series of nouns, adverbs, or prepositional phrases
options.C: A section title and each of its article titles
options.D: A reference standard designation and its edition date

questions.explanation: Beyond compound subjects and predicates, industry guidance also recommends parallel (identical) structure for a series of nouns, adverbs, or prepositional phrases. Parent and subparagraph relationships are governed by punctuation rules, and section or article titles and standard designations are not what this grammar rule addresses.

questions.question: A draft reads 'Apply coating with pneumatic equipment when it is above 40°F.' Applying the rules of pronoun reference, what is the best revision approach?

options.A: Replace 'it' with 'same' so that it clearly refers back to the equipment
options.B: Add a 'which' clause identifying the item that must exceed 40°F
options.C: Retain 'it', because only personal pronouns are to be avoided
options.D: Repeat the intended noun, such as ambient temperature, in place of 'it'

questions.explanation: Industry guidance says pronouns should be minimized or avoided and that repeating the noun is better than risking misunderstanding; its better rewrites name either the equipment or the ambient temperature explicitly. Industry guidance says 'same' should not be used as a pronoun and that 'which' and other relative pronouns should be used sparingly, if at all. The guidance is to minimize all pronouns, not only personal ones.

questions.question: A firm's quality manager asks what should govern how much detail goes into each job's specifications. Specification detail should be commensurate with which of the following?

options.A: The requirements of the project and the method of project delivery
options.B: The scale of the drawing details and the number of drawing sheets
options.C: The size of the design firm and the extent of its office master system
options.D: The experience of likely bidders and the number of bids expected

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that specification detail should be commensurate with the requirements of the project and the method of project delivery. Drawing scale, firm size, and bidder experience are not the factors industry guidance names. Industry guidance adds that the degree of detail is a matter of judgment often tempered by economic considerations.

questions.question: A firm is specifying both a large housing project and a small vacation cottage. Which statement about the two sets of specifications is accurate?

options.A: The cottage specs may use a looser language style because their level of detail is lower
options.B: Both need identical detail, because detail and language style are the same thing
options.C: Housing specs may be more complex, but the same clarity and conciseness rules apply
options.D: The housing specs must use performance methods because of their greater complexity

questions.explanation: Industry guidance contrasts a large housing project, whose specifications may be more complicated, with a small vacation cottage, and says the same general clarity and conciseness rules govern both. Industry guidance also warns that language style should not be confused with specification detail, so lower detail does not license looser style and detail is not the same thing as style. Industry guidance ties no specifying method to project complexity here.

questions.question: A project manager asks the specifier to add explanatory paragraphs to every section so that 'nothing could possibly be left out.' Per industry guidance, which response best reflects when a specification is complete?

options.A: It is complete when every product and step is described in full narrative detail
options.B: It is complete when each Division 01 requirement is restated in every section
options.C: It is complete when the owner's attorney has reviewed it for legal sufficiency
options.D: It is complete when it covers important details without elaborate language

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that a specification is complete when it covers important details without elaborate or unnecessary language, and that the degree of detail is a matter of judgment often tempered by economic considerations. Exhaustive narrative or restating Division 01 adds the unnecessary language industry guidance cautions against, and legal review is not the test of completeness.

questions.question: Where are quality assurance and quality control requirements that are specific to one work result addressed?

options.A: In Section 01 40 00—Quality Requirements, organized by work result
options.B: In the supplementary conditions, under the contractor's general duties
options.C: Within the individual section for that work result in Divisions 02-49
options.D: In the owner-contractor agreement, under the description of the work

questions.explanation: Industry guidance explains that Divisions 02 through 49 consist of individual sections, each addressing a distinct work result, and the QA and QC issues specific to a section are addressed in that section. Collecting work-result quality requirements in a Division 01 section, the supplementary conditions, or the agreement contradicts that arrangement.
questions.source: specifying quality assurance and quality control

questions.question: While editing Division 01 quality sections, a specifier checks what those sections rely on. The requirements in Division 01 are dependent on provisions in which document?

options.A: The Divisions 02 through 49 sections
options.B: The conditions of the contract
options.C: The instructions to bidders
options.D: The cited reference standards

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that Division 01 requirements depend on provisions in the conditions of the contract, reflecting that the contract documents are so interrelated none can stand alone. It does not make Division 01 dependent on the Divisions 02-49 sections, the instructions to bidders, or reference standards.
questions.source: specifying quality assurance and quality control

questions.question: A newly hired specifier is unsure how the quality articles in a Division 08 spec relate to the Division 01 quality sections. An examination of which CSI document helps clarify these interrelationships?

options.A: MasterFormat, which assigns numbers and titles to sections
options.B: UniFormat, which arranges information by building elements
options.C: PageFormat, which governs the arrangement of text on a page
options.D: SectionFormat, which organizes each section's three parts

questions.explanation: Industry guidance says examining SectionFormat helps clarify how article requirements in individual Divisions 02-49 sections relate to the Division 01 sections. MasterFormat numbers and titles sections, UniFormat organizes by building element, and PageFormat addresses page layout, so none of them maps article requirements to Division 01.
questions.source: specifying quality assurance and quality control

questions.question: An owner requires a specific sustainability certification level but lets the contractor decide which points to pursue. Where are the performance requirements for this approach established?

options.A: Section 01 35 63—Sustainability Certification Project Requirements
options.B: Section 01 81 13—Sustainable Design Requirements
options.C: Section 01 35 66—Sustainability Certification Project Procedures
options.D: Section 01 33 29—Sustainable Design Reporting

questions.explanation: When the contractor may select which points to target (performance specifying), industry guidance places the performance requirements in Section 01 81 13—Sustainable Design Requirements. Section 01 35 63 is used when the level rests on specific point targets (descriptive specifying). Sections 01 35 66 and 01 33 29 address certification procedures and reporting under either method.

questions.question: On a certification project, the design team fixes the certification level through a select group of specific point targets (descriptive specifying). Where are the general sustainability product requirements and the particular product requirements specified?

options.A: Section 01 35 63, with particular requirements in the affected sections
options.B: Section 01 81 13, with particular requirements in Section 01 35 63
options.C: Section 01 35 66, with particular requirements in Section 01 33 29
options.D: The affected sections, with particular requirements in Section 01 35 63

questions.explanation: For descriptive specifying based on specific point targets, industry guidance puts general sustainability product requirements in Section 01 35 63—Sustainability Certification Project Requirements and the particular product requirements within the affected sections; the reversed arrangement inverts that. Section 01 81 13 serves the performance approach, and 01 35 66 and 01 33 29 cover certification procedures and reporting.

questions.question: Regardless of whether the certification is specified by performance or descriptively, the owner wants the contractor to track, record, and submit sustainability information throughout the project. Which section could establish these requirements?

options.A: Section 01 35 66—Sustainability Certification Project Procedures
options.B: Section 01 35 63—Sustainability Certification Project Requirements
options.C: Section 01 33 29—Sustainable Design Reporting
options.D: Section 01 78 00—Closeout Submittals

questions.explanation: Industry guidance says that with either method, Section 01 33 29—Sustainable Design Reporting could establish the tracking, recording, and submitting of sustainability information. Section 01 35 66 addresses the procedures the contractor follows to manage the certification process, 01 35 63 holds general product requirements for descriptive specifying, and 01 78 00 covers closeout submittals.

questions.question: A project is not pursuing any sustainability certification, but the A/E and client treat sustainability as a matter of practice. Where can the general sustainability requirements be specified?

options.A: Section 01 33 29—Sustainable Design Reporting
options.B: Section 01 35 63—Sustainability Certification Project Requirements
options.C: Section 01 35 66—Sustainability Certification Project Procedures
options.D: Section 01 35 00—Special Procedures or a suitable Level 3 section

questions.explanation: Industry guidance says that when a project is not subject to a certification program but sustainability is a matter of practice, general requirements can go in Section 01 35 00—Special Procedures or a fitting Level 3 section, with particular product requirements in the affected sections. Industry guidance presents Sections 01 33 29, 01 35 63, and 01 35 66 for certification projects, covering reporting, certification product requirements, and certification procedures.

questions.question: The authority having jurisdiction must issue a specific approval of the emissions control procedures for a coating installation. Under which PART 1 article heading does this requirement belong in the coating section?

options.A: Quality Assurance—Sustainability Standards Certifications
options.B: Submittals—Sustainable Design Closeout Documentation
options.C: Quality Assurance—Regulatory Agency Sustainability Approvals
options.D: Submittals—Sustainable Design Submittals, under Action Submittals

questions.explanation: Industry guidance places AHJ approvals related to sustainability, such as for emissions control, recycling procedures, or posting bonds, under the Quality Assurance article 'Regulatory Agency Sustainability Approvals.' Sustainability Standards Certifications cover documentation of compliance with certification programs such as FSC, and the two submittal types cover product submittals and the certification package.

questions.question: PART 1 'Submittals' of a section with sustainability requirements can include two types of sustainable design submittals. Which describes Sustainable Design Closeout Documentation?

options.A: Information included in the package submitted for certification
options.B: Product submittals that specifically address the sustainable requirements
options.C: Documentation of AHJ approvals for emissions control or recycling
options.D: The contractor's procedures for managing the certification process

questions.explanation: Industry guidance defines Sustainable Design Closeout Documentation as information included in the package submitted for certification. Product submittals addressing sustainable requirements are the other type, Sustainable Design Submittals; AHJ approvals belong to a Quality Assurance article; and procedures for managing the certification process are a Division 01 matter (Section 01 35 66).

questions.question: In PART 1 'Summary' of a section subject to sustainability requirements, what may the 'Related Requirements' paragraph include?

options.A: VOC content limits that apply to each of the section's products
options.B: Documentation that items meet sustainability certification requirements
options.C: Procedures for collecting recyclable packaging from this work result
options.D: References to the general sustainability requirements in Division 01

questions.explanation: Industry guidance says the Summary article includes 'Related Requirements,' which may reference the general sustainability requirements in Division 01. VOC limits belong in the PART 2 Description article's sustainability requirements, certification documentation in PART 1 Quality Assurance, and recyclable packaging collection in the PART 3 Cleaning article.

questions.question: A specifier is deciding where to place Sustainable Design Submittals within PART 1 of a resilient flooring section. Where may this type of submittal be located?

options.A: Under Closeout Submittals, with the certification package
options.B: Under Quality Assurance, with the standards certifications
options.C: Under Action or Informational Submittals, or a separate article
options.D: Under Informational Submittals only, since no A/E action is needed

questions.explanation: Industry guidance lets Sustainable Design Submittals, the product submittals addressing sustainable requirements, sit under either Action Submittals or Informational Submittals, or in a submittal article of their own. Information for the certification package is the separate closeout documentation type, standards certifications fall under Quality Assurance, and limiting placement to Informational Submittals ignores the Action Submittals option.

questions.question: Although PART 2 is where most sustainability requirements are specified, industry guidance identifies only one PART 2 article that explicitly includes them. Which article?

options.A: Manufacturers
options.B: Materials
options.C: Source Quality Control
options.D: Description

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that the Description article is the only PART 2 article that explicitly includes sustainability requirements, under 'Sustainability Requirements.' Materials and related item articles can carry item-specific requirements only when the umbrella article is too limiting, and Manufacturers and Source Quality Control are not identified for this purpose.

questions.question: Division 01 establishes a VOC content limit that applies to all sealants on the project. While editing PART 2 of a joint sealants section, what is the best course of action?

options.A: Reference the Division 01 section in Description rather than repeat the limit
options.B: Restate the VOC limit in the Description article so the section stands alone
options.C: Move the VOC limit out of Division 01 and into each sealant item in Materials
options.D: State the VOC limit under PART 1 Quality Assurance as a certification item

questions.explanation: Industry guidance uses this exact case: when products are subject to a general product sustainability requirement in Division 01, such as VOC content for all sealants, reference that section in the Description article instead of repeating the requirement. Restating it duplicates Division 01, moving it fragments a project-wide requirement, and Quality Assurance covers approvals and certifications rather than product limits.

questions.question: A section specifies several dissimilar items (panels, adhesives, and trim), each with different recycled-content criteria, and a single umbrella paragraph would be too limiting. How should these sustainability requirements be specified?

options.A: In separate sections, one for each item's sustainability criteria
options.B: In Section 01 35 63, listed by item and cross-referenced in the section
options.C: With each item, under the Materials/Mixes/Finishes/Accessories articles
options.D: In PART 1 Summary, under the Related Requirements paragraph

questions.explanation: Industry guidance says that if the umbrella 'Sustainability Requirements' article is too limiting, item-specific sustainability requirements can be included with each item specified under Materials, Mixes, Finishes, or Accessories. Industry guidance does not call for separate sections or for moving item-specific criteria into Division 01, and Related Requirements in the Summary only points to general Division 01 requirements.

questions.question: Low-flow faucets must have their flow controls set after installation so the fixtures achieve the water-use performance required by a sustainability requirement. Which PART 3 article covers this?

options.A: Installation
options.B: Field Quality Control
options.C: Adjusting
options.D: Cleaning

questions.explanation: Industry guidance says that once installation is complete, products may need adjusting to achieve the performance level required for sustainability, citing flow control faucets, under the Adjusting article. Installation/Application addresses actions such as controlling odors, runoff, or discharge during execution, and Cleaning addresses recyclable packaging, waste, and material flush-out; industry guidance does not name Field Quality Control for this adjustment.

questions.question: Division 01 has no building flush-out requirement, but the A/E wants a flush-out after installation of one specific product. Which PART 3 article of that product's section can provide this requirement?

options.A: Installation
options.B: Adjusting
options.C: Protection
options.D: Cleaning

questions.explanation: Industry guidance states that when Division 01 requires no building flush-out, the Cleaning article of an individual section can set flush-out requirements for specific materials or products. Installation/Application covers controlling odors, runoff, or discharge, Adjusting covers tuning products to required performance, and Protection is not among the PART 3 sustainability articles industry guidance lists.

questions.question: A floor coating releases chemical odors and runoff while it is being put in place, and these must be controlled to meet sustainability goals. Which PART 3 article could address these actions?

options.A: Application
options.B: Cleaning
options.C: Adjusting
options.D: Field Quality Control

questions.explanation: Industry guidance lists controlling chemical odors, runoff, or discharge as sustainability actions under the Installation/Application article of PART 3. Cleaning addresses recyclable packaging, construction waste, and product flush-out, Adjusting addresses bringing installed products to the required performance level, and industry guidance does not name Field Quality Control for these actions.

questions.question: A casework section must specify shop joinery tolerances and the tolerances for scribing installed casework to walls. Where should these workmanship requirements be placed?

options.A: Both in PART 1 under Quality Assurance, as workmanship standards
options.B: Shop tolerances in PART 2 and installation tolerances in PART 3
options.C: Both in PART 3, since tolerances are verified at the project site
options.D: Shop tolerances in PART 1 and installation tolerances in PART 3

questions.explanation: Industry guidance says to distinguish product from installation items and place each workmanship requirement under its proper heading: fabrication workmanship in PART 2—PRODUCTS and installation workmanship in PART 3—EXECUTION. Grouping both in PART 1 or PART 3, or putting fabrication tolerances in PART 1, ignores that instruction.

questions.question: NAAWS, jointly published by AWMAC and the Woodwork Institute, establishes measurable tolerances for joinery, surfaces, and clearances. Which grades does it establish that must be selected and specified?

options.A: Premium, standard, and economy
options.B: Custom, standard, and utility
options.C: Premium, custom, and economy
options.D: Premium, custom, and standard

questions.explanation: Industry guidance cites NAAWS as an excellent example of controlling workmanship, with measurable tolerances and grades of premium, custom, and economy that must be selected and specified. 'Standard' and 'utility' are not among the grades industry guidance lists.

questions.question: A draft installation article states 'Install panels with the best possible workmanship.' Per industry guidance, which revision approach best controls workmanship?

options.A: Replace 'best possible' with 'highest quality' to raise the standard
options.B: Require workmanship satisfactory to the A/E in its sole judgment
options.C: Require installers to follow recognized industry best practices
options.D: Specify measurable tolerances and a mock-up as the acceptance basis

questions.explanation: Industry guidance says workmanship requirements should be measurable and warns against generalities such as 'best possible workmanship,' since 'best' is open to many interpretations. Its listed methods include specifying tolerances and requiring samples or mock-ups to establish an acceptable level and a basis for judging later work. 'Highest quality,' the A/E's sole judgment, and 'best practices' remain unmeasurable.

questions.question: An owner upgrades a fabricated handrail from carbon steel to stainless steel, and the specifier assumes the fabrication workmanship requirements must be rewritten. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Workmanship differs from material; both metals may be worked the same way
options.B: Stainless steel requires a higher grade of fabrication workmanship
options.C: Workmanship is set by the material, so the PART 2 material article governs
options.D: Changing materials converts fabrication workmanship into a PART 3 requirement

questions.explanation: Industry guidance says workmanship relating to fabrication should not be confused with the materials used, noting that fabricating a product of copper or stainless steel may not differ from fabricating the same product of carbon steel. Industry guidance does not tie a higher workmanship grade to a material, and fabrication workmanship stays in PART 2 regardless of material.

questions.question: A specifier is outlining where a project's closeout documentation requirements will be stated. Closeout documentation is broadly covered in which documents?

options.A: The owner-contractor agreement and Section 01 77 00—Closeout Procedures
options.B: The conditions of the contract and Section 01 78 00—Closeout Submittals
options.C: The supplementary conditions and Section 01 33 00—Submittal Procedures
options.D: The procurement requirements and Section 01 78 00—Closeout Submittals

questions.explanation: The conditions of the contract and Section 01 78 00—Closeout Submittals broadly cover closeout documentation, including the specific submittals the contractor provides at project close. Section 01 77 00 covers closeout procedures rather than submittals, Section 01 33 00 covers general submittal procedures, and industry guidance does not place closeout documentation in the procurement requirements.

questions.question: A consultant's draft PART 1 'Closeout Submittals' article in a plumbing fixtures section restates all of Division 01's general operation and maintenance data requirements. What is the best course of action?

options.A: Keep the restated text so the section can stand alone if issued separately
options.B: Delete the article entirely and rely on Section 01 78 00 for all closeout items
options.C: Move the restated requirements into the section's PART 3 Cleaning article
options.D: Keep only requirements unique to that work result and delete the rest

questions.explanation: Industry guidance says the PART 1 'Closeout Submittals' and 'Maintenance Material Submittals' articles should address requirements unique to that work result and not repeat the general requirements in Division 01. Keeping the duplication contradicts that rule, deleting the article loses section-specific requirements, and PART 3 Cleaning is not a closeout submittal article.

questions.question: An A/E retains engineering consultants plus specialty consultants for roofing, food service, and hardware. The owner asks whether the A/E's coordination responsibility covers the specialty consultants' sections. What is the answer?

options.A: Yes; the A/E coordinates all of the specifications, specialists' included
options.B: No; each consultant coordinates its own sections with the contractor
options.C: Only for engineering disciplines; specialty consultants coordinate their own
options.D: Only for Division 01 and the conditions of the contract, not technical sections

questions.explanation: Industry guidance says the A/E should assume responsibility for overall coordination of the specifications, including those prepared by engineering consultants and by specialists such as roofing and waterproofing, architectural hardware, and food service equipment consultants. Industry guidance does not shift coordination to individual consultants or the contractor, nor limit it to Division 01 or engineering disciplines.

questions.question: An A/E is about to engage consultants to write portions of the project manual. When should the conditions of the contract and Division 01 be made available to them?

options.A: After their first drafts, for a coordination review
options.B: Before they prepare any of their sections
options.C: At the final coordination review before issue
options.D: Once the drawings are substantially complete

questions.explanation: Industry guidance says the conditions of the contract and Division 01 sections should be made available to consultants before they prepare any of their sections, so they can coordinate properly and eliminate duplications and omissions. Providing them after first drafts, at final review, or once the drawings are nearly finished defeats that purpose.

questions.question: When the A/E gives consultants the conditions of the contract and the General Requirements, industry guidance says the A/E should also request something from them at that time. What, and for what purpose?

options.A: Copies of their office master sections, so formats can be aligned
options.B: Lists of proposed products, so substitutions can be controlled
options.C: Input for Division 01, to avoid duplicating it in their sections
options.D: Their cost estimates, so alternates can be identified early

questions.explanation: Industry guidance says input from consultants for Division 01 sections should be requested when the conditions and Division 01 are provided, which ensures that duplication of Division 01 requirements in consultant-prepared sections is avoided. Office masters, product lists, and cost estimates are not what industry guidance directs the A/E to request at this step.

questions.question: Which pair of words is not recommended for use in specifications at all?

options.A: "Observe" and "supervise"
options.B: "Shall" and "will"
options.C: "Furnish" and "install"
options.D: "Must" and "is to"

questions.explanation: Industry guidance says neither "must" nor "is to" is recommended in specifications. Shall/will, furnish/install, and observe/supervise are all usable when applied with their defined meanings.

questions.question: A draft paragraph reads: "The Contractor must remove and provide new any damaged units as directed." Which element of the sentence follows recommended specification language?

options.A: "must" for the obligation
options.B: "any damaged units"
options.C: "remove and provide new"
options.D: "as directed" at the close

questions.explanation: Industry guidance prefers "remove and provide new" over "replace". "Must" is not recommended, "any" is imprecise, and "as directed" is a phrase with a missing object.

questions.question: Why does industry guidance prefer "remove and provide new" to "replace"?

options.A: "Replace" implies the owner furnishes all of the new material
options.B: "Replace" can be read as reinstalling the removed material
options.C: "Replace" is reserved for warranty corrections after completion
options.D: "Replace" shifts disposal costs to the owner

questions.explanation: Industry guidance: "replace" can be construed as requiring reinstallation of removed materials rather than furnishing and installing new materials.

questions.question: A requirement must reach subcontractors and suppliers who did not sign the owner-contractor agreement. Which term does industry guidance recommend for them?

options.A: Entity
options.B: Party
options.C: Contractor
options.D: Bidder

questions.explanation: A party is a signer of the contract; to include persons or companies that are not signers, such as subcontractors, use the generic term entity.

questions.question: Which line follows recommended specification vocabulary?

options.A: Quantity of the flooring allowance: $25,000.
options.B: Balance of attic stock: Store on site.
options.C: Amount of batt insulation: 2,400 square feet.
options.D: Remainder of unused tile: Deliver to Owner.

questions.explanation: Amount and balance are for money; quantity is for numbers, length, area, or volume; remainder means that which is left over.

questions.question: A specification needs a verb meaning "to make certain in a way that eliminates the possibility of error." Which word has that meaning in specification usage?

options.A: Insure
options.B: Warrant
options.C: Ensure
options.D: Assure

questions.explanation: Insure = issue or procure an insurance policy; assure = give confidence to a person; ensure = make certain in a way that eliminates the possibility of error.

questions.question: The A/E's role is to watch the execution of the work without having control and direction of it. Which term matches that role in specification usage?

options.A: Control
options.B: Observe
options.C: Supervise
options.D: Oversee

questions.explanation: Observe means to watch or view the work; supervise means to oversee and to have control and direction of the work.

questions.question: Where does industry guidance say the definitions of furnish, install, and provide should be placed?

options.A: In the supplementary conditions or Division 01
options.B: In the owner-contractor agreement
options.C: In Part 1 of each technical section
options.D: In the instructions to bidders

questions.explanation: These definitions should be placed in the supplementary conditions or Division 01 - General Requirements.

questions.question: When may "The Contractor shall" appropriately appear in a specification paragraph?

options.A: When the paragraph is in Part 1 rather than Part 3
options.B: When the requirement concerns jobsite safety
options.C: When the requirement exceeds the referenced standard
options.D: When the contractor and the owner or A/E are named in the same paragraph

questions.explanation: Industry guidance: "Contractor shall" is generally omitted in favor of the imperative mood, but when the contractor and owner, or contractor and A/E, are mentioned in the same article or paragraph, "The Contractor shall," "Owner will," and "A/E will" may be used for clarity.

questions.question: Industry guidance criticizes "Equipment shall be installed plumb and level" mainly because:

options.A: Installation requirements belong in Part 2
options.B: "Shall" may be used only for owner actions
options.C: Equipment has no legal duty, so "shall" loses its meaning
options.D: "Plumb and level" is an undefined tolerance

questions.explanation: Shall traditionally means "has a duty to"; in sentences like this none of the subjects legally has a duty, so the use fails the traditional meaning.

questions.question: When two spellings are equally correct, which set shows the spellings industry guidance prefers in contract documents?

options.A: facia, gauge, molding, catalogue
options.B: facia, gage, molding, catalog
options.C: fascia, gage, moulding, catalog
options.D: fascia, gauge, moulding, catalogue

questions.explanation: The shorter of two equally correct spellings is preferred - facia, gage, molding, catalog - but not shortcuts like thru.

questions.question: Which is an accepted exception to the usual caution against abbreviations in specification text?

options.A: Units of measure such as psi, written without periods
options.B: "Galv." for galvanized
options.C: "Approx." for approximately
options.D: "w/" for with

questions.explanation: Accepted exceptions: part of a company's legal name, organization names such as ASTM (no periods), time (a.m., p.m.), time zones, temperatures (degrees F), and units of measure such as psi and mph (no periods).

questions.question: Abbreviations should be limited to:

options.A: Three or fewer letters
options.B: Four or fewer letters
options.C: Six or fewer letters
options.D: Five or fewer letters

questions.explanation: Abbreviations should be limited to five or fewer letters; abbreviations that save only one or two characters should be avoided.

questions.question: Which written form in specification text follows recommended practice for symbols and dimensions?

options.A: 10°F using the degree sign
options.B: 20% (percentage of the contract sum)
options.C: 8'-2-1/2" (feet and inches both used)
options.D: 2 x 4 using the times sign for lumber

questions.explanation: Symbols such as %, the degree sign, +, the times sign, / and @ should not be used; but when feet and inches are both used, use symbols (e.g., 8'-2-1/2").

questions.question: How should a dimension of 8 feet with no inches be written in specification text?

options.B: 8 feet
options.D: eight feet

questions.explanation: Spell out feet when no inches are used (8 feet); use figures, not words, for dimensions.

questions.question: Which phrase follows recommended practice for numbers that define both size and quantity?

options.A: three 1/2-inch holes
options.B: three one-half-inch holes
options.C: 3 half-inch holes
options.D: 3 1/2-inch holes
